I’ve often wondered why certain negative situations seem to impact me more deeply than others. When faced with conflict, failure, or criticism, I tend to get caught between emotional chaos and overanalysis. Instead of allowing myself to fully experience my feelings, I instinctively try to dissect and rationalise them.


While watching the video for this assignment, I resonated strongly with the professor’s reflection on experiencing an “all-or-nothing” mindset, where if things aren’t going perfectly, it feels as though they’re going terribly. I recognised that I often react this way as well. When something goes wrong, even slightly, I tend to magnify
it in my mind. Only once my emotions have settled do I look back and wonder: Why was my reaction so sudden and intense? This realisation made me want to explore my inner dialogue more closely: Why do I respond so strongly to negativity, and what does that reveal about how I process my emotions?


For this assignment, I used ChatGPT (GPT-5) as a conversational AI agent as it tends to be more nuanced and conversational. My intention wasn’t to get advice but to use the AI as a reflective mirror, uncovering the patterns and beliefs behind my emotional reactions. I began by describing a recent experience of receiving a bad grade on an assignment I had worked hard on. My first prompt was:


“Can you help me understand what goes through my mind when I get a bad grade?”


The AI broke my experience into layers: external triggers, internal narratives, and underlying beliefs. This helped me see that my reactions followed a predictable pattern. I refined my prompts to encourage deeper introspection, asking questions like:


“What beliefs might be driving such a strong reaction to a disappointing result?”
“Can you package my thoughts such that they come from my emotions instead of my rational mind?”


These questions helped the AI highlight emotional nuances I normally overlook. I also used chain-of-thought prompting, asking the AI to trace how one event, like a low grade, could escalate into a larger story about self-worth. Through this, I noticed the loop I often fall into: an emotional trigger, followed by self-blame, then rationalisation, and finally emotional withdrawal. This essentially amounted to gaslighting myself out of my own emotions.

One of the biggest insights was recognising how much I intellectualise my emotions.
When something unpleasant happens, I immediately try to understand or explain it instead of letting it unfold naturally. The AI pointed out that “understanding” can sometimes be a way of avoiding discomfort—an observation that felt both accurate and confronting. I also saw how my “all-or-nothing” mindset shows up: I tend to
interpret small setbacks as total failures. When I received the bad grade, my mind jumped to thoughts like “I’m not good enough” or “I’ll never improve.” The AI helped me see that I subconsciously link achievement with self-worth, and that my rigid
internal language (“always,” “never,” “should”) amplifies emotional intensity. Recognising this pattern gave me a way to interrupt it by allowing myself to “feel” emotions instead of pushing them away.


The most meaningful moment came when the AI reframed my overreactions not as weaknesses, but as protective responses. It said:
“Your mind might be reacting so strongly because it’s trying to protect you from feeling inadequate or disappointed. The intensity itself shows how much you care.”
That simple line shifted something in me. Instead of judging myself for “overreacting,” I began to see my emotions as signals of care and sensitivity rather than flaws. This was my true “Ah-Ha” moment: the realisation that compassion for my reactions opens far more growth than constant self-criticism.


I also learned that the quality of the conversation depended on the quality of my prompts. Direct or analytical questions led to surface-level responses, while open,
emotionally grounded prompts led to deeper insight. This highlighted that emotional honesty in my questioning mirrors the clarity of the reflection I can achieve. Moving forward, I plan to use AI journaling regularly to process negative emotions, helping me slow down, articulate feelings, and notice thinking patterns I might otherwise
miss.


Ultimately, this exercise showed me that meaningful transformation can come even through a digital dialogue. By engaging in a reflective conversation with AI, I uncovered patterns in my thinking and developed a kinder, more compassionate relationship with myself. I learned that my “all-or-nothing” reactions are not flaws to suppress, but invitations to pause, reflect, and better understand my emotions.

Personal Area of Awareness:
Consumerism culture has pushed society, including myself, to chase material possessions as a badge of status, belonging, and identity. While I am aware of the pressures and temptations to buy, buy, and buy, the dilemma still perpetuates itself unhealthily: give in to the urge to buy new clothes, skincare, bags, a nice meal (the list goes on), or be fiscally responsible and save the money? Moreover, the rise of the ‘treat yourself’ culture has grown into something bigger that justifies self-indulgence, often through irresponsible spending. Yet, breaking this spending cycle feels insurmountable. Through this assignment, I wish to learn how to better manage my finances.

Designing the Prompt:
In designing the prompt, I wanted help in a few areas:
●What emotions do I feel after spending money?
●What are the hidden triggers behind my spending habits?
●How can I manage finances for the future?

That said, the chatbot should not prescribe financial advice like investment tips, but instead, encourage reflection. I crafted my prompt to be step by step for greater co-creation of meaning, whereby the chatbot can build on my previous responses to suggest tailored ways to reframe my financial habits. Thus, I engineered my prompt to follow the COSTAR format: “Provide step by step prompts (response) for an LLM to help me (audience) deconstruct, understand, and reframe (objective) my unhealthy financial habits (context) in a thoughtful tone, (tone) similar to a reflective finance coach (style).”

Selection of LLM Chatbot:
To reduce familiarity bias toward ChatGPT, I also tested the prompt on DeepSeek to see how it compares to ChatGPT. DeepSeek provided a general 3-stage prompt using the keywords in my input – deconstructing, understanding, and reframing. On the other hand, ChatGPT automatically entered Chain-of-Thought by thinking for 48 seconds and listed a 5-stage process – Exploration, Meaning Making, Values Alignment, Reframing, and Integration. DeepSeek appeared more fact-driven and technical and lacked the conversational ‘human touch’ I was looking for. Thus, I selected ChatGPT for this assignment given its detailed prompt which suits the reflective nature of this assignment.
Being able to read ChatGPT’s Chain-of Thought process also helped me understand how its questions are formed in order to unpack my thoughts. For example, the thought process aimed to find out “emotional, cognitive, and behavioural patterns to guide the user through financial reflection and improvement”. Knowing this enabled me to dig deeper in my past spending experiences and be specific in pinpointing my feelings and needs when splurging. In other words, there was mutual engagement in the conversation which enhanced our transaction.

Main Personal Learnings:
After exploring my patterns toward financial decisions, I could relate it to the dimensional representation of emotions. ChatGPT helped me accept that contradicting emotions can be present at once, like feeling satisfied yet guilty when spending money – rather than a sign of ‘irresponsible spending’, I could reframe it as a way to gauge how much I need the item. For example, feeling greater intensity for guilt could mean the item is an impulse purchase, while a lower dominance

over satisfaction could imply an item that brings me insuppressible joy. Identifying my emotions as such to decide if something is worth buying can promote self-awareness in my finances.
Stage 2: Meaning Making benefitted me most in self discovery. It helped me uncover unconscious inferences that stemmed from my upbringing, where my dad was strict about saving while my mum took a carefree, ‘buy it if you like it’ approach. Recognising this internal tension meant that my relationship with money is driven by conflicting values, likely explaining why I love the joy of spending – it reflects my mum’s self-indulgent behaviour, but often followed by guilt because it misaligns with my father’s values. From now on, I aim to be more compassionate in my financial habits and strive to strike a balance between financial discipline and financial freedom.
While I continued the conversation, I gleaned that my financial needs were shifting. Compared to the past where I had no financial concerns and could spend freely, I now have considerations about my future in saving for housing, emergency funds, and taking care of my parents. It reminded me of the Shaker Room @ Botanical Gardens concept of handling complexities. In other words, as my long-term goals evolve, my current behaviours must shift to make space for things that matter. One thing I appreciated was how ChatGPT assured me that I was on the right track to integrate my financial goals into my current lifestyle which felt encouraging and heartening.
ChatGPT also provided practical and actionable advice to start managing my finances, like implementing a spending cap, a cool-off period before making big purchases, or simple tasks like turning off promotional notifications on my devices to curb temptations.

Overall Reflections:
The conversation provided insights on my emotions, the environmental factors affecting my financial habits, future-oriented outlook on my financial needs, and useful tips to spend less. It was helpful and enjoyable, and it felt like I was talking to a friend. With the non-judgemental nature of the AI, I could revert back to previous stages or ask clarifying questions at any point without feeling like I inconvenienced anyone, which is perfect for introspection and expressing my thoughts freely as they come. This relates back to the conversation design as an ongoing process, allowing me to tweak the conversation to align with their needs. For instance, I could ask the AI to be more humorous midway through the conversation to better suit the lighthearted tone I’m looking for.
The assignment also highlighted that crafting the prompt well and asking the right questions play a pivotal role in getting ideal responses from ChatGPT. However, one downside I noticed was that the AI tends to be agreeable to everything I say, at times lacking nuance. I wonder if this can lead users to develop biased opinions or self-righteousness after engaging with an AI, in turn failing to uncover deeper implications or behaviours. Thus, implying that AI must be used with discretion; we must still take personal ownership when forming conclusions.
While communicating my issues to an AI felt foreign at first, it provided guidance to help me understand my financial habits. I would definitely try this again in the future in other areas of my life.

column2:
The Area of Introspection

 

I have always built my life around optimisation, around systems, routines, automation and flow. It has served me well in life so far, bringing me to law school and helping me carry out life with a certain feeling of control. However, I recognise that this has downsides, a certain level of rigidity, an intolerance for inefficiency, a fear of losing control and a fear of failure that sometimes paralyses me into inaction. 

 

Recently, I met with a friend and junior in law school, and we ended up on the subject of our mutual goals. We spoke for a while about how most people don’t really take the time to introspect. The conversation stayed with me because I consider introspection a core part of my identity. He mentioned that Adler had said that human behaviour is teleological, that we act with purpose towards our goals.

 

Here, I suggest that we can use LLMs as a kind of Adlerian therapist, using teleological reasoning to uncover the underlying purpose behind our behaviour. In my case, I wanted to explore the question of: Why control matters so much to me. 

 

I will use ChatGPT as a reflective partner, it helps me interrogate my assumptions and trace them back to the goals I might be unconsciously striving toward. 

形状

The Framework

 

Teleological reasoning assumes behaviour is goal-driven. The purpose here is to understand the function or goal that “control” serves in my life. 

 

I adopt the CO-STAR Prompt Engineering framework. CO-STAR stands for Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience and Response. The prompt is as follows:

 

Context (C): I’ve built my life around systems, routines, and automation. This gives me a sense of control but also brings rigidity and anxiety about inefficiency or failure. 

Objective (O): You are an Adlerian reflective partner. Help me use teleological reasoning to understand what deeper goal this need for control serves in my life, and how it aligns with/obstructs my growth.

Tone (T): Tone should be reflective, candid, slightly philosophical, but grounded in fact.

Audience (A): Self

Response (R): Lead me through reasoning that identifies (1) the likely purpose that my control-seeking behaviour aims to achieve, how this purpose shapes my mindset, productivity, and relationship, whether this purpose continues to serve me well, and how might I recalibrate that to a healthier and adaptive guiding principle.

Frame your analysis teleologically, treating each insight as a hypothesis about what goal my behaviour is pursuing. Use past context to inform your decision.

 

I then tested this prompt using a “Prompt Evaluator” made by a Senior AI engineer,1 and the results (full chat here) were that the prompt was exceptionally strong.

Learnings from the Chat

The chat attahced here. In all honesty, the answer I got was frighteningly accurate. It verbalised many different thoughts that I had in my head as to why I am the way I am. It accurately suggested several hypothesis for my desire for control. However, the one that resonated with me most strongly was the first hypothesis:

I started thinking as to how this neurosis came about in my life. Looking back, however, things start making a lot more sense. When I was young, my mother had developed a certain spinal condition that required surgery. She went ahead for the surgery, and thankfully, got better. However, the surgery was quite costly, and though my parents thought that they were covered by insurance, in actuality, within the fine print of the insurance agreement, there was a carve-out for such conditions, and thus my family had to bear the heavy costs. This has made me more sceptical about trusting people and institutions. Another situation that hit me was back in Junior College. Because I did not know how the school system operated, I made the mistake of applying for a Hybrid course. Of course, in hindsight it was a great decision as it taught me a lot of interdisciplinary concepts and provided a unique perspective, but from a purely functional perspective, it meant I was restricted as to which courses I could apply to in university. 

 

When I provided that further context to ChatGPT, it succinctly put into words a feeling I harboured for a while. It said “Your childhood and early decision costs taught you that hidden rules and institutional carve-outs are dangerous. Control is the strategy you adopted to defend against that danger.” It also told me that I risk overcorrection.

 

And so, what did the experience teach me?

 

First, that there is much hidden potential in using ChatGPT in unpacking life decisions and behaviour, and a strong prompt framework brings out that potential. I intend to explore further how ChatGPT can be used to improve my life. It also provided me next steps that I can adopt. I intend to do so.

Reprogramming My Thoughts on Love
For this assignment, I decided to explore a deeply personal area: my conflicting feelings about love and dating in university. As someone who values faith as a muslim, commitment, and family expectations of getting an arranged marriage, I often feel torn between craving emotional intimacy and fearing that pursuing romance might lead me away from what I believe is right. I used this conversation with AI as a safe space to unpack the thought: “I’m afraid of love but I crave it so much. My goal was not to seek advice about dating but to understand why I feel so many emotions like fear, insecurity, longing, and guilt and to reframe them into something more digestible.
I designed my conversational AI on ChatGPT, grounding its tone and structure in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) principles. I crafted a detailed system prompt instructing the AI to be a supportive and culturally sensitive guide trained in CBT. It was told to:
1.Ask me to describe a recent emotionally charged situation related to romance or dating.
2.Help me identify unhelpful thought patterns (like catastrophising or all-or-nothing thinking).
3.Challenge those thoughts through gentle reflection (“What evidence supports this?” “Could there be another way to see it?”).
4.Guide me to reframe the thought into something kinder and truer to my values.

This design also intentionally avoided giving advice or moral judgment. Instead, the AI focused on emotional awareness, cultural sensitivity, and faith alignment. I chose ChatGPT because of its flexible tone control and ability to follow structured, reflective dialogue which aligns with the transactional model of communication, where meaning is co-created between both participants, as compared to Perplexity that’s focused more on research and facts.
This experience combined ideas from communication theory, prompt engineering, and AI-human synergy. By designing a CBT-inspired conversational flow, I effectively engaged in rapid prototyping of a therapeutic-style dialogue. The interaction embodied the transactional model of communication rather than a one-way exchange, the conversation became a co-creation of meaning where my emotions evolved in real-time through guided reflection.
In prompt engineering terms, I realised how critical precision and empathy were in the system instructions. For example, including phrases like “avoid assumptions about what is ‘normal’ or ‘right’ in relationships” and “respond with warmth and respect for cultural or religious sensitivities” prevented the AI from defaulting to Western dating norms. This created a psychologically safe space that felt surprisingly human and attuned to my context.
The turning point in the conversation came when I admitted: “It makes me feel like I’m afraid of love but crave it so much.” The AI identified this as a tension between two worlds: one part of me rooted in faith and values such as waiting for marriage, the other yearning for emotional connection in the present. When it named cognitive distortions like catastrophising

(“If I fall in love, I’ll lose myself or my family’s approval”) and all-or-nothing thinking (“I can either honor my faith or experience love, but not both”), I recognised patterns I hadn’t consciously acknowledged.
Through the AI’s questioning, I discovered that what I truly longed for was deep companionship, not casual romance, but the kind of love that aligns with long-term faith and emotional maturity. The reframing exercise, turning “I’m missing out on love” into “I’m waiting and preparing for the kind of love that aligns with who I am”, brought genuine comfort. I realised that patience was not passive waiting but trusting timing.
This insight shifted my mindset. I no longer saw my singleness as deprivation but as preparation. When I concluded the session with, “What they have is beautiful, but one day my turn will come too… there’s greater value in waiting,” I felt a profound emotional release. It was an “Ah-ha” moment: love and faith are not in conflict: they can coexist through patience, self-awareness, and trust.
This conversation reminded me how transformative communication can be, even with AI. It mirrored the transformative dialogue described in the transactional model, a process through which both parties (human and AI) co-construct meaning. Although the AI lacked human emotion, its structured empathy and reflective questioning enabled me to engage in deep introspection.
The experience also highlighted the delicate balance between AI as a mirror and AI as a guide. The AI did not tell me what to think; it helped me see my own thoughts more clearly. Its neutrality made me feel safe to explore guilt and longing without fear of judgment, which can sometimes be harder in conversations with peers or mentors.
From a design perspective, I learned that effective AI-mediated reflection depends heavily on the clarity of the prompt and the emotional sensitivity of its language. Even subtle wording choices (“gently challenge,” “aligned with your personal values”) shaped the entire tone of the conversation, turning what could have been a mechanical exchange into an emotionally restorative one.
In conclusion, through this AI-guided reflection, I developed a new awareness of how technology can facilitate emotional growth when designed intentionally. The conversation not only helped me reframe my fear of love but also reminded me that self-discovery is not always about finding answers, sometimes it’s about learning to sit with uncertainty and trust one’s journey.Moving forward, I plan to apply this method of AI-assisted self-reflection to other areas of my life, such as academic stress and self-esteem. This experience convinced me that AI can serve as a compassionate thinking partner, one that doesn’t replace human connection but enhances it by helping us articulate the meanings and contradictions within ourselves.
Ultimately, this exercise showed me that even a digital conversation can lead to a very human outcome: greater self-compassion, clarity, and peace.
P.S I also gave them some ideas to make the quote image aesthetic (like colour, design and font) and fitting to me so it is something that I might print or use in my everyday affirmations.

However, my day was ruined as I could not control my temper and shouted at my grandmother when she was not listening to my instructions. 

Integration of different topics 

I provided the clear context in my prompt in order to get the most useful answers. I also told the conversational agent my objective of this interaction: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques to reframe my thoughts. This fulfils the C and O in CO-STAR under prompt engineering. 

Chain-Of-Thought: Instead of generating an immediate answer, ChatGPT internally “thinks through” multiple reasoning steps before producing a response. This can be seen in screenshot 5, where after my prompt, ChatGPT thought for 13 seconds before giving me a response. Afterwards, ChatGPT uses a step-by-step reasoning to prompt me for my inputs, customising the output response according to what my inputs are. 

How you designed your conversational agent, including LLM/platform selection and development process.

I chose to use ChatGPT as my conversational agent (screenshots attached below).  I first started off with asking ChatGPT to provide me with prompts for an LLM to bring me through cognitive behavioural therapy techniques to reframe my thoughts. After that, I asked it to combine into a single prompt for me to paste it in another browser’s ChatGPT. I then begin my journey to heal my soul by allowing ChatGPT to comfort me through its various questions and responses. 

The new awareness or insights (if any) that emerged, and how they may influence your life.

Whenever I am feeling stressed or frustrated with my grandmother, I will always remember what ChatGPT told me – “I love my grandmother, but I am human too, it’s okay to feel stressed. One difficult moment doesn’t define me; I’m doing my best.” (shown in the last screenshot)

I will always tell myself this and will motivate myself to do better at both taking care of my grandmother as well as managing my emotions. 

Overall reflections on your process and experience in completing the assignment.

Although conversational agents can be intuitive sometimes and manage to encourage me by providing comforting words, I still prefer to interact with humans and share my thoughts with them. This is because humans can relate to me sometimes, especially when I have friends that experience the same thing as me before. Conversational agent might not have the same experience and feelings, and thus they sometimes cannot provide the comfort that humans want.

column1: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
column2:
The area I wanted to seek greater awareness in was how to manage the stress arising from my school projects. I often felt overwhelmed by the workload and the challenges of collaborating with others. Through talking to a Large Language Model (LLM) I hope to gain insights and develop coping strategies.
When designing my LLM, I began by stating my objectives clearly. I instructed the first LLM to create a prompt for another LLM to act as a therapist to help me manage my stress. Using this prompt, the responses were disappointing as the LLM was returning generic advice such as breathing exercises and recommending me to take a break. After reflecting on this, I went back to the first LLM and told it to generate a new prompt, this time I was more specific with my expectations. I instructed it to design a therapist that can engage more deeply, ask questions to understand my situation and to provide tailored suggestions. This new prompt led to significantly better outcomes, the LLM asked me follow up questions and helped me to better understand and manage my stress. This process has made me realise the importance of prompt engineering in shaping the quality and depth of a LLM’s response.
Several concepts came together in the creation of this conversational agent. Firstly, prompt engineering as described above played a central role. I learnt how small changes in phrasing and structure could alter the LLM’s behaviour. By being specific with my tone, objectives and expectations, I could design more effective prompts.
Secondly, the concept of chain-of-thought reasoning guided how I structured the LLM’s response. By encouraging the LLM to think step by step and to ask clarifying questions, the conversation became more comprehensive and emotionally aware. This approach allowed the LLM not just to respond to my inputs but to reason through them, like how a therapist might read between the lines and understand my underlying issues.
Next the idea of reconstructing social realties, the use of AI chatbots can shape societal views towards seeking help. Although speaking to a LLM cannot completely replace the experience of talking to a real human therapist, the experience of being listened to and guided still had a positive impact on how I deal with stress. This shows how AI can shape social norms around seeking help and normalise discussions about mental health.
While I did not build a full multi-agent system, I did have a simple 2 agent process, where one LLM acted as a “designer” translating my requests into prompts while the other acted as the “therapist” that was helping me deal with stress. In this case, I was the link between the 2 LLMs, allowing me to experience at a much simpler scale how different agents given distinct taskings can collaborate to produce an effective outcome together.
During the conversation, the LLM asked me questions to get more context on my situation. The LLM then helped me to uncover two main pain points causing my stress. The first one which I was already aware of the tight deadlines across numerous projects with overlapping timelines. The second one, which I only discovered through my conversation and reflections with the LLM was my frustration with a groupmate that was not contributing sufficiently. I

realised much of the stress came from not only the workload but also from the emotional burden of managing team dynamics. The conversation I had with the LLM allowed me to see things more clearly. Since I am non-confrontational in nature, I often choose to avoid addressing conflicts directly. The LLM suggested practical solutions for me to advocate for myself and communicate my concerns without being too aggressive. It recommended techniques such as using “I” statements, documenting my contributions and setting clear boundaries. The suggestions by the LLM seem realistic and I intend to apply them to better manage my workload and stress.
This conversation has also changed my perspective on stress management in general. I realised that at times the most obvious issue, the deadlines or heavy workload may not always be the main source of stress. Emotional and relationship factors, though less visible can be significant as well. Through reflecting and listing out all the things that are bothering me, I can better pinpoint the root cause and address them rather than only dealing with the obvious surface level issues.
Beyond the personal lessons that I have learned, this experience has exposed me to how LLMs can be used as reflective tools rather than being a problem solver or information provider. I learnt that with effective prompt engineering, I can create a LLM to facilitate a more reflective and exploratory conversation. Through asking thought provoking questions, listening and facilitating self-discovery, the LLM managed to create a safe and guided space for reflection.
I also realised how much my interactions with the LLM mirror us humans. Just as in real life where we have to convey our expectations and instructions to others when we give them a task. Similarly, LLM also requires clear and well-structured instructions, in this case the right prompt to be able to perform up to my expectations.
Overall, this assignment has allowed me to experience first-hand the process of designing testing and refining a conversational agent. Not only did I learn how to create better prompts for LLMs, I also gained deeper insights on my own emotions and stress triggers. I realised that talking about my stress even if it is with AI, helped me feel better and aware of my feelings. This exercise has shown that when carefully guided LLMs can serve as valuable companions for self-reflection and emotional regulation. The combination of prompt engineering and personal reflection has shown me that with the right questions and honest answers, AI can help us uncover truths that we might otherwise overlook in our daily lives.

Information to Transformation Assignment
Context - Personal Area Explored
For this assignment, I used ChatGPT to explore and examine my growing emotional dependence in a new relationship. As I recently got into my first relationship, I noticed a shift in my moods and emotions. They started to fluctuate based on my boyfriend’s responses or availability. On ‘good’ days when we interact more, I feel uplifted and secure. However, on ‘bad’ days when we interact less, I feel disappointed and anxious. I recognised that such emotional volatility reflected underlying cognitive distortions rather than my partner’s actual behaviour. Thus, I took this opportunity to use an
AI-guided reflective process to gain deeper insight into my internal thought mechanisms. I intended to identify the beliefs contributing to this emotional dependence in my relationship and to explore ways of reframing them. Ultimately, I aimed to foster greater emotional regulation and security in my relationship.
Platform & Agent Design
I used ChatGPT as my conversational AI since I am more familiar and comfortable with this platform, which will allow me to open up more. In coming up with a prompt, I adopted a specific and structured approach to guide the AI’s responses effectively. The prompt I used was: “You are a CBT-trained coach. Please help me to examine my emotional dependence on my boyfriend by identifying my thoughts, feelings and underlying beliefs about relationships. I hope to understand the thought patterns driving this emotional dependence on my boyfriend. I also hope to learn how to reframe my thoughts and work towards a more secure emotional state. Please be objective and help me to grow through this interaction.”.
By explicitly defining the AI’s role and desired outcomes, I engaged in a form of prompt engineering that helped to ensure that responses remained focused and constructive, rather than simply reinforcing my existing viewpoints. By writing out what I hoped to achieve through this interaction, the AI will be able to tailor its responses to my needs. If I were to attempt this interaction again, I would use another conversational AI agent to back up or cross reference so that I can have multiple perspectives on this topic to avoid being in an echo chamber.
Interaction Process
The interaction with ChatGPT was surprisingly fruitful. Since I instructed it to act as a CBT-trained coach, it guided me through reflections step-by-step, using a CBT framework. It started off with a question about a recent moment when I felt emotionally dependent on my boyfriend. It was also very specific to tell me what to describe so that it could ‘understand’ and process my thoughts better.

I learned that asking the AI for step-by-step help led to more practical advice than general questions, through chain-of-thought processing. I learned that specifying ChatGPT’s role as a CBT-trained coach shaped its tone and depth of processing. This revealed to me that framing prompts reconstructs my understanding of reality, by guiding which parts of myself I focus on. ChatGPT was extremely helpful as it helped me to unpack my emotions and used questions to prompt me to reflect deeper and dig deeper in order to find underlying root causes of my emotions. It used starting points such as automatic thoughts in order for me to really think about why my moods fluctuated with my boyfriend’s actions. It also made me feel understood because it was able to explain how I felt without me really spelling it out:

Reflection & Impact
I learned that my emotional dependence creates a fragile link between my boyfriend’s actions and my sense of being loved. With my love language being words of affirmation, my emotional dependence on my boyfriend is rooted in a deep need for security and affirmation. Although I may be very
self-aware, it was very reassuring for ChatGPT to explain my thoughts to me and break down my experiences. I usually feel like I am alone in my thoughts and that I have a problem which I have to deal with on my own. However, when ChatGPT was able to ‘understand’ me, I felt that I was more ready and equipped to tackle my unhealthy thought processes. It was very comforting that ChatGPT was able to empathise with me to a certain extent. I felt that my feelings were validated and I was not being crazy as I have been telling myself the past weeks. I learned that my frustration was due to the tension between my rational mind acknowledging my boyfriend’s love and my emotional mind craving reassurance and visible signs of being prioritised. After talking to ChatGPT openly about my feelings, it then suggested strategies for me to self-soothe and communicate my needs more effectively with my boyfriend. Moving forward, I intend to use the information that I gathered from this process to regulate my emotions and strengthen my sense of self-worth independently. I felt much better after talking to ChatGPT about my feelings since I was able to understand myself better. I understood why I felt frustrated and doubtful over small things. It helped me to reconstruct my reality, and to understand that although my emotional mind may say otherwise sometimes, my boyfriend still loves me. I just need to self-soothe and regulate my emotions when some of my smaller expectations are not met. The encouraging tone that ChatGPT used also made me realise that maybe asking for help is not that scary and is actually a good thing to stop myself from spiralling even more. The sense of empathy and understanding that I felt from this interaction shows how conversational AIs can simulate emotional understanding through linguistic mirroring, even without true affective understanding. However, I still feel that it was lacking a human element. It is definitely not the same as talking to someone face to face and having the human touch to this interaction.
At the end of the day, I was talking to a screen, to a programmed chatbot that I could not see or touch, almost like a void. Although the interaction felt understanding, it also underscored a sense of isolation. I could not see who I was talking to and there was nobody around me physically to comfort me with their presence, reminding me of the irreplaceable comfort that only true human connection can provide. Overall, this experience has taught me that conversational AIs can serve as a mirror, helping me to view my internal processes in more structured ways. Hence, I now view AI as a useful aid for emotional awareness and growth.

column2:
A) 	What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience TED TALK by Charles Hunt (Summary)
Charles Hunt ended the talk with a powerful parting statement: “You have given my trauma a purpose!”.  Charles was brought up in a broken family, struck by trauma and depression at a young age but he did not give up.  With resilience, he managed to convert tragedy into triumph, picked himself up and recovered quickly from adversity by positive adaptation.  He believed that bad things in life were just a process, you either succumb to it or fight back by staying strong and positive.
He shares that belief influences our thoughts, which will direct our actions and responses. Trauma had taught him resilience.  Being prepared will help us address setbacks better. Having a positive attitude and resilience allows us to overcome adversities we face in life to emerge better and stronger.
B)	Charles parents were drug abusers and since young, he had to face with many difficulties and challenging life events.  The loss and traumatic events with losing his parents brought him pain, sadness and depression. These strong adversities faced during those difficult periods of his life had resulted in his strong resilience and positive adaptation.  There are times when he felt like giving up, but he stayed firm. For him, resilience is one of the most important traits and critical to one’s happiness and success.  These traits can be learned (Hunt, What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience TEDx TALKs).
Fletcher’s 2 core concepts (Fletcher, 2013), adversity and positive adaptation closely relate to how he reacted and behaved.   He remained positive and focused on how to move forward and “leap back” to recover quickly from difficult life events (Soans, 2006). He has resilience and a strong belief that “tomorrow could be better than today’s pain”.  This attitude has the positive effect of transforming “tragedy to triumph” as shared in his talk. He could have followed his parent's footsteps, but he chooses to live life differently because of the adverse experiences and adapting changes positively.  Charles’s TEDx talks contents are aligned with what we were covered in the course on resilience, the most common cited definitions on resilience revolved around (Fletcher, 2013) two key components of adversity and positive adaptation.  
Davydov, (Davydov, et al., 2010) resilience mechanisms could further reinforce the alignment of the video contents. Davydov stated that resilience may vary in relation to contextual severity, it may be resilience against everyday stresses (mild adversity) to an extensive stress such as death or illness of a loved one (strong adversity).  The stronger the adversity, the stronger the positive adaptation.  Referring to Charle’s sharing, the intensity of his life adversity was not ordinary everyday stresses but a series of negative life changing events that had resulted in a very high positive adaptation. 
Positive adaptation defined as” behaviorally manifested social competence, or success at meeting stage-salient development tasks” (Luther & Cicchetti, 2000, 858).  A person who is exposed to adversity may react differently to varied circumstances.  Resilience will alter according to the different issues faced. In the same context, Rutter (Rutter, 1981) cited exceptional power to overcome strong adverse circumstances.  
C)	I recalled observing an “abnormal” behaviour of shoppers at NTUC store around March 2020.  Most of the shelves were emptied and check-out counters were unusually crowded.  I could sense that something was “not right” as shoppers were “behaving” differently. Not having experienced any natural calamities or disasters, I was thrown out of my comfort zone and ill-prepared to face the challenges ahead when the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 pandemic and Singapore went into a “circuit breaker”.  Life became more stressful when my late father, who had cancer, became very ill and subsequently became bedridden and required 24-hour home palliative care.  My siblings were able to take turns to take-care of him because work-from-home became a norm during the pandemic.  I had a hard time coming to terms with my late father’s condition and the changes in our way of life during “circuit breaker”.  Mask and social distancing were a chore and unbearable in this humid environment.  To make matters worse, I had an allergic reaction to the mask and sanitizer.  Life became tougher when I had to take up a new role in a new division at work.  Zoom meetings had become a norm then and we had no excuse not to attend virtual budget meetings even when on leave. I broke down during one of those meetings.  That was one of the most difficult periods of my adult life.
As I reflect on those life changing events that took place then, I could closely relate the experience with Richardson’s theory of Metatheory of resilience and resiliency, (Richardson, 2002).  When those events hit, I was unprepared.  The stressors disrupted my homeostasis.  The adversities and positive mindset had given me more strength to move forward.  I was well aware that we had limited time with my late father.  The doctor had told us that it could only be three to nine months and encouraged us to spend more time with him.  That moment struck me hard and the thought of losing him forever was even more unbearable, for the months following, I could stay up all night. Adversities had given me the power of resiliency and perseverance; overcoming the tiredness of my physical body and staying awake throughout the night to nurse him.  My late father passed away six months later.  
COVID-19 persisted, and work became more stable as I found my way around through guidance and learning.  According to Richardson’s metatheory (Richardson, 2002), during the final stage, a resilient individual will achieve “resilient integration”.  I did learn how to cultivate perseverance and resilience through this adversity. I had emerged stronger after that difficult journey.  I could appreciate and relate to some of the strategies shared during the course.  The three strategies shared are optimistic positive mindset that help us to stay focused on our strength.  Be flexible and embrace challenges so that we can leap back quickly (Soans, 2006) and lastly, social support that could make a difference in helping us cope better with adversity.  There are no better ways to get distress than talking to someone you trust. I may not have realised these actions could help at that moment, but with a deeper understanding of this topic, optimism, being flexible and good social support will certainly be very useful when weathering life-changing adversity.  I will share these good ways to develop resilience quickly and encourage those in need.  Last, but not least, by knowing how adversity and positive adaptation could work for us instead of against us could better prepared for any future adverse encounters. Let’s all turn “Trauma into Triump” like Charles. (Hunt, TEDx Talks, Youtube).

Choice of TED talk: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
(a)	The TED talk features Nina Nesdoly (“Nesdoly”), a researcher specialising in work stress and burnout prevention. She presents three key strategies for effective stress management: letting tension out, limiting information intake, and lowering the barrier to entry.
	Nesdoly emphasises the importance of prioritising stress-relief before tackling tasks, using these strategies:
1.Letting tensions out through activities such as exercise, mindfulness breathing, journaling, or talking to a friend.
2.Limiting information intake by reducing exposure to work-related or stressful social media content during breaks.
3.Lowering the barrier to entry with quick and easy activities like dancing at home or simple journaling (in forms of doodling or bullet points).
Through compelling examples demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating stress relief into daily life, Nesdoly encourages her audience to prioritise stress management as an integral part of their routine, rather than waiting until all tasks are completed. This approach can lead to an increased energy, focus, and overall well-being.
(b)	The premise of TED talk by Nesdoly on “How to Relieve Stress When You’re Overwhelmed” provides a practical stress management strategies which could be incorporated into daily life and work routines. During the talk, she introduces three key strategies: letting tension out, limiting information intake and lower the barrier into entry, as part of stress-relief activities before diving into the tasks. Nesdoly’s TED talk similarly aligns with Chapter 2 of NCO112 Peak Performance as both contents focus on managing stress to promote positive outcomes. 
While Nesdoly’s proposed solution may potentially be useful for many, it however may not be universally applicable. Depending on individual work environments, the effectiveness of stress relief techniques may vary. The TED talk does not adequately address these potential differences as she has addressed the issue in general. One example of which Neslody’s solution may not be useful is when the environment of a person’s workplace becomes an influence. Inappropriate work environment such as working with outdated technology or workplace with strict hierarchy culture, may not find Neslody’s stress relief techniques useful. 
Firstly, finding a solution to improves the work environment issues will potentially be a better stress relief strategy. According to a recent report conducted by TELUS Health, fifty-seven percent of workers in Singapore have not used Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) tools as part of their work and this group of workers have shown to have the lowest mental health score in comparison to workers that used AI in their workplace (TELUS, 2024).
Secondly, in August 2022, a survey has been conducted in Singapore which revealed that in 1 out of 2 had experienced workplace discrimination in the past five years (AWARE, 2022). In the same report, it shows that the impact of workplace discrimination is serious which led to twenty-nine percent of those who had reported the discrimination and twenty-eight percent of those who did not, eventually quitting their jobs. Therefore, in this case, Nesdoly’s stress-relief strategies may not potentially be a useful technique in improving the overall well-being.
	While Nesdoly generally provides a good strategy on overcoming stress before approaching the necessary tasks, the approach may not be useful to certain environments or situations as prescribed above, and more extensive research will be required in order to tackle such scenarios when managing stress and when addressing a wider audience that comes from different backgrounds.
(c)	In my department at work, I am widely recognised as someone who holds a highly stressful role due to the demanding responsibilities that come with my position. This year marks my fifth year in the department, and I have noticed that my ability to handle stress has been rapidly declining due to poor mental health. Recently, I came across NCO112 Peak Performance course online, and for the first time in a long while, I felt hopeful. I believe this course could help me overcome my fear of stress and regain confidence in my ability to excel in my role.
	During the online seminar, I finally understood the root cause of my work-related stress. It stemmed from the fact that the demands placed on me often exceeded my available resources and capabilities. To address this, I adopted the ‘problem-focused’ coping technique which was introduced during the seminar. Now I start each day by allocating specific time slots for different tasks and ensuring that I follow through with my schedule. (a)From the list of TED TALK links, I will be choosing the talk on stress by Nina Nesdoly on ‘How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed’ The youtube link as follows: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc 
After watching the TED talk, the speaker Nina Nesdoly is trying to convey that we should take breaks to relieve stress when we are feeling overwhelmed. She also shared the three main ways on how to incorporate the breaks into our life. 
The first one will be to let tension out of our body for example, by going out for exercises, and practicing mindfulness. Followed by limiting information into our brain as it can also contribute to stress. Lastly, will be to find easy ways to relieve stress. 

(b)From what we have covered in the course on stress in chapter 2, we can use the 2 dimensional coping framework to identify and develop strong and robust coping strategies. 
There are two different coping strategies focusing on problems or emotions and approach or avoidant. The three strategies shared by the TED talk falls under the following:
1st strategy: let tension out/take a break, the speaker listed a series of tension relieving activities such as exercise and movement, creativity or journaling, talking to a friend, meditation or mindfulness, or even a hug. I identified these as emotional coping strategies as they are used to improve emotional response to the stressful situation. I then tried to classify them as approach or avoidant coping, it was not clear initially as these strategies do not necessarily always produce positive emotions and sometimes be just numbing the emotional pain, however, based on definitions given in the text, the strategy falls much closer into approach coping than avoidance coping, i therefore conclude that the strategies and examples speaker shared falls under emotion focused-approach coping.
2nd strategy: limit information. I found the strategy to be related to the stress process of the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping that is explained in the course chapter 2.2. Speaker states that information can contribute to stress, such as news, social media posts that leave us comparing ourselves to others, or disturbing videos, and this draws parallel to the start of the stress process “Potentially stressful situation”. By limiting information that could lead to potentially stressful situations, we put a lid on the number of stressors that our mind has to deal with.
3rd strategy: lowering the barrier. This strategy does not fall into the models or framework in chapter 2, but instead, the speaker simply reminds the audience that we need not wait to cope with stress, as emotional focused-approach coping can be as low cost and simple as a 10-mins call or doodling.
In summary, the speaker provided examples and relevant scenarios that we can identify parts within the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping and Two-dimensional coping framework.



(c)I recall a time when I felt overwhelmed with stress was when I had my first full time job after graduating from polytechnic. 
It was my first full time position at a public hospital pharmacy and multiple responsibilities; mainly to do reception, picking of medications as well as dispensing out to the patients. 
Due to the lack of knowledge and real life experiences, it was hard for me to adapt quickly as the workload in the pharmacy is very high, and I also had anxiety talking face to face with the patients for the first time. These are my potentially stressful situations according to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping. 
I used to cope by taking sick leaves because I was stressed out. I now see that it is an avoidant coping mechanism according to the two-dimension coping framework.
From what I learned during the course as well as from the TED talk, I should have known that learning takes time so it will not be possible for me to adapt quickly, and that I have my seniors to learn and count on. I would have perceived that there are sufficient resources to cope at the second appraisal and not have caused myself so much distress per the model.
Instead, I should have asked for guidance from the seniors as well as resources for me to improve and understand the workflow better. Also by practicing mindfulness, such as deep breathing in and out before dealing with the patients might have also helped to manage the anxiety. These are problem focused and emotion focused approach coping respectively in the framework.

In the talk  “How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), she begins with a somewhat counter-intuitive personal anecdote of partying to overcome overwhelming academic pressures, to introduce 3 key tenets of effective stress relief. The first is to let tension out during consciously scheduled breaks, either physically through exercise and breathing techniques or via creative and mindful outlets such as journalling. The next is to limit information intake by reducing exposure to potentially stressful media and work-related content during breaks. Nesdoly supports this with neuroscientific research, demonstrating how taking regular breaks estranged from work-related activities that provide genuine downtime can prevent the accumulation of stress and improve cognitive function, attributing to lower burnout rates. Finally, an effective stress relief technique should be accessible and easy to implement in daily routines. Nesdoly thus encourages the audience to pick 1 stress management tool that offers tension relief, avoids information overload and possesses low barriers to entry.

	Nesdoly's emphasis on individual strategies for stress relief partially aligns with Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, which posits that stress results from an individual's appraisal of a specific situation and their perceived ability to cope given limited resources (Ong, 2025, p. 19). Nesdoly’s three keys to stress relief can be seen as ways to influence both primary and secondary appraisals in the Transactional Model. For instance, "letting tension out" through activities which have low “barriers to entry” could be viewed as a form of emotion-focused coping ability, which aims to regulate emotional responses to stressors. An individual with a self-perception of high personal ability to let off steam when necessary may view themselves as possessing the ability to cope emotionally, thereby increasing the likelihood of experiencing eustress as opposed to distress. Similarly, "limiting information" could be interpreted as a way to modify the primary appraisal of potential stressors, potentially reducing the perceived threat or challenge. Nesdoly's suggestions thus allow individuals to reframe one's mindset towards stress, corresponding with the concept of cognitive reappraisal in this model, where altering one's perception of a stressor could mitigate its impact.

	The 3 keys also coincide with The Two-Dimensional Coping Framework by Nes and Segerstrom, which categorizes coping strategies along 2 axes: problem-focused vs. emotion-focused, and engagement vs. disengagement (Ong, 2025, p. 19). While her opening anecdote can be categorised as behavioural disengagement and problem avoidance, her other strategies primarily fall under the engagement coping category, as they involve active attempts to deal with stressors or their emotional impact. Her emphasis on "letting tension out" aligns with both problem-focused and emotion-focused engagement coping, depending on the specific activity chosen as well as the problem it is intended to resolve. To illustrate, exercise could be seen as problem-focused if it is aimed at improving overall physical resilience, or emotion-focused if it is utilised primarily for immediate emotional relief. However, in this particular talk, Nesdoly does not explicitly delve into disengagement coping strategies, which can sometimes be useful in certain situations, particularly when dealing with uncontrollable stressors.

	While Nesdoly's talk provides practical advice consistent with these theoretical models, it primarily focuses on immediate, individual-level interventions. Critically, her approach could overlook broader systemic or environmental factors contributing to stress, which are also important considerations in comprehensive stress management. For instance, workplace stressors such as excessive workload or lack of support may require organizational changes beyond individual coping strategies (Pham, 2024). Additionally, research by Nes et al. (2010) suggests that personality factors such as optimism and conscientiousness can impact self-regulatory capacity and stress resilience. This indicates that a one-size-fits-all approach to stress management, as in the generalised 3-key approach suggested by Nesdoly, may not be universally effective.

As such, while Nina Nesdoly's talk offers valuable, practical strategies for stress relief that align with aspects of established stress and coping theories. Her emphasis on accessible, engagement-focused coping strategies could be especially useful for immediate stress relief and as part of a broader stress management approach. However, a comprehensive approach to stress management should also consider the full range of coping strategies outlined in the Two-Dimensional Framework, and the role of individual differences and environmental factors in how an individual perceives stress. Nesdoly’s suggestions should be complemented with a deeper understanding of systemic changes to reduce stressors at their source, as solely focusing on individual coping mechanisms without addressing underlying antecedents of stress can lead to a cycle of temporary relief without long-term solutions, encouraging the potential recurrence of distressful situations.

As a university student, I have encountered numerous stressful situations, but one that stands out occurred during my second year when I was juggling exam deadlines, part-time work, while dealing with decreased immunity after repeated COVID-19 infections. During this time, I experienced high levels of stress, manifesting as sleep disturbances, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. Applying the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, I can now recognize that my primary appraisal of the situation was that I perceived a high level of threat to my academic and future success. My secondary appraisal led me to believe I lacked sufficient resources to cope effectively due to regularly being physically unwell and lacking enough time to accomplish academic, professional and personal tasks, exacerbating my stress levels.

Initially, my coping strategies were largely ineffective. I often engaged in what the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework would classify as emotion-focused disengagement coping, such as procrastination and avoidance. a)  	In her talk, Nina Nesdoly - a work stress and burnout prevention consultant - discusses stress and stress relief. Citing various neuroscience studies and theories, she expounds on three key strategies for effective stress relief and management: Letting Tension Out, Limiting Information In, and Lowering the Barrier to Entry. 'Letting Tension Out' refers to engaging in activities that can physically release stress, often involving releasing something from our bodies. Be it the sweat when we exercise, the creative thoughts when we journal, or the words when we speak to our friends; these activities can aid in releasing tension and stress relief. 'Limiting Information In' refers to reducing input to your brain and preventing information overload. Information from social media and distressing news can overwhelm our brains, contributing to mental stress and fatigue. By allowing our brain to focus on one task at a time, stress levels can be greatly improved and managed.
Finally, 'Lowering the Barrier to Entry' refers to making stress relief easy and accessible. By choosing simple actions that are easily doable, stress relief can be integrated into daily life.
(How to Relieve Stress When You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)

b) 	In general, I believe that Nesdoly's talk largely aligns with what we have covered in the course. In her talk, she mentions that "exercise and movement" releases tension in the body, thus helping to relieve stress. Be it a run, jog or swim, there is much evidence to show that physical exercise does indeed help in relieving stress. Exercise has been shown to improve "attention and processing speed, executive function, and memory" (Smith et al, 2010). As cognitive function and information processing capabilities improve, the pool of available mental resources similarly increases. This would make it easier to find a balance between the demands that an individual faces, and the resources that the individual possesses to cope with the demands (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). Self-confidence in one's capabilities will also grow as cognitive function improves, thereby allowing for challenges and demands to be perceived as less stressful. Moreover, exercise has also been shown to reduce the stress hormone cortisol, resulting in improved sleep outcomes and in turn, better stress management (De Nys et al, 2022). Therefore, I agree with Nesdoly that exercise and tension release are good ways to relieve stress.
	In her talk, she also opines that the information that we take in on a daily basis can be a contributor to stress. These include disturbing TV shows or movies, negative news articles, or even social media, which leaves us constantly "comparing ourselves to others". Therefore, reducing the intake of overwhelming information can result in better mental faculties and improved stress management. Studies have shown that limiting the usage of social media can greatly enhance the mental health of young adults, resulting in significant improvements in their psychological well-being (Faulhaber et al., 2023). By experiencing brighter emotions and having an optimistic view of life, greater self-confidence is fostered. This allows one to perceive that they possess the coping ability to deal with stressful situations more often, and as a result, experience eustress (Lazarus and Folkman, 1984). Hence, it can be seen that 'limiting information in' is indeed an effective strategy for managing stress.
	Nesdoly mentions that taking frequent breaks can enhance focus and reduce stress. Indeed, taking micro-breaks can have benefits in improving mental health and personal well-being (Albulescu et al., 2022). However, there may be certain circumstances where taking a break becomes counter-productive instead. In a heavy workload environment, workers taking frequent breaks may feel increased pressure to meet deadlines, causing them to rush tasks post-break. This in turn results in increasing stress and workplace errors (Engagedly, n.d.). It is also important to ensure that breaks do not turn into attempts at procrastination. Defined as putting off a task "intentionally and habitually" (Merriam-Webster, n.d.), procrastination of a task is detrimental to productivity, which leads to increased stress levels. On the two-dimensional coping framework developed by Nes and Segerstrom (2006), procrastination can be classified as a form of avoidance coping, where the procrastinator hopes to ignore and/or avoid the situation at hand (Ong, 2025). Avoidance coping is considered to be a maladaptive practice as it often exacerbates stress without dealing with the root causes (Dijkstra & Homan, 2016). Therefore, it is important to ensure that breaks do not develop into a habit of procrastination. This can be done by setting time limits, planning specific activities, and motivating one's self to re-engage with the situation when the break ends.
	In conclusion, Nina Nesdoly's talk largely aligns with what we have covered in the course and other studies done on the topic of stress and stress management. This is especially true for her points on releasing tension through physical actions and limiting social media to prevent information overload. However, it is important to ensure that her suggestion of taking frequent breaks does not devolve into task procrastination. Her speech also focuses more on stress management techniques, which may serve only as temporary solutions if root causes are not addressed. Therefore, in addition to Nesdoly's strategies, problem-focused coping approaches should also be employed in order to achieve a long-term solution to the stressor.

c)	One of my personal experiences relating to stress was during the COVID-19 pandemic circuit breaker when I was a final-year tertiary education student. During the circuit breaker, I was thrust into an unfamiliar world of remote learning via Zoom calls and social isolation. Although I technically now had more "free time", I would find it harder to complete assignments and maintain focus. Instead of working on important tasks, I found myself endlessly doomscrolling on social media and the news. More often than not, these included updates on the worsening pandemic, economic downturn and even social unrest in other countries. It was during this period that I often felt tired and fatigued, not just physically but also mentally drained.
	After the first week or so, I was able to reconnect with my friends and classmates (outside of classes) through applications such as Discord and Skype, as it took some time to exchange account information and contacts. Although the social interactions we had were not in-person, the ability to chat with friends 'face to face' was a huge step up from what was almost total social isolation. Our lecturers also conducted small 'stretch sessions' breaks during our remote learning sessions, encouraging us to get up from our desks and stretch. It was during this period that I realised that I was able to cope better with my situation and assignments. I was also able to stay focused for longer periods and enter a flow state more often, as I spent less time on social media and consuming negative news.
	Looking back, I now realise how those small actions aided in my stress management and mental well-being. By stretching more often, video calling friends, and seeking social support, I allowed my body to release built-up tension – a key point in Nesdoly's talk. This in turn created noticeable stress relief, allowing me to perform better cognitively and achieve a better mental state. Nesdoly's point on limiting information intake was also another reason why I was able to manage my stress effectively. I now realise that although staying informed about the pandemic was necessary, the constant exposure to distressing news was adding anxiety and stress. By taking a break from social media and negative information, I was able to better utilise my cognitive resources on important tasks, such as assignments and knowledge retention.
	Before, my impression of stress management was that it required structured activities such as going to the gym, yoga classes or even extended meditation sessions. However, after listening to Nesdoly's talk, I realised that small, low-effort activities can also have a significant impact. In future high-stress situations, I will try to keep Nesdoly's three key strategies in mind as I try to manage stress through approach-oriented coping methods.

How to make stress your friend – Kelly McGonigal
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU

The TED Talk by Dr McGonigal was an insightful one where she talked about the common perception that stress is harmful for you may be wrong. The common interpretation of stress is that being in a prolonged state of stress puts you at a higher risk of falling sick and your body will present signs of physical manifestation of the stress, like catching the common cold bug, suffering from cardiovascular diseases. Based on a study conducted with almost 30,000 people, those that experienced stress and believe that stress is bad for their health had a 43% increased risk of premature death. (Keller, Litzelman, Wisk, et al. 2012) 
Dr McGonigal theorise that when you changed your mind’s perception about stress, you can change your body’s response to a healthier stress response. Another interesting point that Dr McGonigal pointed out was the neuro-hormone, Oxytocin, is not only a “Cuddle Hormone” that induces social bonding but also a stress hormone. It is your body’s natural stress response, and it protects the cardiovascular systems from the effects of stress by helping your blood vessels stay relaxed when you’re stress through its anti-inflammatory properties.

Relating to our course materials, I find that the course materials and the TED talk by Dr McGonigal was somewhat in line in terms of the way we cope with stress and the negative impacts of stress. However, the TED talk helped cast a wider lens on how our perception of stress can tip the scale between positive and negative impact of stress and how we should perceive stress as a form of motivation, rather than a stumbling stone in order to attain the benefits of stress.
In class, we were taught about the negative effects of stress, and how it can lead to diminished performance at work for adults and academic results for students. It can also lead to poor interactions between loved ones and causing intergenerational trauma, where parents’ reaction and responses to stress are often mirrored by their children – i.e. getting frustrated whenever things do not go his/her way. The course materials also mentioned about coping mechanisms that we can use to help identify the appropriate action to take to overcome the stressful period – which is a method to mitigate the negative impacts of stress.

As backed by many studies and research done before, people who are in a prolong state of stress are more likely to have an impaired immune system and as a result, suffer from illness more frequently. (Khansari et al., 1990). Our body gets into a “Fight-or-Flight” mode when we are stress and because of this, the body diverts its energy into more critical areas such as muscle skeletal system and brain, priming the body to respond to any physical altercation. Our heart pumps faster to get more oxygenated blood into the muscle skeletal system – which explains the palpitating heartbeat and flushed face one will feel whenever they feel stress. (Schneiderman, Ironson, Siegel et al. 2005). Imagine our heart, repeatedly pumping at a higher rate than normal, will wear out faster than an average person, thereby resulting in a stress induced premature death due to cardiovascular diseases.
I feel that Dr McGonigal’s theory makes logical sense to me. How we choose to perceive the stressor (event that causes stress) will make a difference on how we respond to the stressor. In a study done by students at Yale University, they found that by shifting one’s mindset about stress, it can lead to how they respond to stress and the amount of stress or severity of the stress does not matter as “stress mindset” can be a distinctive variable that influences stress responses. (Crum, Salovey, et al. 2013).

If we see stress as a motivation to become better, stronger, our response to the stress will change dramatically and the change in response may result in a different outcome. For instance, I am in the construction industry and I went through a period of immense stress in the 4th quarter of 2024 where I was assigned to a 2nd project towards the end of my first project. The construction industry’s busy periods are usually at the initial phase and handing over phase of each project where quality paperwork is required to ensure a smooth kick-off/handing over and it is paramount to the overall success of the project. As a subcontracting company, the majority of our workforce consists of permit holders, while the main contractors are predominantly locals. As the only local engineer on both projects, I was being hounded daily by the main-contractors from both sides for drawing submissions, method statements and test reports. There were times where I had to work way beyond my working hours just to churn out the urgent documents for submission and I was bitter about it, constantly worrying about being unable to meet the expectations of these main-contractors as the locals in the industry are rare and easily identifiable. After nearly 2 months of struggling, I was able to clear most of the submission and things began to wind down on my 1st project, but this “success” came at the expense of sleep deprivation and time with my family. The stress of fulfilling my work commitments made me crankier than usual, losing my patience with my child over small issues and this took a toll on my relationship with my family. Looking back, I felt that I should be able to handle the negative impacts of these stress better if I had known about the two-dimensional coping framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006) taught in class. By targeting my emotional response to stress and being task focused, I should be able to shut off the negative emotions welling up inside and focus on completing the task at hand.

While the course materials can help to solve the immediate problem of these negative effects of having stress, the insight I gained from the TED talk video by Dr McGonigal can help me further when I come across such stressful events in the future. By changing my mindset about stress and viewing the stress of being easily recognised in the industry as a motivation to do better and strive harder, I can avoid being trapped in the realm of “unhealthy stress response” and make use of the stress responses like heighten brain function and adrenaline rush to complete my assigned task efficiently.

The association with health and mortality. Health psychology : official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association, 31(5), 677–684. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026743
