I watched Nina’s TED talk titled ‘How to relieve stress when you’re overwhelmed’. Nina shared three keys to stress relief in everyday life. Firstly, she suggested “letting tension out” by engaging in physical or social activities to release built-up tensions in the body. Secondly, Nina proposed “limiting information in” by decreasing constant social media intake. Overconsumption of these increase cortisol levels, deplete cognitive resources and make people feel more overwhelmed. Nina explained that cognitive depletion is due to our brains being wired to focus on one thing at a time. Finally, Nina suggested “lowering the barrier to entry” as the third key to stress relief. This is achieved by incorporating small and easy activities into daily routines to increase the likelihood they will be done. Overall, Nina emphasized stress relief techniques can be practiced in daily life through small steps do not require perfect conditions or big changes.
From the TED talk, the key ideas of stress relief echo the NCO112 topics on stress. Using the transactional model of stress and coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1986), stress happens when daily life demands are greater than a person’s coping resources. Nina’s advice to think of lowering the barrier is aligned with the secondary appraisal of stress, by influencing our perception to realize that we can take actions, even if they are small. According to Nes and Segerstrom (2006), seeking emotional support by letting tension out and actively limiting information are forms of emotion-focused coping approach, because they do not solve the root cause of stress but provide emotional relief by providing calm acceptance and reduce negative emotions like anxiety or anger from stress.
However, the stress reliefs suggested in the TED talk are definitively reliefs. They are short-term actions that provide temporary comfort but do not address the root cause of the stress. Nina did not address problem-focused coping approaches to stress, such as time management or seeking active assistance to their problems. Furthermore, even though Nina’s stress relief techniques are approach-oriented, it is arguable that these techniques may oversimplify stress management and may not work on everybody as her suggestions indicate. Although her suggestions to step away from stress to release tension or practise small steps appear to be approach-oriented, consistently turning to stress relief can distract people too much from resolving their stressful demands and even add more stress when their problems persist. 
Alternatively, evidence has suggested mindfulness as an alternative to Nina’s stress relief approach. Regular mindfulness exercises promote better wellbeing and increased problem-focused coping approaches (de Vibe et al., 2018), as compared to the TED talk’s stress relievers. Mindfulness help ease stress by increasing one’s self-awareness to the present moment and opportunity to self-regulate emotions. After a mindfulness breathing exercise, one can be calmer and then more likely to be able to re-appraise the stressful situation more meaningfully and resolve their demanding situation. It aligns with the transactional model of stress and coping. During primary appraisal, being in a mindful state can allow a person to reduce an automatic perceived threat to a non-judgemental awareness. Mindfulness can also make the secondary appraisal more manageable, as people perceive a threat as a challenge rather than a disaster, increasing the capacity to cope and increasing the likelihood of eustress. Therefore, mindfulness can help to overcome stress and helps increase resilience by optimizing our attention and memory capacity (Jha et al., 2014).
In summary, Nina’s TED talk provides helpful tips that most people can adopt to relief stress in the short term and is aligned with NCO112 emotion-focused coping methods. On the other hand, mindfulness offers an alternative form of emotion-focused coping approach that can indirectly contribute to problem-focused approach by providing calmer emotions to solve problems more objectively. 
One personal experience of stress I encountered recently is during peak assignment period while I was juggling multiple responsibilities at work and juggling parental duties. As a full-time employee in a lean team and a part-time student with two young daughters, I sometimes felt waves of overwhelming demands that happen all at once. During an assignment where I had to complete a 2,000-word essay, managed heavier workload when my manager resigned and my youngest daughter was hospitalized for prolonged fever due to Kawasaki disease, I recalled sleep disruptions at night, mental haziness in the day, falling sick due to weakened immune system and a very irritable temperament.
Understanding the transactional model of stress and coping made me appreciate that the stress is due to the result of overwhelming demands of life from work, school and parenting, and the limited resources of time and energy that I have. I saw the situation as a threat in the primary appraisal phase to my mental well-being and academic performance, while during the secondary appraisal, I felt a lack of self-confidence and almost feeling helpless to cope with the stressors. I coped by focusing my attention of my parental duties on emotion-focused coping approach by sharing my emotional anxieties with my spouse to regulate my emotions and accepting my daughter’s illness without self-blame or blaming others. I planned my time to focus between parenting and school assignment using problem-focused approach and successfully submitted my assignment in time, ahead of schedule. However, it was a mixed to negative response at work. Feeling frustrated from isolation without immediate manager support (she left), I distanced myself from the team at work, procrastinated and reacted passive-aggressively at work outside my scope. I scrolled through my phone a lot as a distraction, compounding my stress due to the loss of focus and time. In retrospect, I practised an avoidant coping emotion-focused approach when it came to work.
The TED talk provided me with quick stress relief tips which I could easily start to implement, no matter how small the action is. In letting out the tension, I could plan for walks around the office to ground myself and to feel calmer. Secondly, limiting information in can help me to clear my mind from anxiety of doomscrolling on social media, which over-aroused me with negative mood like pessimism and increased anxiety. Lastly, in lowering the barrier to entry, I could incorporate mini exercise routines and use my Apple Watch feature of mindfulness to remind myself to pause and practise 100 repetitions of small exercises or a 3-minute mindfulness exercise in a safe and comfortable space. 
I realized that my coping strategies were a mix of emotion-focused and avoidant coping methods and came to realize from research that frequent use of avoidant coping strategies not sustainable for long-term outlook on my stress management (Chao, 2011). I learned to realize that building resilience is about overcoming adversity using positive coping such as problem-focused approach.
Looking back, this experience reminded me that stress is something which cannot be avoided, but I can control how I respond and interpret it. The transaction model of stress and coping is a constant reminder to be aware of how I appraise stressful situations and to evaluate options by improving positive feelings to enhance my wellbeing by accumulating enough emotional resources to combat stressful situations in the future. Nina’s TED talk also reminded me that I do not have to wait for the perfect moment to react to stress but take small meaningful actions to relieve the stress pressure periodically. I plan to practise more mindfulness to improve my self-awareness in reacting automatically to stress by being less reactive, calmer and accept that I cannot control the situation, but I can control how I handle it. I aim to be better, no matter how small, than yesterday.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People | Speaker:  Lucy Hone 
Question 1a)
TED speaker, Lucy Hone who is a resilience expert, had shared a personal traumatic experience in 2019. She had lost her daughter, her daughter’s best friend and the friend’s mother in a car accident. She had become the victim, instead of the giver on how to be resilient. Further sharing that she had decided to proceed to experiment on how to overcome her grief, using the three-resilience advice.

	First, the acceptance of suffering, in which adversity can happen to anyone, at any time. Understanding it and accepting it helps in part of resilience process. Secondly, the ability to focus, this refers to the attention to focus on matters which the individual can change. Simultaneously, to minimize the focus on what one cannot change. Finally, the constant ongoing evaluation to consider the actions or decision undertaken, whether it is beneficial or not.

Question 1b)
Reference to the TED talk, there are several points which are aligned to our course of study; first on Fletcher and Sarkar (2013) had presented that resilience involves two components, adversity and positive adaption. The adversity would relate to first advice, to accept that adversity would occur to anyone, and this aids the individual from feeling being singled out, as there are also others who have encountered similar traumatic experience. While Lucy’s other two points, the ability to focus on matter which an individual can change and to constant evaluate the decision making in a resilience process, whether it helps or harms oneself Both aligns to the concept of a positive adaptation to adversity. Secondly, the study guide had reference to Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR; Richardson, 2002), that an individual starts from a state of homeostasis, which is a comfort zone. Thereafter stressors, such as traumatic, challenging life events takes place which alters the state of homeostasis. It was presented that there are four possible outcomes that may arise after the mentioned disruption, which are resilient reintegration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss and dysfunctional reintegration. It was further elaborate that resilient reintegration being the ideal outcome, while dysfunctional reintegration is the least ideal. 

Further mentioned, there are resilience factors such as protective factors, which Hone had shared, as an individual’s mindset, having a positive mindset. There are also factors which hinder or deter the positive development of resilience, such as economic hardship, poor parenting and lack of social network support. Based on Hone’s talk, there is an oversimplification that resilience by just accepting, focus on being positive and making decision to do right. It is observed that developing resilience is a dynamic process which requires individual protective factors as well as conducive external resource to further support. In Hone’s case, she has not mentioned, that external resources has to be in place as well, such as economic stability, professional counselling and support.

In a recent 2021 meta-analysis on social support and posttraumatic stress by Wang, A. Y., et al. (2021), indicates that a social support act as a protective factor, in reducing the post-traumatic stress order (PTSD), while PTSD also forms a risk factor in a relationship, in the case of severe symptoms, such as irritability, emotional withdrawal would affect the frequency and amount of social support, be provided such as family members and close peers. This presents that relying solely on external support may deemed insufficient, on a prolong basis. It also requires individual’s commitment in developing positive mindset and attitude, concurrently with sufficient external support provided. This would greatly increase one’s development to a better resilience trait as well as the outcome.  

Question 1c) 
Eight years ago, at a company which I had worked less than five months, there was a planned shift of work scope and reshuffle of team members. Previously there were total of five work teams, all handling various regional Asia payrolls. The proposed change was to allocate three teams handling Singapore payrolls, while the other two teams handling Hong Kong payrolls. The rest of the Asia payrolls to be reallocated to our Philippines office. 

The new teams’ members and team leads were made known one week prior. I am positive to the change, given my team lead remain unchanged. And I have a strong working relationship with her. On the planned date of change, my new team excluding me was called to an ad hoc meeting with the Operations director and Human resource business partner. Twenty minutes later, the rest of the four teams and myself were called in to the conference room, excluding my new team members. It was announced, due to company restructuring, the 4 members, including my team lead were asked to leave the organization.

This impacted my mindset, as it is my first hand experiencing a retrenchment in the organisation.  There were quite a few unknowns, the sudden involuntary loss of colleagues, how would the work allocation be like?  Further reshuffle placement other teams, re-adjustment to new team lead. And the biggest concern, would be job security, whether would it be my turn in next few months? It did not occur me back then, but it was my first work experience as survivor’s guilt.
	
Firstly, by applying from Hone’s first tip, to accept the suffering, the loss of my colleagues and team lead, and my new team, posed a moderate mental block that took me about two weeks to overcome. I was unsure how to interact with them; a positive tone would likely to be interpreted that I am relieved it had happened to them and not me.  If I were to appear sad, it would worsen their emotional burden.
	 
By applying the MRR model, which was discussed earlier in Q1b, on resilience factors such as external support. The initial two week, I have shared with my family, as well as close friends. Their encouragement and willingness to listen to my concerns, particularly the uncertainty of the company’s action, had brought me comfort and support during the difficult times. In addition, by focusing on the new portfolio of clients and transitioning out my current non-Singapore related payrolls to my Philippines colleagues. This has diverted my focus on the adversity, while allowing me to redirect to a more meaningful work purpose. 

These self- reflections had provided me better clarity on my initial coping mechanism in adversity. Given the increasing volatile political, economic and technological trends. This has led me to a continuous effort to nurture a proactive resilient mindset and exploring appropriate external resources. These actions would further strengthen my capability to handle adversities much effectively.

Stress 
1.How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly 
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)  

(a)The speaker, Nina Nesdoly, who is a work stress and burnout prevention speaker, started the talk with an example of a highly stressful and overwhelming situation. She then gave three options to the audience on what people normally choose to do. They are, push it through, curl up into a ball or go to a party. Nina then explained on three keys that the audience can relieve stress.  Firstly, let tension out. This can be in a form of various activities that physically get the tension out. Examples are, going for a run, talking to a friend or writing down our thoughts in a diary. Secondly, limit information. Usually our brains get exhausted from us taking in information. This includes scrolling through social media, listening to news and so on. We will need to take a break or create a space that we don’t take in information or limit the information that we absorb.  The last key is to lower the barrier to entry. For example, if one of the ways we relieve stress is to talk to a friend, then instead of waiting to schedule a lunch with our friend, we can consider having a short video call instead. This is because when we are overwhelmed, lowering the barrier will make it much easier to relieve the stress. Nina concludes that by following these three key points, we will be able to relieve our stress and in turn, focus on our work more. 
(b)The TED talk offers coping strategies which align with what was covered in the course. We learnt that there were four coping strategies in the two dimensional framework which are problem vs emotion and approach vs avoidance. From the TED talk, for the first key point of letting tension out, depending on the action taken, it can fall either into problem focused approach or emotion focused approach. If a person chooses to let the tension out by talking to a trusted friend about the problem, it will fall under the emotion focused approach. If a person decides to confront the problem to let the tension out, it will fall under the problem focused approach. 
For the second key point of the talk, it was to limit information. I feel that this may fall  under problem-focused avoidant coping. However, it may not be so as from the TED talk, when one is to limit information, the speaker was not talking about avoiding the issue. She was referring to having a space for oneself to take a break from things where information was not given or absorbed by our brains. For example, a person may think that taking a break from a stressful situation may be to scroll through social media. However, as the person is scrolling through social media, he/she is still absorbing information from it. Thus, this will not help the person with relieving stress. On the other hand, if the person is facing a stressful issue and decides to disengage by having alone time somewhere, it can also be considered as avoiding the issue, especially if the person prolongs the disengagement.
For the last key point of the talk on lowering the barrier to entry, I feel that this can fall under different parts of the framework, depending on the action taken. For example, in the case of a difficult senior colleague. For a problem focused approach, it could be to talk to the senior colleague with several other colleagues. However, this might take time and to ‘lower the barrier to entry’, the person may consider talking directly to the senior colleague. For an emotion focused approach, instead of talking to other colleagues over lunch, one may consider messaging the colleagues for advice or support. 
As such, even if the coping mechanisms were explained differently in the TED talk and what we have learnt in our course, the essence and approach to it is the same.Thus, the content in the TED talk aligns to what we have learnt in the course. 
(c) There was a period in my life when I was not doing well financially and emotionally. This was, unfortunately, due to me having a relationship with a person who was emotionally abusive towards me and used my feelings towards the person as leverage to get what the person wanted. If I decide to draw a boundary, the person will start to gaslight and will even turn our arguments around and make it seem like I was the one causing all the trouble between us. It had gotten so bad, that I had lost so much weight and I had mild depression due to the nature of the relationship. The stress had built up and I could not focus much on my work, and even with my own family. They advised me against continuing the relationship, but as I was conditioned to believe that anyone who was against the person, was against me, I dismissed their advice. 
When I had to make big purchases such as buying a house, I had to calculate if my CPF was enough as the person was not in a stable job, and thus unable to pay for the monthly loan. The relationship had been causing me so much stress and having to make big decisions also added on to the massive stress that I was already undergoing. 
When I finally realised that the person did not love me, as the person was caught cheating repeatedly, I decided to take action to get myself away from the person. This included involving my family, close friends and work as well. My family and close friends helped with the emotional support and my direct supervisor helped me with transferring me to another department so that the person could not find me at work to harass me. 
Applying what I learnt from the course, I was already facing most of the negative impacts of continuous stress. They were, reduced work performance, affecting my family relationships and unhealthy related behaviours. Knowing the different coping mechanisms from the course and the TED talk, it could have helped me manage my stress better during the course of the relationship so as not to affect my relationship with other people. It might have also helped with my mild depression, as having that much stress did not help with my spiraling thoughts. It would also help me identify that certain prolonged coping mechanisms may not be healthy in the long run such as the avoidant forms. Knowing this could have made me look for other coping mechanisms. Also, knowing that to limit information when relieving stress, would have helped me as well back then. Previously, I would try to take a break by scrolling on social media but that usually drained me and it did not help me with my stress.

Chosen TED Talk on resilience: ‘The Three Secrets of Resilient People’ by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
(a) In Lucy Hone’s TED talk, she drew upon her academic insights in resilience research, her experience working with her local community, and her application of staying resilient while navigating her toughest time, losing her only daughter. Hone shared that resilience can be a cultivated skill that can help one navigate life’s inevitable challenges. 
Her first strategy to be a resilient individual highlights the acceptance that suffering is inevitable and is part of the human aspect. She believes this strategy stops individuals from feeling isolated when challenges arise. Her second strategy underscores the importance of attention control to be resilient. While humans are naturally predisposed to focus on negative instances, staying resilient involves learning to redirect their focus from a negative to a positive lens, thereby cultivating optimism and gratitude. Hone referenced a 2005 study, which postulated that individuals exhibited higher gratitude and happiness levels when they reflect on positive things occurring daily. For her last strategy, she suggested that one should habitually ask oneself whether one's actions and thoughts are helping or harming. This reflective question empowers individuals to appraise their own responses in adversity, giving them power in decision-making, and facilitates recovery and growth.
Collectively, Hone’s three strategies articulate ways that resilience can be learned and strengthened over time. She believes that by adopting these strategies, individuals can endure and flourish through life’s inevitable adversities.

	(b) Hone’s TED talk closely aligns with the resilience concepts outlined in the iSmartGuide. Her first strategy regarding the acceptance of suffering reflects the American Psychological Association (APA) Dictionary of Psychology’s definition of resilience as the ability to practice positive adaptation through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility (APA, n.d). This mirrors the iSmartGuide’s emphasis that resilience arises from the interaction between adversity and positive adaptation (Ong, 2025). By framing hardship as a universal human experience, it reinforces that disruptions are essential catalysts for the development of resilience. However, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) acknowledges less favourable outcomes (Ong, 2025), suggesting that this strategy may overstate the inevitability of growth, as acceptance of suffering does not guarantee resilience.
	Her second strategy, regarding attention control, corresponds with the areas of resilience identified in iSmartGuide, particularly optimism, positive emotions, and cognitive flexibility. Both perspectives show how resilience can be cultivated by training the mind to adopt a constructive perspective during difficult circumstances to enable individuals to reframe adversities. Consequently, her third strategy, asking oneself if their thoughts and actions are helping or harming, aligns with the iSmartGuide’s discussion of practicing active coping and self-reflection (Ong, 2025). Both highlight the role of deliberate self-awareness in evaluating and adjusting one’s responses to foster adaptive outcomes during adversity. 
However, while Hone’s three strategies align with the iSmartGuide’s content, which offers practical insight into achieving resilient integration, her talk simplifies the MRR’s theory by overlooking the possibility of other outcomes after adversity. Both converge on the idea that resilience is not a fixed quality but a dynamic process that can be fostered through deliberate reflection, adaptation, and the cultivation of positive psychological resources.
	My research on resilience led me to Regan, who opined that people cope differently with adversity and perceive challenges in various ways (Regan, 2017). Regan also mentioned some techniques, such as being aware of unhelpful thoughts, to reduce anxiety. This aligns with Hone’s second strategy of managing attention to focus on positivity to strengthen resilience. The iSmartGuide reinforces this by highlighting positive emotions and cognitive flexibility (Ong, 2025). Though Hone presents this as a habit, both iSmartGuide and Regan stress that resilience also depends on how adversity is interpreted by and shapes individuals.
Conversely, in The Resilience Workbook, Schiraldi posited that recovering from adversity often requires strategies beyond mere acceptance of suffering. He highlights practices such as writing about past trauma to release unexpressed emotions, reducing the fatigue of secrecy, and alleviating the isolation that comes with avoidance (Schiraldi, 2017). In addition, he emphasises self-compassion and forgiveness as vital methods to foster recovery. While Hone’s first strategy acknowledges the universality of hardship, this new perspective offered by Schiraldi suggests that resilience may require complementary approaches to navigate adversity more effectively to transform adversity into growth. 

(c) One of the most defining moments of resilience in my life occurred last year when 
I was preparing for the Singapore International Band Festival (SIBF). In secondary school, I played the bassoon, an instrument I learned and mastered largely on my own, as no one else in the club played this instrument. However, when I entered Temasek Polytechnic, I decided to learn the violin to expand my musical experience, and ended up playing for three years.
 After I graduated, an opportunity arose to participate in SIBF, and I decided to challenge myself to switch back to the bassoon after a four-year break. This was a tough period as I only had three months to relearn the fingerings and adjust from treble to bass clef. Moreover, the pieces we performed had a solo for my instrument. At times, it felt overwhelming, and many people doubted me as I could not even play a bar of the songs properly. The pressure of representing my school heightened this sense of adversity.
However, rather than withdrawing, I committed myself to the challenge and attended all the practices and even brought my instrument home for additional practice despite working. Over time, I regained fluency in the bassoon and could play as well as I used to in secondary school. This effort paid off when the band achieved a gold award at SIBF, a huge improvement from the previous SIBF, where the band achieved a silver award. Furthermore, the judges also commented that my playing sounded resonant. That outcome was significant as an external success and as a personal testament to what resilience looks like in practice. In this case, my consistent effort, adaptive learning, and self-belief were successful.
Upon reflecting on my experience, it became clear that I interpreted my success as a matter of discipline and persistence. However, after understanding Hone’s strategies, the iSmartGuide, and my additional research, it broadened my horizon and gave me a more nuanced lens, which helped me identify what I did well and what I could have done better.
To begin with, Hone’s first strategy of accepting hardship aligns with my choice to embrace the challenge of switching instruments. Additionally, the MRR shows that adversity can result in individuals stepping out of their comfort zone (Ong, 2025). While my experience reflects resilient reintegration, I recognise that it is insufficient without active coping, echoing Schiraldi’s suggestion on practicing self-compassion during setbacks.
Hone’s second strategy of shifting attention helps me reflect on how I focused on practice and progress rather than others’ doubts. Although this focus supported my reintegration, the over-practice led to fatigue. Regan’s (2017) advice made me realise that I can acknowledge negative thoughts while redirecting my focus on constructive actions. Applying the resilience factors mentioned by Ong (2025) taught me that sustainable resilience requires both disciplined focus and reflection for my personal growth in the future.
In essence, peak performance results not only from persistence, acceptance, and reflective action, as mentioned by Hone, but also from adopting a multi-pronged approach involving emotional awareness, self-care, and adaptive habits. By adopting a growth mindset and applying strategies to manage mental and physical demands, one can thrive under pressure, transform challenges into opportunities, and achieve sustainable resilience.

Mr Hunt shares about how he not only survived but thrived through a life racked by adversity through resilience. He grew up amidst anti-black racism and poverty, and both his parents being involved with illegal activities. He lost his mother to drugs and father to a fight within jail before hitting puberty and was raised by his abusive grandmother for a decade before moving out in the middle of schooling (Hunt, 2025). Despite his adversity, he was the first in his family to complete undergraduate studies and get a masters. He believes knowing why instead of how is important to having resilience. To him, the most important resource is our minds: that the resilience to survive has the power to change one’s life. He believes that this kind of resilience can only be learnt through hardship, but that is not to say that we must be alone. With perseverance, an internal grit, and partnership, the support of others when you need them most, we get resilience: proper perspective and positive attitude create power. However, that is not to say he has no hidden agendas. He is the founder of Audacity Firm, which provides self-development services to foster resilience and promote upscaling. Inducing the will to better oneself in others would increase demand for services like Audacity Firm. Thus, Mr Hunt would want people to seek self-help courses rather than, for example, seeking assistance or welfare services from others. 
However, resilience is not a miracle cure to trauma. Mr Hunt was lucky that he managed to improve his adverse circumstances through resilience, but to expect such of other marginalised people is unrealistic (Suslovic & Lett, 2024) especially without proper support, and similar adverse childhood experiences often lead to them spiralling deeper into their suffering, raising the rate of social and health problems (Abate et al., 2024). 
NCO112 also adds a similar perspective to Mr Hunt’s of the power of resilience. With the metatheory of resilience and resiliency (Richardson, 2002), it sheds insight on how one in homeostasis can respond to an external stressor, leading to varied outcomes. The ideal one is resilient integration, where one can not only overcome the stressor, but improve themselves after with the experience gained. In order to achieve resilient integration, one must have resilience. Resilience is made of two parts: an external adversity that disrupts and positive adaptation, the response to the adversity (Morgan et al., 2013). There are also other ways resilience has been deconstructed. According to Kunzler (2020), can also comprise of the combination of social support, sense of coherence and meaning of life. Social support when someone fosters a reliable network of people that can help through hardship, so that they can have people to fall back on if they are unable to cope with their adversity, which has proven to reduce interpersonal conflict and stress (Caines & Treuren, 2024). While resilience does involve intrinsic strength, it is not solely about one’s own strength. When they are unable to cope, resilience also involves knowing when to turn to others for help to ensure they can continue striving towards their goal. Sense of coherence is strengthening the capacity to make sense of life’s obstacles, understanding and coming to terms with the challenges presented, but not merely wallowing in an inability to solve it, but rather to figure out and curate solutions for the problems faced. Lastly, meaning of life is understanding the purpose of one’s life and creating guiding principles for one to follow, which reaffirms one’s purpose for tolerating and undergoing the hardships associated with learning new things and having new experiences that lead to growth and development (Ackerman & Levontin, 2023). These experiences are part and parcel of life, and seeing them as challenges to grow from can have positive impacts (Horikoshi, 2023) and foster greater resilient integration.
When comparing NCO112 and Mr Hunt’s talk, similarities surface. Partnership is similar to having social support, as both focus on relying on external support when needed. Meaning of life is similar to looking having perseverance and understanding the “why” instead of the “how”. When you seek to understand the reasons behind your actions instead of only just learning how to achieve your goal, it provides a stronger sense of purpose. This sense of purpose helps one to reaffirm their reason and beliefs for coming this far. Lastly, sense of coherence is related to positive attitude. Both focus on confronting, rationalising and understanding one’s hardships without succumbing to them and giving up. Having an optimistic view can help to reframe one’s thinking and allow them to rationalise and find new ways to view and tackle their problem. 
My adverse experience was when I started my second year in Junior College (JC), and swapped teachers for Chemistry as my first teacher only taught first year students. My classmates and I were very upset on this change as we had heard this teacher was less competent than our old teacher. This demoralised me greatly, and made me rather pessimistic, which likely contributed to my grades falling. Looking back, I focused on trying to maintain a passing rate despite having the curiosity and enthusiasm to learn more. I have always had poor study techniques, which led to me often getting poor results for examinations as I was not used to the stress of the examination.
While eventually I managed to pull my grade up to pass my A Levels with lots of pain and struggling, the content of both Mr Hunt’s talk and NCO112 have concepts that would have benefited me if I had utilised them and possibly helped me get either a better grade or not suffer as much. Understanding the meaning and reasoning behind the importance of getting good academic grades for my future can help me be more persistent in trying to achieve my goal of getting high grades, giving me the drive to push on. Remembering that good grades allow me more options for university can help me be more focused on trying to do well for school, rather than trying simply to get through JC and get an A level certificate. Being optimistic and trying to make sense of alternate ways to solve my troubles could also help me remain more driven and productive, and instead of pessimistic views such as focusing solely on the incompetence of my teacher being the cause of my poor grades, I can try to be optimistic and problem-solve, such as trying to seek one-on-one consultations with her, other teachers or even classmates if I find it unhelpful, to focus on improving myself, or perhaps researching online to find more effective study materials. Not giving up even when it seems hard will help me be more likely to study more effectively. If those fail, having good social support and reliable partnerships can help me fall back on trusted people when I find it hard to go on alone, such as asking my classmates for advice as well as finding people to organise study groups with and share our knowledge, notes or methods of studying. This might have exposed me to techniques to cope with my troubles or even get solutions to my woes, as well as fostered my confidence and determination to study harder and not give up in the face of a difficult situation. These factors in combination could have helped me cope better in JC and possibly achieve better results, as they can help improve how I coped with the situation.
In conclusion, to quote Mr Hunt, resilience is something that can be spoken to “the adolescent you, the college you, the corporate you, the professional you, the future you”.  Resilience is a powerful asset one must have to succeed through hardship, past and present and future. Having resilience protects from the drawbacks of high-stress environments such as burnout, sleep deprivation and depression (Shatte et al., 2017). Not only that, resilience improves quality of life, such as areas of physical and psychological health, and forge stronger relationships, and improve the clarity of priorities (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 2004). It is more important than ever to develop resilience in an increasingly volatile world rife with challenges and hardships. Even when it may seem hopeless, unless we give up, it is never impossible that we can overcome our hardships with enough tenacity and support. Even if the chance of success is low, the chance of success is zero if we lack the resilience.

TED Talk chosen: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly 
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)  
(a)Summary of the video:
This video highlights that managing stress can make life easier for us. Nina discusses three primary methods for stress relief. The first key is releasing tension. Some ways to relieve stress can be journaling, chatting with a friend, and meditation. Taking a real break allows our body and mind to recharge, letting tension fade away from every part of our body. The second key is to limit information in. Our media consumption (social media, news, etc.) can increase stress without us realising.  Without taking a break, even our most enjoyable work can lead to exhaustion. Intense focusing on tasks has been shown to increase blood pressure and cortisol levels. Taking an actual break allows our minds to recuperate and boost productivity. The final key is lowering the barrier to entry. Relieving stress should be done in a simple and easily accessible way in our comfort zone, making us more willing to do it. For instance, doing something small, such as making a short call to a friend to vent. 
(b)The TED talk by Nina aligns closely with what was covered in this course. The three strategies highlighted in the talk were releasing tension, limiting information in, and lowering the barrier to entry. All these align with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), mentioning that stress develops when demands placed on someone exceed the resources available to balance them. Nina emphasises strategies for rebalancing the situation and enhancing one’s coping ability by promoting practices such as exercising, journaling and relaxation. 
Subsequently, Nina mentioned that stress can affect a person physically, which can be supported with articles. Stress can have negative impacts on our body’s vital systems, inclusive of our brain and immune system (Yaribeygi et al., 2017). This supports Nina’s view that tension should be released as soon as possible instead of bottling it all in. Long term psychological distress can damage our health, especially for those who are already ill or older. This accentuates the value of getting therapy and recovery. (Schneiderman et al., 2005), indicating evidence that managing stress is crucial to both our physical and mental well-being. 
Based on a survey conducted by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), nearly one-third of youths suffer from depression, anxiety or stress (The Straits Times, 2024). Some factors that contribute to it are the excessive usage of social media, the rise in cyber bullying and people not seeking help due to fear of stigma. 
Having said that, not all stress is necessarily bad. Both HealthHub (2022) and VeryWell Mind (2023) mention that “eustress” or moderate levels of stress, can help serve as a useful motivation to encourage people to reach their main goals and be more productive. According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance will improve under stress but to a certain extent, before it starts to deteriorate (VeryWell Mind, 2023). This point suggests that having a good balance of stress is beneficial rather than removing it completely. 
In conclusion, Nina’s speech addresses the importance of recuperation and preventing excessive workload while providing helpful stress relief tips backed by academic resources. Her advice is relevant to the Singapore survey that was mentioned, as local youths show significant levels of stress. Although her presentation can be further improved by stating that not all stress is always bad, and having a good balance would be the optimal goal for maximum productivity and efficiency. 
(c)In my final year of polytechnic, I had a 6-month internship at a hotel as a pastry intern. From the very start, I was treated like a full-time employee which made me feel overwhelmed. My shift starts from 6 am to 3 pm, and I wake up at 4.30 am daily to catch the staff transport. However, there was not a day that I ended on time; I usually worked till 6 pm. There were instances when I clocked a 15-hour shift, or when I worked ten days straight.
During the same period, I was going through my first ever breakup. It felt like the whole world was crashing out on me, I worked on 2 hours of sleep daily and had many emotional breakdowns.
There was one incident that is permanently stamped in my memory. It was a busy Saturday, and we were short of manpower. My executive chef instructed me to take charge of the afternoon tea service alone that day as it was her rest day. The afternoon tea desserts must be sent out before 11 am and I was overwhelmed with pressure as I was doing a two-person job. It did not help that it was a weekend and the busiest day of the week. There was no one free to help me as they all had their own responsibilities. I still remember my hands shaking while piping the desserts, each of which required individual decoration as they were bitesized. There were six different types of desserts, which all needed precise garnishes. I needed to rush, but at the same time, I couldn’t sacrifice precision and I needed to ensure that every dessert looked identical. 
With two months in, the pressure took a toll not only on my mental health, but also my physical health. I developed alopecia, which resulted in multiple bald spots all over my head. This became another component to my distress, as I felt very self-conscious and even more stressed out whenever I looked into the mirror. Chronic stress can cause hair loss because it prevents the hormone corticosterone from activating hair follicle stem cells, which are crucial for new hair growth (Bryant, 2021). 
Reflecting back, if I had more support, I feel that I would have managed the situation with a more positive attitude.  In fact, research has shown that interns with heavy workloads and little support often feel more stressed and less engaged (Azila-Gbettor et al., 2022). 
Even so, I know that I am not the only person going through this type of struggle. One out of three youths struggle with poor mental health, showing signs of depression, anxiety or stress, based on an article from The Straits Times (2024). Many young people my age struggle to cope when demands are overloaded. 
Looking back now, with reference to Nina and the course contents, I realised why I was struggling so much. According to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), it explains how stress increases when demands exceed perceived coping resources. It relates to my situation as my responsibilities and emotional burden were too much for me to handle with the limited to no strategies that I had. Instead of releasing tension, I suppressed it and ignored it, thinking that it would go away over time, which only worsened the situation and negatively impacted both my body and mind. Nina’s point to “let tension out” resonates deeply, as I had no healthy outlets, and that likely contributed to the physical symptoms that I experienced. Additionally, I did not “take a real break”. During my rest days, I stayed at home and thought about work or my breakup repeatedly, reenacting what-if scenarios and how I would have done things differently if I had another chance. I am sure that going for a walk or journaling would have helped me release some of the tension. In the future, I will face stress with strategies such as practising mindfulness or talking to a friend about my worries. From this course, I learned that ignoring stress creates more issues and learning to balance it out is the optimal solution.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
(a)The speaker of this TED talk, Lucy Hone, was sharing not only in the perspective of a resilience research expert but also as a mother who experienced the loss of her daughter in a car accident. She highlighted that adversity can happen to anyone and it is possible to recover from it through resilience. She believes that resilience is not a fixed trait but something that can be learned through an easy process. Mainly, she focused on sharing three strategies that makes someone resilient. Firstly, people with resilience understands and accepts that suffering is part of life instead of questioning it. Secondly, they focus their attention on things that can be changed rather than stressing over those that cannot. This can be done by being more grateful and by reducing negative thoughts. Thirdly, resilient people reflect by asking whether their action is actually helping or harming them. This helps them gain more control over their decisions and practice self-compassion.
(b)The content of Hone’s sharing was mainly aligned to the resilient reintegration outcome of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) where individuals positively adapt and achieve growth after facing challenges. This is the best among the four outcomes that can occur which are homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss and dysfunctional reintegration respectively (Richardson, 2002). I do agree with her point that resilience is not a fixed trait and can be learned when someone faces an adversity that disrupts their homeostasis. However, while Hone claims that resilience can be learned easily using her strategies, I think that it is definitely not as easy as said. The NCO112 course highlighted the term bouncebackability which describes the ability to recover and achieve resilient integration after a setback (Collins English Dictionary, 2023). There are ten important qualities associated with this achievement (Kunzler et al., 2020). While Hone’s strategies do cover qualities like hardiness, optimism, positive emotions, cognitive flexibility and self-efficacy, they do not fully utilise other qualities such as social support, active coping, meaning in life, sense of coherence and religiosity which might be equally important and useful for us.
Her first strategy revolves around asking us to accept suffering as part of life and that everyone will experience tough situations. She justifies by saying this mentality of acceptance would prevent individuals from being consumed by the “No, why me?” thinking. This does align with the hardiness quality which helps us be mentally prepared to deal with difficult situations and increases our commitment to overcoming the hardship. However, this could risk being misunderstood as passivity or resignation when individuals simply accept their fate and lose confidence in life. Research showed that resilience is not just about acceptance, rather it is about building motivation and skills needed to address the problem (Passfield, 2019). Similarly, NCO112 emphasises on establishing a meaning in life and having a sense of coherence to contribute to the growth of resilience.
The second strategy suggests to only focus our attention on what can be changed and direct our limited energy to things that we can be grateful for and find happiness in. Although cultivating optimism and positive feelings does help to foster greater resilience, overly ignoring our weaknesses seems like an avoidance of the problem. The NCO112 course highlights the importance of having active coping skills, which is to find different ways to solve the challenge rather than escaping from them. It was found that avoidance coping not only fails to develop resilience, but could also create more stress and anxiety (Arsenault, 2025; Scott,2024). Hence, while wasting too much energy on negativity is bad, it is equally important to not overly withdraw from our challenges. 
The last strategy is a reflective question on whether one’s actions is beneficial or harmful to oneself. This action of reflecting does demonstrate active coping, self-efficacy and cognitive flexibility, but it is important to note that simply deciding to stop the harmful action does not help someone become a resilient person. The journey of growing and recovering emotionally requires more than just removing the source of stress, it has to be paired with other coping mechanisms in order to achieve resilience integration. Some of such coping mechanisms covered in the course would be tapping on social support and religiosity. Both the NCO112 course and additional research has found that religiosity and social support has a positive correlation to strengthening resilience in individuals (Gan et al., 2023).
Overall, Hone’s strategies are accurately aligned to the course content to a large extent. However, by simplifying it into just three strategies, she could not fully cover the complex process for building resilience which sometimes not only depends on individual mindset but also on environmental and support factors.
(c)Reflecting on my experiences, I faced one of the most difficult and draining project work experience which lasted an entire year in JC. I had an extremely demanding, emotionally unstable and inconsistent teacher. I remember one occasion when we had to submit a personal reflection for our report, she already approved some of my work on my first draft which led to me editing only the parts that were not approved before submitting again. To my surprise, when she returned to me for the second time, it was harshly deemed as completely wrong and unacceptable, including the parts that were previously approved. I felt really confused, worthless and mentally tired. I tried to seek my classmates’ advice and questioned on whether I misunderstood her instructions, but even after that I could not figure out what was wrong. Out of desperation, I submitted the exact same draft again. This time, she approved everything and praised it as extremely well done. Dealing with her unpredictable feedbacks and standards drained my energy and took a toll on my self-confidence. At the same time, I had uncooperative groupmates who often do their part last minute and refuse to follow the internal deadlines. For instance, I would send reminders to finish their parts by 23:59 so that I can print out the report for submission before bed. However, they would still miss the deadline, leaving their parts completely untouched. As a result, I would have to wake up extra early to print a 60 pages report for them using my own printer ink. To make matters worse, my teacher would put all the blame on the group leader when we could not submit on time, and nothing was done despite knowing about my groupmates’ attitude. On top of this project, I was facing other challenges in life such as heavy workloads from other subjects, sleep deprivation and a long travelling time to school. Everything left me feeling so stress that I was on the brink of burnout and felt like giving up. At that time, social support was an extremely important factor for me. I would not have survived without relying on a group of friends who listened to my worries and comforted me. They reassured me that things were not my fault and made me feel like I was not alone.
Eventually, I coped by telling myself to not put so much burden and weight on my shoulders. Similar to Hone’s strategies, I realised that some of my actions were harming me. For example, I stopped tolerating unfair requests and told my groupmates to print the report themselves instead. I also focus more on things that I could change by trying to find ways for things to work out. For instance, I realise I could assign work that would better suit their abilities by observing their strengths and working style. Regarding my teacher, I tried to go with the flow and not take things so personally. 
Looking back, it was still a very painful experience but I realised that I was actively demonstrating the qualities mentioned in NCO112 such as active coping, self-efficacy, hardiness and social support, which helped me achieved resilient reintegration. Although I initially felt very frustrated and disappointed, I am glad that I managed to bounce back from that adversity.

The TED talk I have chosen is The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw). The main message of this talk is that pain and suffering can and will happen to anyone, though we do not have to spend our lives wallowing in them forever as there are 3 easily accessible strategies that we can employ to lessen the grief that we are facing. The first strategy is to recognise that suffering is a natural part of life for everyone and that the pain we are experiencing is not unique to us. Realising this prevents us from being stuck in a victim mentality that makes overcoming grief tougher. The second is knowing which areas to put our energy into and looking on the bright side in dark situations. While pain cannot be immediately erased, we can choose to focus our attention on the good left in our lives. The third is actively identifying if our thoughts and actions are benefiting us. By being intentional with our decision-making, we can better control our emotions and choose to do what is best for our well-being. 

This TED talk has many similarities with the topics being covered in this course. Firstly, in the TED talk, the base circumstance that activates resilience is adversity, that can range from many different events that cause a person pain and distress. From there, resilience is the process in which people overcome their negative emotions and push to better their situation. This is similar to the 2 components of resilience covered in this course, which are adversity and positive adaptation (Ong, 2025). Both the TED talk and course material describe adversity as a natural occurrence in life. Secondly, a similarity the TED talk and course material share is that consistent and conscious effort must be put in for resilience to be grown. A strategy in the TED talk was actively choosing to do and think about things that benefit a person’s well-being and steering clear from negativity. Similarly, one of the nine areas associated with resilience is active coping, which includes actively solving problems that bring us down, to uplift ourselves (Ong, 2025). 

The premise of the TED talk is that no one is immune to adversity and hardships, though we can strive to grow from them and be able to protect ourselves from future difficulties. While the TED talk did provide useful insights and tips on how to increase resilience, it still missed out on some notable areas that are contributing factors to resilience growth in different people and situations. 

One example is how the TED talk focuses more on individual strategies and neglected to highlight how vital community support can be in helping people bounce back from hardships. In a study by Dr. Micheal Ungar, it is shown that environmental factors hold much importance in the development of resilience in people. Social connectedness and reliance on others, whether it is for emotional support or for resources, have proven to aid in the ability for people to better recover from hardships (Ungar, 2011). Additionally, social support, one of the areas associated with resilience, also highlights the importance of community in strengthening a person’s resilience, with how community can make stressful situations easier on people through kind words or actions (Ong, 2025). This viewpoint is especially pertinent to people suffering from extreme situations like poverty, where a person alone may not be able to overcome their circumstance. Instead, they would benefit from a supportive community that can provide emotional and tangible support. This differs from the TED talk, which focuses more on how individuals can handle suffering internally, and instead highlights the need for a strong external support system to recover. 

Another example is that not everyone may be capable of processing the thoughts required for the 3 strategies to work, especially those who are facing extreme hardships that affect their cognitive functions. While the tips from the TED talk may be practical for most people, it may be inaccessible to some groups of individuals that are facing more complex issues that cannot be healed through those tips. Long-term exposure to certain negative environments may have permanent effects on a person’s mindset and ability to think flexibly. A study on how continuous economic hardships affect cognitive function in young people shows that when exposed to economic hardships for a long time, the cognitive function may be worsened and the higher the risk of premature aging (Zeki Al Hazzouri et al., 2017). These factors may impair the ability of people to properly self-reflect and conduct the tips from the TED talk, showing that the tips may exclude certain people. In extreme cases like this, the tips may also be ineffective in helping people develop resilience from their suffering due to their simplistic nature. 

Overall, while the strategies from the TED talk may be effective for some types of hardships that people face every day, they may not be suitable for people facing more extreme hardships that have long-term and cause them permanent physical or mental damage.  

My personal experience, relating to resilience, was one I had in secondary school. During my secondary school days, my Co-Curricular Activity (CCA) was choir. I was very passionate about being part of the club, which gave me the desire to serve as a co-president of the club. Subsequently, I tried to prove my worth through actively participating during our practices, aiding my peers in sounding out notes they had trouble producing and contributing to various club related activities like hosting our open house booth. When the executive committee positions were announced, I was disappointed to receive a smaller role of events head. It felt like all my efforts were ignored or simply insufficient, which made me feel deeply dejected. Afterwards, I found myself participating less enthusiastically during practices. Eventually, I managed to let go of my disappointment and regained my interest in singing, though my passion for choir was dimmed. 

The topics covered in this course and the TED talk have helped me better understand my mindset, relating to this experience. Firstly, the course material has taught me that I was lacking in hardiness when faced with my disappointment. I now see that my lack of it made me more susceptible to the pain and stress that came with the disappointment (Ong, 2025). Consequently, I was overwhelmed with the negative emotions of failure which caused my withdrawn behaviour during practice for a period. I now recognise the importance of being hardier. Increased hardiness would have allowed me to focus more on things within my control, like taking charge of club events and doing them well and viewing this experience as a challenge to work harder at contributing to the club, instead of letting it bring me down. Secondly, the TED talk has taught me the importance of regulating my thoughts and emotions through intentionally choosing the habits I act on. When I found myself stressing over why I did not receive the position I wanted, I could have consciously chosen to embrace a more positive mindset. I now recognise the importance of intentional decision-making. I see that actively steering myself away from negative thoughts of the experience could have allowed me to better focus on embracing my given role and move on from the disappointment more quickly and effectively.

TED Talk: How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal 
In her TED talk “How to Make Stress Your Friend”, Kelly McGonigal (Kelly), a health psychologist, challenges the traditional notion that stress is predominantly harmful. Kelly cited a study that illustrated that people who experienced higher levels of stress have a higher mortality rate only when they believed that the stress that they experienced was harmful to them. Conversely, those who viewed stress as a bodily human response to the event or situation, had a lower risk of dying when compared to those with less stress. Kelly elaborated that stress pre-empts the body to prepare for the challenges ahead and this allows the person to increase courage and resilience when it is interpreted positively. Kelly also covered concepts such as stress hormones like oxytocin which promotes social connection and empathy which motivates people to seek human connection and support. To conclude her talk, Kelly stated that stress can transform our physical and emotional experience but only if we were able to change how we view and adapt to the stress we face on a day-on-day basis. This turns stress from a negative response to a positive one which enhances our own performance and improves our connection with friends and families.
Kelly’s TED talk aligns with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). According to the model, stress arises from a perceived imbalance between the demands required from a person and the resources that avails to them. Kelly’s message of viewing stress as a positive physiological response is identical to the primary and secondary appraisal phase in this model. When a person views stressors as a good challenge rather than a threat and they believe they have adequate resources to cope, this experience will lead them to experience eustress instead of distress. Kelly’s TED talk is thus identical to the appraisal phases of Lazarus and Folkman to promote adaptive responses and outcomes.
Kelly’s TED talk also mirrors what was discussed on the concept of eustress and performance. The performance-arousal curve illustrates that when moderate stress is managed effectively, it enhances motivation and a sense of achievement within the individual. Kelly’s claims that stress could increase courage and foster stronger support systems aligns with the idea that stress activates certain physiological responses that are designed to enhance performance. 
The idea of flow which is “an optimal and positive psychological state attained through deep concentration on the task in hand and involving total absorption” (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990) also comes into play. Kelly’s ideas align with what Csikszentmihalyi had presented as when stress is perceived as manageable, the individual may reach a state of “peak performance” where they are in deep focus on their performances and the results positively reflect it. 
However, Kelly’s TED talk simplifies multiple aspects of stress sciences. Chronic stress that is built up over a longer timeframe are results of sustained stressors such as debt, caregiving or long-term illnesses (Birk, 2023). Repeated activation of the stress response takes a toll on the body eventually. Research suggests that chronic stress promotes the formation of artery-clogging deposits and causes brain changes that may contribute to anxiety, depression, and addiction (LeWine, 2024). This signifies that Kelly’s examples focus on short-term stresses that aligns with eustress rather than chronic stress and the failure to differentiate the two stress types could lead to an individual being unable to act on the advice brought up by Kelly. As such, individuals should accept Kelly’s ideas as a complement for other appropriate coping strategies to have an all-rounded approach to tackle the multiple facets of stresses that they face in their lives.
A personal experience of mine which induces stress would be when I play football. Before stepping onto the pitch every match, I will often experience stress while thinking (and sometimes overthinking) about my performance on the day and my failures (misplaced passes, poor decision making) from the past. In the past, I have always seen these feelings as signs of anxiety and self-doubt which had negatively affected how I played and decreases the enjoyment I get from playing football.  However, Kelly’s TED talk and the concepts taught in the course had allowed me to view such situations differently. 
Lazarus and Folkman’s Transactional Model of Stress and Coping states that stress will occur when we perceive that the demand of a situation exceeds the resources (ability and support) that we have to cope. For my case, I used to appraise my football matches as “threatening” situations where I could disappoint my teammates by failing to make a pass or scoring a goal which results in distress. However, I am able to reappraise my stress now to the form of eustress which ignites a motivating energy within me that prepares my body for maximum performance. As I feel my heartbeat accelerating before the whistle goes, I will constantly remind myself that this stress is my body’s signal that it is ready to go and I can trust it to react to every passage of play and stay focused. This is similar to Kelly’s ideas and claims that she mentioned in her TED talk. 
Additionally, instead of trying to suppress and ignore the stress that arises, I could use problem-focused coping strategies to allow me to take control of the resources that avails to me. Such strategies include having 1 on 1 training sessions with my defensive partner to allow both of us to understand the strengths and weaknesses of our respective games. By understanding each other’s weaknesses, we are able to cover for each other when we get the sensing that the other player is going to be exposed during the match. At the same time, I could also apply emotion-focused approach coping. By taking deep breaths and engaging in self-talk, I can take control of my emotions and use that to calm my nerves every time I am feeling stress. Hopefully, these methods could allow me to transform my distress into eustress which allows me to be ready to enjoy the game that I love.
Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of flow resonates deeply within me when I play football. In moments when my team requires the midfield to be composed and collected, I am able to properly enjoy my football as I am able to dictate play from my position and slow and hasten play as I deem fit. Instead of feeling the pressure that the game is centred around how I play my game and who I pass to, I am able to enjoy the moment without feeling external pressure which allows every decision that I make to feel natural and “automatic”. As I read more on the concept of flow, I release now that such moments where I am in the zone was possible as I had been able to use stress positively to my advantage as opposed to seeing it as an obstacle that could hold me back.
Through this reflection, I have learnt that we should not view stress as a negative physiological response but instead, credit should be given to it to properly acknowledge that it is part of who we are and how we respond to the different situations in our lives. Personally, stress is something that I see as a good challenge and is a constant reminder that what we are doing is worth doing and we should continue to enjoy the things that we do even if it brings us temporary discomfort. By combining Kelly’s proposal of shifting one’s mindset and the various concepts by Lazarus and Folkman and Csikszentmihalyi, I am now better equipped to manage the stress that I faced and will face, not just in sports but also in other aspects of my life when I am placed in situations where a huge load of stress could present itself. 
Kelly ended her TED talk with the line: “Go after what it is that creates meaning in your life and then trust yourself to handle the stress that follows”. This is something that I resonate with as I would always choose something that I love, even if it causes me temporary stress and discomfort as opposed to thinking about the what ifs.

Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1990). Flow: The psychology of optimal experience. Harper and Row.

TED Talk chosen:
Stress
How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU)


Speaker Kelly McGonigal conveys the idea of stress being helpful rather than harmful and puts forward the idea of changing how you think about stress can make you healthier. An example she gave was that in a typical stress response, your heart rate goes up and your blood vessels constrict, which is why chronic stress is associated with cardiovascular disease. But in a study, participants who viewed stress response as helpful had their blood vessels relaxed despite a pounding heart rate which resulted in a much healthier cardiovascular profile. She also mentions oxytocin – a neurohormone that helps relax your blood vessels during stress and strengthens your heart and that its physical benefits can be enhanced by human connection to increase resilience. She concludes that pursuing meaning will result in a healthier lifestyle than trying to avoid discomfort, and to trust that your body is able to handle the accompanying stressors.
Stress can be defined as the existence or perception of a threat. The TED talk does align with some topics that was taught in class. In particular, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984) states that eustress and distress results from the existence of stress, combined with a secondary appraisal of whether there are sufficient resources to cope with the threat. In the speaker’s examples, stress is present and if left alone, will by default lead to a perceived lack of resources to cope. However, by introducing human interaction and social connection, they can “distribute” and lessen their stress, and as a result will have a perception of having sufficient resources to cope with their stress. The resulting eustress is a motivating and positive form of stress that can help you to grow and improve.
For this reflection, arousal can be defined as the ratio between stress and the perceived resources available to cope with the stress. According to Yerkes & Dodson (1908), performance is enhanced by moderate levels of arousal, but declines with too little or too much. If there is too little arousal, there is no stress and there is no motivating factor. If there is too much arousal, it means that there is a perception of insufficient resources available to cope with the stress, resulting in distress. This aligns with what the speaker is pushing for, which is to leverage on moderate amounts of arousal to enhance performance through healthy stress levels.
The speaker cited a study which suggests that one's belief about stress alters its impact. There is another study done by Bosshard and Gomez (2024) that found that teaching people to reinterpret stress arousal and to maintain a mindset that stress can enhance performance, can help slightly under pressure, which supports the speaker’s views that reframing how you view stress can help mitigate the effects of distress by turning it into eustress. And personally, I have experienced this as well. Last semester, while I was extremely stressed for an examination, I was able to channel my racing anxiety into quicker thinking by reinterpreting in my own mind that the jitters I was having can enhance my thinking speed and ability. While it could have been a placebo, the effects felt real to me.
In the course materials, we were presented with the two-dimensional coping framework (New & Segerstorm, 2006), and we were taught to lean into approach focused coping as Compas et al. (2001) found that avoidant coping strategies generally leads to poorer outcomes. Although McGonigal’s coping strategy of choice is an emotion-focused approach which is linked to generally better outcomes compared to avoidant coping strategies, Muñoz-Cruz et al. (2024) confirmed that problem-focused coping is more consistently linked to improved outcomes, compared to emotion-focused coping. Moreover, the course materials advise that using both problem and emotion-focused approaches are appropriate, but McGonigal only asserts the latter.
During the course, we learned about the flow state (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990) and how conducive it can be for peak performance by maintaining an optimal amount of stress and arousal. Her concluding statement may seem like she is advocating for having an optimal amount of stress to improve performance, but she does not explicitly address the concept of flow, and the three prerequisites (balance between being challenge and capability, clear goals, immediate feedback) for entering the flow state were also never directly mentioned by her. This omission may lead to an oversimplified understanding, and although her talk promotes embracing stress, it overlooks the fact that unmanaged or poorly directed stress cannot facilitate flow and, on the contrary, disrupt concentration and performance instead. Hence, despite McGonigal’s optimistic views about stress aligning with the eustress concept taught in the course, it conflicts with the concept of flow state, which additionally requires a set of structured environmental and challenge conditions to sustain peak performance, and not just a positive appraisal of stress.
Personally, I have always been chasing the flow state. As a former parkour athlete, I used to tap into the flow state to perform incredible acrobatic feats where the smallest of mistakes could lead to injury. In that state, I felt a complete sense of control and immersion where time seemed to slow down while I was mid-air. And now, as a student aspiring to be a software engineer, I experience a similar sensation when I’m deep into my coding sessions. Hours would easily pass without me noticing, and I feel fully and completely absorbed into the task at hand. Despite having entered the flow state many times, it is only after taking this course that I realised how I am able to enter it.
The course materials states that there are three prerequisites for entering the flow state. The first is to face a challenging situation and to ultimately overcome and accomplish it. In other words, there needs to be a balance between the difficulty and your capability. If the difficulty is way higher than your capability, you will not be able to overcome it and you could give up or feel burnt out at the end. If your capability is way higher than the difficulty, then it would be too easy and you will get bored. An example from my parkour days was when I was learning to front flip. I have never done a front flip before, so the difficulty is high. But the challenge is not insurmountable, as I have already been equipped with the technique necessary to complete a front flip. I already knew how to forward roll, jump, and tuck. And strength wise, I was capable enough too. So my capability was almost matched with the difficulty.
The second is to have a clear goal to be able to inherently strive towards. This can be achieved when one is able to visualise the path to take towards achieving the singular outcome. In the parkour example, my clear goal was to jump, do a front-flip and land on two feet. I already knew and could visualise what the end result was going to be, and I only needed to tweak the details.
The final prerequisite would be the ability to respond to immediate and continuous feedback, in adjusting your actions when conducting a task. This means that you are constantly aware of how well you are doing and can instantly make quick corrections to keep yourself on track to the final goal. In the same parkour example, I am able to immediately sense why I wasn't landing the front flip properly – if my takeoff angle was wrong or if I was untucking too early, which let me correct it immediately on my next attempt.
Something that I found really cool that was mentioned by McGonigal, was the fact that participants who viewed stress response as helpful had their blood vessels relaxed despite a pounding heart rate. This was extremely relatable as a parkour athlete, because we had to maintain a certain level of physical activity, which meant an accelerated heart rate. But at the same time, we had to maintain our composure; to keep our cool, so that we could perform at our best. And although McGonigal did not mention the flow state, I did find her overarching idea that stress can be harnessed aligns with the concept of eustress in achieving the flow state. In my parkour practice, I also realised that the adrenaline from mild stress actually sharpened my focus, enabling me to enter a state of flow.
