Title and Speaker: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Dr Lucy Hone
Link:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw

In her TED Talk, Dr Lucy Hone presents three key strategies practiced by resilient people. Firstly, they accept suffering as an inevitable part of life. This prevents feelings of unfairness, reduces risk of adopting a victim mentality, and counters the “why me” mindset often fuelled by entitlement and social media’s distorted portrayal of perfect lives. Secondly, they consciously direct their attention by realistically appraising situations, focusing on what they can change, and accepting what lies beyond their control. Rather than dismissing negativity, they actively engage in finding ways to also appreciate what is good, a strategy aligned with the psychological concept of benefit finding, directing their attention towards positives as well. Lastly, resilient individuals often ask themselves whether their thoughts and actions are helpful or harmful, enabling them to reclaim control over their lives and navigate challenges with greater strength and adaptability. Adversity does not discriminate, and resilience is accessible to anyone willing to cultivate it.
	
Both the course and the TED Talk conceptualises resilience as a dynamic process, or the outcome of such a process, rather than a fixed personality trait. As Dr Hone explains, “resilience isn't some fixed trait” and instead “requires very ordinary processes” that individuals engage in over time to cultivate their capacity to adapt to adversity. By framing resilience as a dynamic process, it highlights that resilience is developed and maintained through ongoing, deliberate efforts, rather than being an inherent or static trait. More importantly, this perspective demonstrates that resilience is accessible to everyone, since it is not limited to those born with certain psychological traits, rather it can be nurtured through continuous maintenance.

As discussed in the course readings, Fletcher and Sarkar (2013) identify adversity and positive adaptation as two central components of resilience. This parallels Dr Hone’s TED Talk, which highlights the behavioural and psychological strategies resilient individuals employ. Both perspectives acknowledge adversity as a universal, unavoidable aspect of life, and part of resilience. Positive adaptation is illustrated by Dr Hone’s emphasis on consciously focusing attention on what can be controlled, practicing benefit finding, and regularly evaluating whether one’s thoughts and actions are helpful or harmful. These strategies reflect the positive adaptation Fletcher and Sarkar identify as core to resilience, reinforcing that resilience emerges not from avoiding hardship, but from actively engaging with it to promote growth and agency.

Similarly, both the course and the TED Talk emphasises the fundamental role of mindset in shaping how resilient individuals respond to adversity, whereby one’s perception of circumstances is more important than the circumstances itself. Together, they illustrate that resilience arises from a mindful and intentional mental approach, rather than from external events alone. 

However, the course extends the discussion by exploring environmental risk factors that can hinder the development of resilience (Sameroff & Rosenblum, 2006).  It is observed that in such environments, where social support is lacking, children often struggle to adapt positively to adversity. This highlights the importance of social support in facilitating the development of resilience, an aspect not addressed in Dr Hone’s TED Talk.

According to Connor & Davidson (2003), resilience refers to the combination of personal qualities and social resources that positively influence outcomes in the face of adversity. Receiving strong social support from other people can increase resilience to stress, safeguard mental health, and reduce the likelihood of developing trauma-related issues (Ozbay et al., 2007). For example, in the aftermath of the Great East Japan earthquake and tsunami, adults with higher pre-disaster social support were associated with reduced likelihood to develop post-disaster depression among adults, whereas experiences of loneliness corresponded with heightened negative stress responses (Sasaki, 2019).

In contrast, Dr Hone’s framework primarily focuses on personal cognitive strategies rooted in an individualistic approach to resilience, centering on the individual’s internal mindset while overlooking external systemic factors, such as social support, that also influence one’s coping capacity. This neglects the reality that individuals exist within broader social systems, which themselves vary in resilience and in their capacity to facilitate adaptive psychological functioning (Southwick et al., 2016).

Recounting a personal experience related to resilience, I recall my journey of applying to university. The first time I applied, I was rejected, which left me feeling bitter and dejected. The following year, I applied again, only to be rejected once more. The second rejection was even more demoralising than the first, causing me to struggle with intense self-doubt and question my own worth, especially since I had closely tied my self-worth to academic achievements and success. As a result, I felt like a failure and struggled to cope, withdrawing from others, and isolating myself.  My feelings manifested more as self-hatred, where the negative feelings and emotions were internalised. During that period, I was overwhelmed by negative thoughts and allowed myself to succumb to despair. However, the turning point came when I took an honest and reflective look at myself and realised that continuing to wallow in self-pity was more harmful than helpful. I recognised that I had been in denial about the outcome, avoiding the reality of the situation. Understanding that acceptance was necessary, I chose to honestly face the results, embrace them, and shift my focus towards moving forward positively. Thereafter, I reconsidered the meaning of self-worth and success and directed my efforts toward achieving it.

Reflecting on this experience, I recognise that I have demonstrated strategies mentioned by Dr Hone. I consciously redirected my attention by accepting the reality of my university rejection and focused on what I could control in the future, rather than dwelling on an unchangeable outcome. I also critically evaluated my harmful thoughts and emotions, such as the self-hatred I projected onto myself, and chose to adopt a more constructive mindset. These strategies enabled me to reclaim control over my life and demonstrated resilience. In retrospect, I recognised that I could have benefited from seeking support from my friends and family during that period, rather than withdrawing and isolating myself. 

Ultimately, resilience for me involves maintaining an internal locus of control by not allowing emotions to overwhelm me, while consciously choosing thoughts and actions that support emotional balance and positive adaptation in adversity. At the same time, I acknowledge the vital role of social support in reinforcing my capacity to cope with adversity more effectively.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw) 
a)	 Drawing from both empirical research and her own lived experiences, resilience researcher Dr. Lucy Hone presents three cognitive reappraisal strategies anyone can adopt to cope with loss and cultivate resilience (TEDx Talks, 2019). The first strategy is acceptance, where recognising that suffering is an unavoidable part of life. Doing so prevents the chances of individuals feeling unfairly targeted whenever misfortune strikes, reducing their negative affectivity. The second strategy Hone discusses is benefit finding, where resilient individuals can identify the positives of the situation by focusing on the things they can realistically control. The third strategy is regaining control, where individuals pause and reflect to assess if their actions or thoughts are harmful or beneficial. To conclude her talk, Hone emphasises that resilience is not a fixed trait but a mindset that can be learned.   

(b) 	In today’s ever-evolving world, resilience remains a relevant topic as adversity stays a constant in everyone’s lives. In Hone’s TED talk, she uses both her research work and own lived experience with loss to illustrate three strategies of resilience in hopes of inspiring others (TEDx Talks, 2019). With reference to concepts introduced in NCO112, this essay aims to discuss Hone’s approach through the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) and the salient factors of resilience. 
Through the lens of Hone’s approach towards resilience, her three strategies align well with resilient reintegration. Richardon’s (2002) MRR introduces a paradigm that posits that a disruption could pull an individual out of their comfort zone, or homeostasis state, which instigates either four responses: resilient reintegration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss, and dysfunctional reintegration. Being the most ideal outcome out of the four, resilient reintegration is the positive process where an individual successfully adapts and recovers from the disruption with growth and insight that will increase their initial level of homeostasis. Hone’s second and third strategy—benefit finding and reflection—exemplify how resilience can be internalised as a learned mindset rather than an innate trait. By focusing on what can be controlled and intentionally pausing to reflect, individuals can cultivate lasting protective values like gratitude and self-awareness, and meaning-making (Helgeson et al., 2006; Park, 2010). In this way, Hone illustrates resilience as an ongoing process of growth that will enhance subjective well-being and strengthens one’s capacity for future adversity. 
This process of resilient reintegration can be further understood through resilience factors, which act as underlying mechanisms that enable positive adaptation (Kunzler et al., 2020). Hone’s first strategy of acceptance, for instance, fosters a sense of coherence by helping individuals make sense of suffering and sets a foundation for positive growth. It also develops cognitive flexibility and optimism as it encourages individuals to positively reappraise challenging circumstances rather than viewing them as insurmountable. Hone’s second strategy, benefit finding, aligns well with active coping since it encourages individuals to problem solve and actively deal with the situation at hand. Finally, the third strategy, reflection, supports the development of positive emotions by promoting emotional regulation. Collectively, the three strategies Hone proposes shows potential to enhance psychological qualities that can promote resilience. 
However, while Hone’s TED talk effectively distils resilience cultivation into relatable and actionable strategies, her focus on cognitive reappraisal and emotional regulation primarily centres on the individual aspect of resilience building and overlooks the social and environmental dimensions of adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). This is because human responses to adversity are not formed in isolation but depend heavily on the resources and support systems available within one’s community, promoting well-being and lasting resilience (Ozbay et al., 2007; Sippel et al., 2015). From this perspective, resilience depends as much on external supports as it does on internal cognitive reappraisal. 
Ultimately, while Hone succeeds in inspiring individuals to take ownership of their growth, an approach that considers the social and psychological approaches must be acknowledged in support of resilience cultivation. 

c)  	The first personal experience that related to resilience would be my final-year project focusing on dementia care. The project spanned over six months, and was deeply personal to me as both my paternal grandparents suffer from severe dementia. Having to witness their deteriorating condition and the stress brought onto my family had me feeling powerless at times, and motivated me to focus my research on caregivers—a vulnerable group that is often overlooked in Singapore’s healthcare landscape. As a design student, translating insight gathered from both quantitative and qualitative research into a physical space was extremely tough, and had me caught in phases of self-doubt. However, it was through the challenges faced that grew my resilience. 
Watching Hone’s TED talk allowed me to recognise how I had already implemented the three strategies proposed. The first strategy, cognitively reframing that adversity is inevitable, was one I frequently employed whenever unexpected challenges arose. Whether it was the sudden loss of progress due to software malfunctions or scheduling conflicts, I reminded myself that such setbacks were normal and that peers, seniors, and even lecturers experienced similar obstacles. Hone’s second strategy, benefit finding, was also a habit I cultivated throughout the six months of working on the project. The technical and logistical issues I faced encouraged me to strengthen my problem-solving skills and identify positives within each situation. Finally, Hone’s third strategy, assessing whether one’s actions were harmful or beneficial, was another practice I applied. During moments of self-doubt or procrastination, I would pause to take a break or redirect my focus towards another task. This helped me challenge irrational thoughts, regulate my emotions, and regain a more constructive perspective, effectively engaging in cognitively reframing the challenges faced. 
Through the implementation of these strategies, I recognise resilience factors contributing to the process of resilient reintegration taking place, where adversity faced in my final year project led to personal growth, self-awareness and a more resilient mindset. Reflecting through the concepts of resilience introduced in NCO112 deepened my understanding that resilience is not an inherent trait but a dynamic process of continual adjustment and reflection in response to adversity.

MY SELECTED TED TALK:
Resilience: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)


Question (a): In her TED talk, Lucy Hone explores the nature of resilience and provides three keys that enable people to survive and recover from profound trauma. Building upon her academic study and her personal tragedy-the sudden death of her daughter-Hone underscores that resilience is not an innately possessed quality but a set of skills that one can learn. She begins by accepting the fact that suffering is part of life, and respectable people simply accept this truth, feeling no one has victimised them. In contrast to asking “Why me?” they have come to understand that suffering is an experience all human beings go through. It is this acceptance that becomes the fertile ground for the emergence of resilience from which one is able to stop fighting the reality and start thinking effectively about response. 
Hone's second and third strategy dealt with attention regulation and self-reflection. Resilient individuals choose deliberately where they place their attention; they focus only on what is within their power and acknowledge that there are matters outside their sphere of control. They then embark on a conscious pursuit of the positive as a compensatory way of viewing at least some good from bad situations. The mixture of realistic acknowledgment with hopeful expectancy can help dissolve the feeling of helplessness and seed gratitude during periods of sorrow. Finally, she stresses the importance of frequently asking oneself whether a particular thought or action is helping or harming them. This simple but potent question immediately instils a sense of control in individuals and forces them to focus on making the right decisions during dark moments in life. In Hone's talk, she communicates that resilience is about regular, everyday processes that anyone can practice and through which people can live fully with joy while mourning with equal depth.
Question (b): In her TED Talk titled “The Three Secrets of Resilient People,” Dr. Lucy Hone proposes three strategies that she says are the very basis for building resilience: (1) understand that suffering is part of life; (2) focus on what you can control; (3) and choose where you put your attention. The personal tragedy she suffered created a powerful narrative combining real-life experience with lessons to be drawn. Although such ideas are emotionally persuasive and intuitively right, a thorough examination of her point of view through the framework of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2002) and the more current literature on the subject shows that this view, while useful, is an incomplete one and is lacking theoretical rigor in some important aspects.
The central argument in Hone’s talk about resilience is not being a trait, but a set of skills people can learn and practice, is consistent with the core principles behind resilience theory. According to the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, resilience is seen as a dynamic process during which an individual adapts positively in the face of adversity, in turn, shaped by protective factors and reintegration (Richardson, 2002). Hone’s emphasis on agency (for example, deciding where to put one’s focus) supports the concept of “resilient reintegration,” where an individual not only bounces back from stress but becomes strengthened by it. Her idea that “resilient people ask: is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” reflects the metatheory that individuals strive to pursue adaptive strategies in response to disruption.
The TED Talk diverges from the metatheory in a few major respects. Hence, Knowles' model is missing from the systemic and ecological depth given to academic frameworks for resilience. The Metatheory of Resilience emphasises a biopsychosocial approach of taking into account the biological, psychological, and environmental factors involved in adaptation. Hone's suggested strategies are sound within the psychological realm and may work with some individuals, but within the social-ecological realm, they seem to miss some essential interventions that provide resilience, such as community networks, socioeconomic status, or even cultural context (Windle, 2011). To frame resilience from this individualistic standpoint contributes to situating resilience within a mindset that could conceal structural barriers and potentially place unwarranted blame on individuals unable to “bounce back” (Ungar, 2011).
Additional criticisms, of course, are to be found in recent empirical research. For example, Southwick and Charney (2012) stress the neurobiological undertones and adaptive functioning (e.g., flexibility, optimism, and moral compass) that work in the affirmative for a resilient human being. While some of Hone's advice runs parallel with some of these findings (especially cognitive reframing), it has not come to terms with the neuropsychological level or even with the large empirical basis of resilience. Her talk would have been richer if she had considered the role that physiological regulation, such as that mediated by the autonomic nervous system, may play in stress response and the building of resilience, as has already been hypothesised in Porges (2009) Polyvagal Theory.
Yet her TED Talk does translate higher psychological theory into plainly applied advice very well. For public education, where very often the use of academic jargon distances lay audiences, her Talk was extremely important. Her use of narrative, a well-known teaching strategy within psychology (Green, Strange, & Brock, 2002), creates a durable and emotional imprint in the memory of watchers or listeners. From an educational vantage point, the talk affords a meaningful backdrop to formal resilience theory by touching on the affective domain as well as fostering emotional literacy.
In summarising, Dr. Hone’s TED Talk indeed provides a heartfelt, practical view of resilience at the same time disallowing a simplified model for an insufficiently complex construct of resilience as the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency has conceptualised. Her talk is consistent in many ways with the metatheory regarding positive adaptation and agency, but in other ways, falls considerably short with respect to acknowledging ecological, cultural, and systemic factors involved in shaping resilience. In order to foster resilience and to defend it in plural, especially vulnerable populations, a wider framework as opposed to the metatheoretic principles and empirical research needs to exist; whereas in this regard Hone’s talk remains a viable conceptual stepping-stone for individual reflection and public reckoning, it remains sufficient only in the most foundational sense in need of supplementation from an academic view for a fuller coverage.
Question (c): In her TED Talk, “The Three Secrets of Resilient People,” Dr. Lucy Hone talks about what she sees as the three practical strategies central to resilience: recognising suffering as part of life, focusing on what one can control, and consciously choosing where to direct one's attention. Drawing upon personal bereavement, she offers an emotionally evocative yet psychologically anchored account. While the idea seems intuitively correct and does offer valuable guidance, it warrants closer scrutiny-a closer look through the analytical prism of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2002) and the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984) provides for a richer and more nuanced picture of resilience that supports and problematises Hone's overly simplistic framework.
The core premise of Hone’s talk—that resilience is not provided at birth whereas strategies are cognitive-behavioural strategies-would synergise well with the cornerstone theories in resilience. The Metatheory of Resilience describes resilience as a dynamic and recursive process where individuals are disrupted, activate protective factors, and eventually reintegrate into a better-functional or even an enhanced state (Richardson, 2002). This resonates with Hone’s strategies, particularly the focus on attentional control and adaptive cognitive framing, as a form of “resilient reintegration”. As such, the message also aligns with Lazarus and Folkman (1984) in terms of the perspective that one's cognitive appraisal of stressors and the coping strategies they choose have a strong bearing on psychological outcomes.
In my life, I had one unquestionably trying period through which my very core of resilience was tested. I was moving abroad for an international assignment I had worked for years in preparation. Then, just weeks before I was to be on a plane with my bags for the airport, my very best childhood friend was diagnosed with a terminal illness. Grief poured forth from me. As if time had stopped, that heavy silence in the apartment, the phone almost slipping from my tremulous hands as I sat there, tears dripping down my cheeks-the heavy sorrow of impending separation and living with that stark reality-weighed down upon me so deeply. Balancing the excitement and pressure of a new beginning with the sorrow and guilt of leaving someone so dear was a profound internal struggle. I still remember those dark days full of self-doubt and anxiety questioning whether pursuing my dream was selfish in light of such tragedy. But as I wrestled with these dark thoughts, Lucy Hone's TED talk on resilience kept playing in my mind, giving me clues. Her message about acceptance, realistic optimism, and meaning helped me shift my perspective: instead of thinking about resilience as “bouncing back,” I saw it as an ongoing process of adapting and finding meaning in the midst of adversity, integrating grief with growth. After this reframing, I started to look at our impending transition not as a defeat but as a classic example of vulnerable strength.
At the height of this experience, and quite unwittingly, I was undergoing what Lazarus and Folkman (1984) describe as secondary appraisal-the process of evaluating one's resources and options for coping. I began to compartmentalise my time with disciplined intent, using planning apps, breath-work, and social support from a few close friends. When I finally acknowledged that I had no control over the prognosis of my family member, emotion-focused coping kicked in: instead of holding my breath over “what ifs”, I found myself in the here-and-now, supporting where I could. Hone's suggestion to focus on what is within our control struck a chord with me; I discovered her TED Talk much later, and she provided a retroactive validation for the strategies I had been employing all along.
Her concept, “choosing where to focus attention,” gave a name to something I had once only practiced instinctively. I began focusing my attention more intentionally on anything good that had happened with tasks accomplished, no matter how small, rather than catastrophising about what could go wrong. This delineation is paralleled in the approach of Lazarus and Folkman (1984): coping is never a single act but rather an ongoing process of adaptation influenced by appraisal and reappraisal. In hindsight, Hone's talk brilliantly crystallised an essential message: whereas certain aspects of the outer world are beyond our control, the internal orientation to those same circumstances through attentional focus and interpretation is where personal agency begins.
However, Hone’s model is also a bit limited in certain areas. Her methods may empower individuals but can risk oversimplifying the resilience process if they do not adequately consider the structural and social-contextual forces at play. According to the Metatheory of Resilience (Richardson, 2002), resilience stems not solely from internal coping mechanisms but also from external support and opportunities to reintegrate. In my own personal journey, the support of a flexibly minded supervisor and considerate coworkers greatly served as a buffer against stress. This situation showcases what Ungar (2011) characterises as the “social ecology of resilience,” consisting of the interaction between intrapersonal assets and systemic enablers. Without these external accommodations, I doubt that my internal mechanisms would have been sufficient. 
Another critique I would venture is that the narrative that Hone unfolds is definitely situated within a Western inclination that honours individualism, thus perhaps not being able to touch on the realities of collectivist worlds where resilience may also be construed as relational. For instance, many Southeast Asian regimes, including my own Singaporean upbringing, do not always define resilience in terms of individual assertive coping but rather interdependence, duty, and emotional suppression in the interest of making a collective whole happier. Thereby, putting emphasis on internal control, as Hone does, might rub against cultural paradigms that see resilience as either a social or a collective opposition rather than a solitary one (Ungar, 2013).
Still, Hone's TED Talk remains a valuable addition to the field of resilience, particularly in the popularisation of psychological concepts and their application. In turn, this allows for the creation of personal meaning, which is at the heart of resilient reintegration in Richardson's framework and an emotion-focused coping strategy in Lazarus and Folkman's model. Here Hone puts it simply: “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” The heuristic is one that anyone facing hardship can apply quickly. Her framework helped me retrospectively more sharply define an experience that had been understood only at a visceral level. It gave me a scaffold from which to reflect on that cave-like journey of coping in a more structured, psychologically coherent way. 
To conclude, Dr. Lucy Hone's TED Talk gives some useful tools for building resilience, but it presents only one small piece of a much bigger, very complex psychological construct. The stress and recovery experiences in my own life underline that real resilience emerges from a dynamic negotiation between internal coping abilities and external supports and is ideally understood through an integrative model such as Richardson's Metatheory and Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model. The applicability of Hone's insights is maximised when they serve as a springboard for deeper exploration, thus assisting a person in grounding their struggle and pertinent responses within a broader, evidenced framework.

How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc) 
In her TED Talk, Nina Nesdoly posits three ways to relieve stress in everyday life and at the workplace. Firstly, let tension out, which can be achieved in various forms such as physical activity, exercising creativity, or socialisation. The focus of this technique is to let something out of your body such as sweat, thoughts, or spoken words. We are then supposed to feel relief if done correctly, such as the alleviation of tension in our necks. Secondly, limit information in, the human brain processes a lot of information daily and receiving certain forms of information can add stress. Therefore, effective stress-relieving breaks require focus on activities that prevent receiving additional information. Lastly, lower the barrier to entry, which is the idea that stress relief activities come in a spectrum of intensity so one can incorporate breaks in their schedule with flexibility. For example, if you feel stress on a particular day at work, you can simply take a ten minute break instantly, instead of waiting for the end of work to go for a jog.
With this summary in mind, similarities between the three coping strategies and the course content can be derived. But before further analysis, one must first understand what is stress and coping to appreciate the nuances of the TED Talk and course content. According to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984), stress is a mental strain that an individual experiences when they lack resources to cope with demands. And the act of coping involves cognitive and behavioural efforts to manage stressors (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).
One alignment between the TED Talk and course content is that letting tension out can be interpreted as emotion focused coping – a determinant of coping strategies in Nes and Segerstrom’s (2006) two-dimensional coping framework. This form of coping entails emotional responses to stress which is what letting tension out focuses on. However, I notice that letting tension out is not intrinsically approach or avoidant focused – approach coping being the active seeking of remedy to a stressor and avoidant coping being the passive act of avoiding the situation (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). After a person takes a break to let tension out, a person can choose to face their stressors or run from it, which would result in different cascading effects. This highlights the importance of the self in stress management, one may successfully manage external sources of stress, but stress can also come from the individual if one proceeds incorrectly. In Fritz et al. (2013), different types of work breaks like vacations, weekends, evenings after work, and short breaks at work, have all been found to have positive effects on wellbeing but they can also be negative experiences if not exercised correctly by the individual. This relates to the second point by Nina Nesdoly in her TED Talk, where ideal coping strategies should limit information in.
The positive effects of limiting information could be explained using the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, where it revolves around the balance of cognitive resources and demands. Logically speaking, if one is already experiencing stress from imbalance, then one should at least stop the influx of demands to prevent further imbalance. Other studies have also supported limiting information albeit in different contexts. For example, in a study on a digital workplace where employees are constantly working with information, Marsh et al. (2024) found that information overload and the fear of missing out significantly affected workplace stress. The fear of missing out was the greatest risk factor for mental health as employees constantly seek information for job performance (Marsh et al., 2024). When this pursuit for information outweighs their resources to cope, it eventually leads to stress. An extension of this study could test the effects of limiting information consumption by employees. Nina Nesdoly also mentioned avoiding the use of social media and Li et al. (2024) validates this strategy with their findings that one can experience information overload through social media due to the processing of various information and result in social media fatigue. While the relationship between social media fatigue and stress was not specifically studied, the study did find an elevation in anxiety and overexertion of cognitive energy. These findings are relevant as anxiety and stress have neurobiological links in that acute stress can generate state anxiety response, amongst various relationships between the two (Daviu et al., 2019).
Nina Nesdoly’s final point on lowering the barrier to entry was to me the most important and thus makes for a fitting conclusion to her TED Talk. The previous discussions helped address the why and how to cope with stress, but this final point addresses the where and when. It helped me perceive stress coping as a form of emergency response, where you should administer it as soon as possible with whatever resources you have on hand – if you do not have much, so be it and do it anyways, if you have a lot, good for you and give yourself a nice long break.
Having learnt the underpinnings of stress and coping strategies, my enrolment in this module seemed right on time as my last significantly stressful episode occurred in the examination period of April. I had three exams to prepare for, which was by far the most I had to face in my academic journey in SUSS. And two of those tests were back-to-back, this was a concern of mine with regards to memory retention as I must now study for two modules concurrently, possibly mixing up their content during the exams. During my revision, I was also guilty of procrastinating and admittedly, I could have revised more. While the first test was manageable, the back-to-back tests were stressful as I only had little more than a week to revise for both. Eventually, I could not sleep well before the tests as I was worried about my performance and struggled to recall lesson content during the tests.
Additionally, as appointed by the school, I had to clear my work attachment requirement in the upcoming semester so I was busy applying, interviewing, and worrying about the applications throughout the month.
Reflecting on that month, I could have minimised the amount of stress I faced by cutting away distractions. One major source of stress I faced was from the imbalance of content I had to study and the lack of time to study everything. By procrastinating, I further reduce my resources to cope (time) and create a larger imbalance – eventually causing me insomnia the night before my tests as I knew I did not study enough and worry about my performance. If I was fully focused but did not study finish in time, at least I had more time to cope than to study with distractions, resulting in lesser stress.
On a day-to-day basis during that period, my breaks from studying consisted of mealtimes or browsing social media as short breaks. However, these social media breaks would go from an initially planned five minutes to thirty minutes or even an hour. Looking back, browsing social media did not help in stress relief and instead I dread studying when I stop browsing, Nina Nesdoly helped me realised that was because I was not destressed and therefore not willing to face more obvious sources of stress.
As of writing this paper, I have received my results indicating that I have passed all my tests and have also secured an internship, causing me great relief. I cannot help but think that I got lucky this time as the quality of my answers during the tests was, at least to my judgement, inadequate. I had trouble sleeping the night before the results were released and I would not have been surprised if I failed my tests. Moving forward, having been through the lesson content and the TED Talk, I would like to avoid this harrowing experience by maximising my resources to cope in any stressful situation and find a stress-relieving activity that works for me, keeping in mind the three keys that Nina Nesdoly have taught. Whenever I am in a stressful situation, I will identify what constitutes as coping resources in that context, then actively safeguard and monitor how stressed I feel. Additionally, I would take short and effective breaks as soon as I can and actively avoid social media or my phone altogether.

a) Summary of the TED Talk
In her TED Talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal argues that stress is not inherently harmful and argues that our mindset significantly influences its impact on our health. She cites a study that tracked 30,000 adults over eight years, revealing that those who experienced high levels of stress and believed it was harmful had a 43% higher risk of death. McGonigal uses this to argue that seeing stress as bodily signs of readiness, not danger, can lead to healthier physical reactions and more resilience. McGonigal also highlights oxytocin, a stress-related hormone that promotes social connection and resilience. Overall, McGonigal encourages viewing stress as a natural, helpful response to life’s challenges, fostering greater well-being.
b) Evaluation of the TED Talk
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk, “How to Make Stress Your Friend,” aligns closely with key psychological concepts from NCO112. Her central proposition echoes the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping framework by Lazarus and Folkman (Eysenck, 1985), which conceptualizes stress responses into two categories: primary and secondary appraisals. McGonigal’s focus on reshaping how we perceive stress aligns with the primary appraisal stage, where individuals assess whether a situation is threatening, challenging, or harmless. By promoting a healthier mindset toward stress, McGonigal’s encourages a more adaptive interpretation that enhances perceived control and supports effective coping in the secondary appraisal phase, thereby improving overall well-being. Her approach also reflects the emotion-focused strategies within the Coping Strategy Matrix discussed in Seminar 2. This is further supported by a meta-analysis by Nes and Segerstrom, which found a correlation between dispositional optimism and approach-oriented coping, suggesting that individuals with a more optimistic outlook in life are likely to manage stress constructively rather than avoid or suppress it. (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).
From a physiological perspective, McGonigal explains that positively reinterpreting stress responses can lead to healthier bodily states. She highlights research showing individuals who interpret stress responses – such as a pounding heart and rapid breathing – as helpful tend to exhibit improved cardiovascular patterns, such as the dilation of blood vessels. Similarly, another study by Pascoe et al. (2019) found that students with negative perceptions of stress and poor coping strategies were more likely to experience adverse health effects, including elevated blood pressure and a weakened immune system (Pascoe et al., 2019).
While McGonigal presents a compelling and evidence-based narrative, it is not without limitations. She cites a study estimating that 182,000 Americans deaths resulted from believing that stress was harmful. While this claim is attention-grabbing, it is based on correlational data, yet framed in her presentation as causal, demonstrating a classic example of the correlation-causation fallacy. In reality, chronic stress is rarely determined by mindset alone, but by complex factors such as socioeconomic conditions and systemic issues (Slavich, 2016), which were not adequately addressed by McGonigal. By overlooking broader social determinants, McGonigal risks oversimplifying the causes of stress and implies that mindset alone can resolve deeply rooted or systemic challenges.
The second area of contention lies in the assumption that mindset-based strategies are effective across all stress contexts. While McGonigal’s approach may benefit those facing short-term or manageable stress, it overlooks those facing persistent pressure, especially those raised in chronically adverse environments. Over time, prolonged psychological stress can lead to dysregulated stress systems, limiting one’s ability to benefit from cognitive reframing (Repetti et al., 2002). This highlights that positive thinking alone is often insufficient, and structural solutions are necessary alongside these individual-level strategies.
Overall, Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk offers a valuable perspective of stress, encouraging individuals to reframe their perceptions of stress as a catalyst for self-resilience and growth. While McGonigal presents an unorthodox narrative that challenges traditional beliefs, her approach aligns with the psychological frameworks taught in NCO112 and is supported by empirical evidence on the effectiveness of adaptive, approach-oriented coping strategies on stress. However, her message falls short of addressing the complexities of chronic or systemic stressors, where psychological agency alone may be insufficient to overcome. To effectively address stress, mindset-based interventions must be part of a holistic approach that includes policies targeting socioeconomic and structural factors. This empowers individuals not just to cope, but to thrive in environments that support lasting mental and physical well-being.
c) Personal Reflection
As someone who recognizes having a relatively low stress tolerance, I often struggle to maintain emotional equilibrium when faced with academic deadlines, social obligations and work-related pressures. My typical physiological responses – such as heart palpitations, rapid breathing and a tensed body – were always seen as signs of personal inadequacy or a malfunctioning nervous system. I developed a negative narration about myself, which reinforced a self-perpetuating belief that only intensified my stress responses.
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk challenged this narrative, offering a space for introspection where I began rethinking the meaning I assigned to these bodily reactions. I began to see them as signs of engagement, my body’s way of preparing me to rise to the occasion, rather than indications of dysfunction. This shift marked a turning point in how I approached high-pressure situations, moving from a mindset of avoidance to embracing stress as an opportunity for me to tap into inner resilience and develop greater self-efficacy.
Reflecting on McGonigal’s talk and the concepts taught in NCO112, I realized many of the strategies that I use to manage stress – such as meditation, short walks, diaphragmatic breathing techniques – were forms of emotion-focused coping. However, I had not adjusted my primary appraisal of the stressor. According to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, my habit of framing stressors as threats constantly triggered my flight-or-fight response. This helped me understand why my nervous system was always on edge. Without reframing them at the primary appraisal stage, my strategies were merely short-term band aids, offering only momentary relief.
This shift in appraisal aligns with the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, which outlines how individuals respond to adversity through varying forms of reintegration (Richardson, 2002). My past stress responses reflected homeostatic reintegration, where my coping strategies focused primarily on restoring emotional balance, without fostering meaningful growth. McGonigal’s reframing of stress offered a roadmap towards resilient reintegration, where adversities in life can be seen as opportunities towards personal development rather than dysfunction.
Nonetheless, while McGonigal’s TED Talk was empowering, it also made me realize that lasting change requires broader systemic and contextual support beyond individual mindset shifts. I believe that truly addressing stress requires a holistic approach, one that combines approach-oriented coping strategies with collective efforts to create supportive environments, reduce structural stressors, and foster long-term well-being.

(a) Summary of TED Talk 
In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk on “How to Relieve Stress when You’re Overwhelmed” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), she highlighted that relieving stress can be challenging when overwhelmed as it may seem like another task to complete. To address this challenge, she emphasised three keys to stress relief. The first strategy is to let tension out of one’s body through physical activities, such as meditation or exercise, lowering cortisol levels. The second strategy is to limit information when feeling overwhelmed by taking breaks from constant input and allowing the brain to rest or engage in calming activities. The third strategy is having a low barrier to entry by selecting accessible and low-effort activities to encourage participation. By incorporating these strategies into daily life and work, individuals would experience reduced stress levels, increased energy, prevent burnout, and improved work productivity. 

(b) Alignment and Critique of TED Talk with Course Content on Stress and Coping
In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, she talked about stress and its negative effects on the body. Stress is defined as a state of “mental or emotional tension or strain” (Collins English Dictionary, 2023). First, she highlighted her personal experience of stress which arose from high coursework demands that exceeded the insufficient time and energy needed to complete them. Similarly, the concept of stress was discussed in the Transactional Model (“Model”) of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) in NCO112 where it arises from an imbalance between the demands that an individual faces and the resources needed to cope with it (Ong, 2025). Additionally, Nesdoly discussed the negative effects of stress by presenting the results of a longitudinal study showing how continuous work without breaks can lead to stress accumulation, exhaustion, and reduced work productivity. These effects were also covered in the Model where negative stress can be detrimental to mental health. While Nesdoly highlighted the negative form of stress whereby there is an imbalance between demands and resources needed to cope with the stressful situation resulting in detrimental effects, her content did not cover eustress which is a positive outcome that can arise from a potentially stressful situation as covered in the Model. Eustress is a positive form of stress that helps individuals to achieve peak performance and promotes growth (Ong, 2025). To achieve eustress, the Model states that individuals must perceive that they have sufficient resources, such as adopting adaptive coping strategies, to better cope with the stressful situation for improved well-being.

In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, she emphasises three keys to stress relief when overwhelmed, which involves letting tension out, limiting information in, and having a low barrier to entry. Nesdoly provided an example of how overwhelmed individuals could relieve stress by choosing an enjoyable activity that requires little effort and time, such as meditation or journaling, as it would increase the likelihood of engaging in it and alleviate stress levels. Similarly, these keys are aligned with Nes and Segerstrom’s (2006) Two-dimensional Coping Framework (“Framework”) discussed in NCO112, specifically emotion-focused approach coping strategies, which involves individuals actively trying to improve their emotional responses to the stressful situation (Ong, 2025). While Nesdoly highlighted emotion-focused approach coping strategies for immediate stress relief, these keys do not address the root causes of stress. In contrast, the Framework considers both emotion-focused and problem-focused approach coping strategies for effective long-term stress management and improved holistic well-being. By utilising problem-focused approach coping, individuals can find solutions and address the root causes of their stress to prevent reaching the distress stage. For example, students could prepare for their examinations earlier to avoid last minute revision, reducing feelings of stress, overwhelm, and anxiety. This helps them to manage stress more effectively as they have the time and energy to cope with exam demands, thus reducing the likelihood of needing immediate stress relief from feeling overwhelmed. Similar to the Framework, George Engel’s (1977) Biopsychosocial Model posits that well-being is the combined influences of biological, psychological, and social factors, suggesting that stress can lead to poorer mental and physical outcomes. To effectively reduce stress, individuals take holistic approach to address emotion-focused (psychological) and problem-focused (social) coping strategies.

(c) Reflections and Summary 
The previous semester was stressful as I struggled to balance part-time tutoring commitments on top of demanding coursework. During the coursework submission period, I was nowhere close to completing assignments that had tight and even overlapping deadlines. I desperately needed more time to focus and complete them. However, due to my tutoring commitments, my study sessions were constantly disrupted as I had to pause and provide tuition. Furthermore, internal pressures such as my poor time management, procrastination, high self-expectations for academic excellence, and perfectionist tendencies resulted in additional stress. As deadlines caved in, I felt increasingly stressed by the overwhelming workload, while needing to maintain tutoring obligations. To have more time to complete my assignments, I indulged in quick social media breaks and neglected proper rest leading to prolonged stress and exhaustion. 

The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) covered in NCO112 highlights that stress is a product of the imbalance between the demands that an individual faces and the perceived resources to cope. From the model, I learned that I was stressed due to an imbalance between high coursework demands and perceived insufficient time and energy needed to cope with it. Learning from that experience, I realised that my maladaptive coping strategies of neglecting proper rest to obtain extra time for coursework completion were ineffective as it only resulted in poor physical and mental health. 

Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk addressed the challenge of relieving stress when overwhelmed by emphasising three keys to stress relief which can be incorporated into daily routines. These keys involve letting tension out through physical activities, limiting information by taking intentional breaks from excessive information by allowing the brain to rest and immersing in stress-relieving activities, and having a low barrier to entry by choosing activities that are accessible and attainable, encouraging participation as it requires low effort and time. Reflecting on my experience, it was challenging to relieve stress and take breaks during my hectic coursework submission period due to insufficient time and lack of energy. Furthermore, I lacked knowledge on effective stress management especially when overwhelmed, where I pushed through the stress without proper breaks. 

Moving forward, I would utilise Nesdoly’s three keys of stress relief. Instead of taking social media breaks, I would disengage from work and take an intentional ten-minute stroll around my neighbourhood which relieves stress, reduce information input, and increase focus levels. While these are short-term practical strategies, I would also adopt Nes and Segerstrom (2006)’s Two-dimensional Coping Framework, specifically approach coping, which is defined as “an active form of coping that seeks to improve the situation that the person is in and reduce the negative impact of the stressor” to effectively cope with stress from a long-term view. There are two types of approach coping. First, problem-focused approach coping aims to problem solve, like working on coursework earlier, breaking down tasks into smaller parts, and discussing tuition cancellations with parents to reduce unnecessary last-minute stress. Secondly, emotion-focused coping aims to regulate emotional reactions, like talking to a friend about my stress for emotional support. By adopting these adaptive coping strategies, I would have sufficient time, more energy, and sustained motivation to cope with future work demands.

TED talk selected: What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience 
Speaker:  Charles Hunt
YouTube link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg 
In this Ted Talk, the speaker, Charles Hunt shared about his own experience about trauma. The trauma included having a drug addict as his mother and his father being a pimp. While having not so desirable family background and un-ending trauma experiences over the course of his lifetime, he was able to grow strong mentally and be the successful person he is now, holding a ‘Bachelor of Science in Business Administration (Purchasing & Materials Management and New & Small Business Ventures) from California State University, Hayward (East Bay); a Master of Science in Financial Analysis from Portland State University; and also completed the Cornell Certified Diversity Professional (CCDP) program at Cornell University.’ (Winters Group, n.d.). In the TED talk, he also shared ways and perspectives that helped him overcome the traumas. For example, he shared about how it was perfectly fine with how if someone ‘was a victim but not being a victim’, suggesting that one way to deal with adversities was to choose to focus on the future and what can be changed instead of immersing yourself in past troubles. Also, another way to overcome challenges is to ask for help, through partnerships.
According to the APA Dictionary of Psychology, resilience is defined as the “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA,2020). Hunt’s experience mirrors this definition. From youth, he encountered advertises such as undesirable family background and losing his loved ones. However, he was able to adapt to those situations and not let it drag him down by seeking support from others and focusing on step-by-step improvements.
We also learn in this course, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2022). In this theory, one starts at the stage of Homeostasis, which is the comfort zone for most, and a disruption may happen, which is a stressor or a difficult life event. Eventually, there can be 4 different outcomes: Resilient Integration, Homeostatic Reintegration, Reintegration
with Loss, Dysfunctional Reintegration. Firstly, resilient integration is the ideal outcome when one grows stronger where they have acquired new skillsets and strength and improve their situation beyond what it was originally. Secondly, homeostatic reintegration is where, while the disruption does not carry about repercussions, the individual does not gain much from it either. Thirdly, reintegration with loss happens when the individual returns to homeostasis, albeit with certain permanent damage to their lives. For example, the trauma may cause one to lose confidence in their own abilities and thus become withdrawn. Lastly, dysfunctional reintegration, which is the worst outcome where the individual does not successfully cope and adopt harmful behaviours or habits such as drug abuse, alcoholic tendencies, etc. Drawing parallel to Hunt, we can see two different outcomes when adversities happen. Hunt, facing all these undesirable backgrounds was able to reach resilient integration where he was able to move out of that environment and becoming an inspiring figure for many. However, we can also see dysfunctional reintegration in the case of his parents. Hunt’s parents, likely faced certain traumas previously, resorted to substance abuse which led to them landing in prison. More specifically, Hunt’s mother created an even worse situation where her family was thrown out of the social initiative due to the discovery of her drug abuse. Hunt’s father also faced a bad situation where he was jumped in prison and died from that without being able to see his son before his passing. Hence, we can observe that while one may face disruptions in their lives, it is important to choose the way we cope with it as it may lead to differing outcomes.
However, while Hunt’s TED talk is motivating and empowering as he was able to succeed despite all those traumata, it may undermine the importance of environmental risk factors in cultivating resilience. Sameroff and Rosenblum (2006) found that economic hardship, antisocial peers, poor parenting, and living in low-resource communities are environmental risk factors which stifle the development of resilience in children. While Hunt was able to break out of the poverty cycle through his mental resilience, many others don’t. Without the proper guidance and necessary support, it is highly likely for one to find it more comfortable to succumb to the temptations of settling into such situations and not finding ways to improve. From research, it is concluded that ‘poverty and income inequality are each associated with violent crime’ where ‘homicide and assault may be more closely associated with poverty or income inequality than are rape and robbery.’ (Hsieh & Pugh, 1993) Hence, while it is possible for one to overlook their hard natural circumstances, these circumstances often break individual, causing them to adopt extreme ways to cope with the stress.
From personal experience, there are many times where I face problems, often sudden and unpredictable. However, there was one incident that struck my mind when I first see this assignment. For context, I was always deemed and viewed as one of the ‘smarter’ one in class, someone who only needs to read the textbook 30 minutes before the test to ace the test, someone who would not face troubles in his studies. In primary school and secondary school, this was often the case. I was what many called, a ‘genius’. Naturally, this cultivated a sense of pride in me, causing me to have an extremely bad study habit where I do not engage in active revision. After all, why revise 1 week before the test when I can do it the night before and still ace? This situation continued for both PSLE and ‘O’ Levels where I achieved results many others, who have been putting in efforts, dreamed of. Hence, I brought this habit into Junior College (JC). However, JC is a whole other ball game compared to primary and secondary school. Revision the night before was no longer sufficient. Not listening in class was detrimental. Minimal efforts were costly. Before long, I realised every lecture was just me going into class and listening to my teachers speaking in alien. Going for test was a torture, the papers was filled with words that, while separated I could recognise, combining them made me completely clueless. Despite all that, I still managed to scrap by all the test and still managed to pass papers that others could not. The balloon of ego slowly expanded, launching me into the deep black hole of false security. Well, as all story needs an end and life is not a fairy tale, my balloon popped. This came during the release of the ‘A’ Level results. On the certificate, I could only see ‘C’s and ‘D’s. Academically, this was one of the biggest setbacks I encountered. Me? The mighty genius? The feeling of despair and upset was overwhelming. How am I going to go into a local university? While I thought this was the end of my life, I was lucky. I had a group of friends that was there for me, ready to continue the journey with me. The same people I thought lightly of when they were putting in the hours revising was the same people who encouraged me in this dark time. Eventually, after much encouragement by my friends and advice given by my family, I decided to retake my ‘A’ Levels. While the journey to retake my A levels was filled with hardships and obstacles that will take up another whole 5 page, I was able to triumph this time with no credits to myself but to everyone that was with me. Hence, through this experience, I learnt that while it is inevitable to make mistakes and have a giant trip in life, it is important to find out ways to get around the obstacle. It can be as simple as taking a small break when things get chaotic to asking for help from trusted ones. What matters is, always take action. Afterall, the problem and trauma would not solve itself, would it?

Youtube Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc 
Title: How to Relieve Stress when You’re Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
Speaker of the TED talk: Nina Nesdoly

(a) The video encapsulates three strategies to relieve stress in emotionally charged situations. Strategy one focuses on alleviating tension through physical activities. For instance, when  individuals journal, they can sense the stress being released from their bodies through words. Hence, they can assuage their stressful emotions and cultivate a positive mindset. The second strategy emphasises the importance of resting one’s mind between tasks. It is suboptimal to engage in information processing activities during breaks, as the brain fails to rejuvenate. For instance, it is not ideal for individuals to listen to a professional development podcast during their breaks at work. Nina encourages individuals to engage in calming practices like meditation to release stress during breaks. The third strategy argues against the slogan, ‘work now play later’. Individuals can engage in dopamine inducing activities such as doodling, instead of continuing the task with overwhelming emotions. Therefore, individuals can revitalise themselves with the energy to complete their tasks efficiently. 
(b) 	The video introduced three strategies on relieving stress by focusing on the overwhelming emotions. In the following paragraphs, I will present my observations regarding the relevance of the video with my course materials and the effectiveness of the strategies.
            The video correlates to a section on stress in the course materials. Nina introduced three stress relieving strategies which centres around emotion focused coping techniques. Similarly, the study guide explains the transactional model of stress and coping by Lazarus and Folkman(Ong, 2025). However, the video lacked substantial information about the concept of stress. For instance, the course materials cover a greater scope such as problem focused, emotion focused, approach and avoidance coping. Moreover, it emphasises how stress can be managed to reach a flow state for optimal performance (Ong, 2025). 
Strategy one proved to be beneficial amongst the other techniques, based on other research conducted. According to Schultchen et. al. (2019), their research proved that physical activity reduces stress. This is because dopamine, serotonin and endorphin hormones are secreted which account for mood regulation. Therefore, there is substantial evidence to support Nina's strategy whereby engaging in physical activities reduces stress and redirects negative emotions. 
However, I made three critical observations regarding the video and I will share my explanation hereafter. Firstly, Nina’s strategies do not cater to a wide spectrum of her viewers. Her techniques only benefit individuals who are stressed while completing a task, which can be observed through her examples. It does not benefit individuals who are suffering from other forms of stress such as episodic acute stress, chronic stress and psychological stress (Kapur, 2021). Therefore, these individuals would not relate to the video, and would deem the strategies unsuitable for their stressful situations. Secondly, the video showcased three strategies which support emotion focused coping techniques, but failed to incorporate any problem focused and approach focused coping strategies. Since the video title mentions ‘overwhelmed’, Nina focuses on intense emotions instead of the situation being the reason for such feeling. By introducing problem focused coping techniques, individuals will understand that they can cope with stress by focusing on cultivating positive emotions or the root cause of the situation. Otherwise, Nina could introduce approach coping techniques which aim to target the root of the problem and manage the negative emotions (Ong, 2025). Lastly, Nina failed to mention the possible implications if strategy three is not utilised strategically. For instance, if an individual decides to engage in social activities each time they face stress, they would feel a sense of dopamine and it alleviates their tension (Samuel Centre for Social Connectedness, 2017). Thus, they would begin their task with a fully rejuvenated state of being while utilising the refound energy to focus. However, this has the potential to be an avoidant coping mechanism as they would constantly crave the sense of pleasure. Individuals would choose to escape from their stressful duties which eventually leads to procrastination. In due time their stress levels are bound to accelerate, further inducing overwhelming emotions. Nina should address the possible implications of the strategy and ways to channel stress into a motivating factor. 
In conclusion, the strategies appear easy to follow but upon closer observation, it is not informative and lacks depth for individuals to understand stress. Therefore, the strategies are not highly effective for individuals to follow to reduce their stress in overwhelming situations.
(c) 	After obtaining my A levels certificate, I applied to all the autonomous universities. However, I was faced with multiple rejection letters. It was one of the most stressful periods in my life as I believed that I was a disappointment to my parents. It felt as though I had lost my sense of direction in life. I was stressed as I searched for alternative university options which were suitable for me. I isolated myself from my friends to avoid feeling embarrassed and a sense of inferiority amongst them. Fortunately, a family friend introduced me to SUSS part time university and motivated me to pursue this path. I found a full time job as an assistant preschool teacher and applied to SUSS with a successful application outcome. Eventually, I was able to redirect my life. However, I would have been able to manage my distress with the strategies mentioned in the Ted Talk video and course materials.
	Nina introduced a strategy which encouraged individuals to release their stress through physical actions. This would have been a healthy coping mechanism to release my overwhelming emotions, pertaining to my experience. I enjoy acrylic and watercolour painting, but failed to utilise that as a coping technique to de-stress. For instance, I could play calming music and let my brush flow with different colours on the canvas. It could simply be splashes of red or black paint to reflect my stress. It is not necessary to paint with a reference as that would defeat the purpose of expressing my inner emotions. This would have provided me an avenue to release my stress and reframe my mindset regarding the situation (Wang & Abdullah, 2024). I resonate with strategy one introduced in the video as it would have been an ideal emotion focused coping mechanism, rather than my initial avoidant coping.
The course explains the fundamental concept of stress by introducing the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman. It explains that stress derives when one’s expectations are not met due to the lack of capabilities one possesses (Ong, 2025). The course made me understand the reason for my distress. I was stressed as my expectations of pursuing a  degree at an autonomous university failed, because I was unable to attain remarkable A level results. Furthermore, the course made me realise that I should have used emotion focused, problem focused or approach coping. I would have been able to manage my negative emotions and navigate the root cause of my stress, respectively. In my perspective, both the sessions of the study guide on stress and managing expectations should be read conjointly as it complements each other. When an individual sets highly unrealistic expectations, they are bound to face disappointments when they do not attain it. To reinforce this idea, Kao (2024) highlighted that stress derives from having high expectations. 
	The course and Ted Talk video provided me with a deeper understanding of the stressful situation I faced, while searching for a university path. I realised that my high expectations were the reason I faced such tensions and negative emotions. Henceforth, I know that I have to set SMART goals and consider my capabilities to avoid setting unattainable expectations. This would significantly protect my mind and body from stress.

column2:
Kelly McGonigal talked about how perceiving stress positively can improve our wellbeing. She cited a study revealing that individuals who experienced high stress but did not view it as harmful had lower risk of dying than those who perceived stress negatively. Believing that stress is detrimental can be more harmful than the stress itself. She also stated how our body’s reaction changes as we change our view on stress. For example, our blood vessels remain relaxed during stress when we view stress as helpful, which is healthier for our cardiovascular system. When going through stress Oxytocin is released, a hormone that encourages social bonding and support seeking behaviour. Oxytocin helps protect our hearts too, by reducing inflammation and aiding in heart cell regeneration. McGonigal mentioned that individuals who spent time helping others show no stress-related increase in dying, highlighting the protective effect of social support. She also emphasises that pursuing meaningful activities is beneficial for health. She advices that choosing a path that aligns with one’s values and trusting oneself to handle the associated stress leads to better outcomes than avoiding stress altogether. 
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk connects well with the ideas covered in NCO112, especially the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984). This model says that stress doesn’t just come from what happens to us, it depends on how we see the situation. First, we ask ourselves if the situation is a threat (primary appraisal), and then we ask if we have what we need to handle it (secondary appraisal). In her talk, McGonigal encourages us to change how we think about stress, like seeing a fast heartbeat not as panic, but as our body preparing us to cope. This idea matches what we’ve learned in class about reframing our thoughts (cognitive reappraisal) to help us feel less overwhelmed.
She also talks about how stress can be a good thing, which relates to the difference between eustress (positive stress) and distress (negative stress). McGonigal shares research showing that people who think stress is helpful actually live longer, even if they go through a lot of it. This connects with the coping strategies we’ve studied, especially approach based and emotion focused coping. When McGonigal says we should face stress and talk to others, she’s describing the kind of healthy coping we’ve learned about in this course.
However, while her message is uplifting, it may come across as too simple for real life problems. Changing your mindset is helpful, but not always enough, especially if someone is facing long term stress like financial problems, family issues, or illness. For example, Pascoe et al. (2020) found that students dealing with long-term school stress often experience anxiety, poor sleep, and low grades even if they try to stay positive. In the same way, Colligan and Higgins (2006) found that stress at work can cause burnout and people missing work which these are not something that mindset alone can fix.
Another important point comes from Robert Sapolsky (2004), who studied stress in animals. He found that long term stress can harm the body, weaken the immune system, and even damage the brain. And these effects happened no matter how the animals “thought” about the stress. This shows that while changing how we think is helpful, it’s not enough on its own. People also need real life help, like support at work, mental health services, and fairer systems.
In conclusion, McGonigal’s TED Talk shared many useful ideas that match what we’ve learned in NCO112. Her focus on mindset and support is backed by theory and research. But to truly handle stress in a healthy way, we need both a positive mindset and changes in the systems around us. Reframing stress is a good solution but it is not the complete solution.
There were many moments in my life where I experienced stress. The most recent one would be the past semester when I first started university. I felt completely overwhelmed as everything was new to me. I had lectures, group assignments, and individual assignments all piling up and everything felt so foreign. During the assignment submission and exam period, I barely had time to rest, and I started getting headaches and couldn’t sleep well. Back then, I saw my stress as a sign of weakness and that I wasn’t doing well enough. I honestly thought it meant I just wasn’t suitable for university.
After learning about stress in the NCO112 course, I realized that I was using avoidant coping strategies. I was putting things off, kept my worries to myself, and imagined the worst. The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping helped me understand now why I felt so helpless. I kept thinking the challenges were too big and that I do not have the capacity to handle them, what the model calls a negative secondary appraisal.
Watching Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk changed the way I look at stress. She said that things like a racing heart or anxiety before a big task don’t mean we’re failing, they mean we care. I remember the night before my Statistical Analytics exam, I couldn’t sleep and my heart was pounding. Looking at it now, if I convinced myself that it was my body trying to help me get ready and told myself that this means I’m prepared and I care, it may have helped me calm down and complete my exam with confidence. That time, even after the exam I was still feeling the stress and anxiety. I talked to my girlfriend about how I was feeling, and her support made a big difference. She reminded me that I didn’t have to deal with stress all on my own.
Now, I would try to doing things differently by breaking big tasks into smaller steps, planning ahead, and reaching out when I needed help. Like now when I am doing this assignment, I feel more in control, and I got into this deep focus where time just flew by. That’s something we learned about in class, a flow state, where you’re so focused and engaged that you lose track of everything else. It showed me that stress, when handled well, can actually help us perform better.
Now, I see that resilience doesn’t mean having no stress it means knowing how to work with it. This course and the TED Talk taught me that I don’t need to fight stress or fear it. I just need to understand it, change how I respond, and build support systems around me. In my road ahead, I would definitely still get stressed, but I would try not to see it as a weakness but as a part of life, one I can manage and even use to grow.
