The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)
(a)Lucy Hone conducts this TED talk in Christchurch, and she covers the major reasons for overcoming tough situations and trauma through the value of resilience.
She begins her talk by asking the audience if they have ever faced some form of misfortune or unfortunate event. Most audience members stand up; Lucy highlights a strong and valid point: adversity does not discriminate. She explains that you must confront some tough times if you are alive. Lucy Hone studied resilience research ten years ago at the University of Pennsylvania. She enrolled in this course when the university accepted a contract to train 1.1 million American soldiers to be mentally fit, just as they are physically fit. After completing her studies in America, she returned to Christchurch to continue her doctoral research. It was at that time that the Christchurch earthquakes struck. She had to pause her research to engage in community aid work. Just when she thought it was her moment to apply her valuable research, she faced the ultimate test of time. She lost her daughter in a tragic car crash. She became a victim of her line of work. She had to confront societal pressures as those around her negatively affected her situation. At that moment, Lucy needed to find light at the end of the tunnel. She took proactive steps to understand her grief and dared to conduct a self-experiment based on the research she had undertaken. Research has shown that parental bereavement is one of the most difficult losses to endure. Despite this, Lucy emerged from that adversity five years later. Drawing from her real-life experience, she advocates that anyone can rise from grief through the proven techniques and strategies she has utilized. She employed three methods to navigate some of her darkest days.
Firstly, Lucy states that resilient people accept that adverse events are bound to occur and are a part of our life journey. Understanding this concept helps individuals avoid feeling discriminated against during tough times. Secondly, resilient individuals are thoughtful and wise in directing their attention. They focus wisely on changing things while accepting those they cannot. Lastly, self-regulation through asking questions that help put the positive in perspective, for example, “What am I doing, helping or harming myself?”—is beneficial. She practiced “benefit-finding,” as it is called in psychology. To conclude, Lucy’s takeaway message is that living and grieving coexist. It is not a trait but rather a set of behaviours. Altering our mindset towards adversity is crucial for our mental and physical reactions to pain and suffering; we can change how we perceive these situations.

(b)(b) The TED talk covers specific resilience areas that were taught to us during our first seminar. Let me discuss the shared values and ideas presented in Dr. Lucy's TED talk, which align with the course content. Dr. Lucy explained how resilient people employ three strategies to cope with trauma. Before that, she mentioned that adversity does not discriminate. This aligns with our course content, emphasizing that resilience is a positive adaptation during adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). In Dr. Lucy’s coping mechanisms, she also addresses concepts like those discussed in the course. In her talk, she mentions “benefit-finding” and changing how we think in response to adversity. These ideas resonate with our course content, which explores the metatheory of resilience and resiliency (Richardson, 2002). In this theory, we examine the disruption of homeostasis leading to the most desired outcome of resilient integration. To elaborate further, one way to build resilience is to identify the positives in adverse situations. This is what Dr. Lucy meant by “benefit-finding.” 

Self-efficacy is another concept that Dr Lucy shared that aligns with what we learned. She smartly phrases, “What am I doing? Is it helping or harming me? "This question invites reflection on how motivation and behaviour influence one’s ability to succeed in specific situations. It also provides a sense of agency.
Through my research, I found similar notions shared by other resilience researchers who believe in the value of resilience and its impact on individuals facing severe adversity, as Dr. Lucy teaches us.

The theory of resilience (APA PsycNet, n.d.-b) synthesizes four resilience patterns from the individual resilience literature: dispositional, relational, situational, and philosophical. In this context, Dr. Lucy’s discourse explores the philosophical pattern of resilience, which examines the individual's worldview and life paradigm. It revolves around beliefs such as optimism, self-awareness, and purposefulness.

However, I have a drawback to this oral discourse. Through my personal story of overcoming trauma, I feel that resilience encompasses more than just a positive mindset shift and redirecting attention to relevant aspects. The healing process is a delicate phase for anyone, and the types of interactions, conversations, and people we choose to associate with make a significant difference. Apart from emotional regulation and having a growth mindset, turning the tables and fostering meaningful connections with diverse individuals is equally pertinent. External factors also impact how resilient one can be. This was absent in Dr Lucy’s scenario.
Research has backed this perspective of mine. Resilience as successful adaptation relies on effective responses to environmental challenges and ultimate resistance to the deleterious effects of stress. Therefore, a greater understanding of the factors that promote such effects is relevant. (Wu et al., 2013) Other factors that affect resilience, apart from mindset building, that were not discussed in the TED talk, include Genetic factors, which contribute significantly to resilient responses to trauma and stress. A range of human genes and polymorphisms associated with NPY, HPA axis, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, and serotonergic systems, and BDNF have been linked to resilient phenotypes (Feder et al., 2009; Russo et al., 2012). 

Genetic studies on resilience provide new insights into the interaction between genes and the environment (Genes × Environment). The development of mental disorders has long been associated with genetic predisposition combined with an individual’s past and present life experiences and environments. Even more surprising is evidence that social experiences can lead to substantial and enduring changes in gene expression that may affect a person’s later behaviour and be transmitted to the next generation. Herrman et al. (2011)

Hence, in this TED Talk, Dr Lucy talks about the personal and systemic sources of resilience; however, she does not explore the environmental and biological sources. 
 
(c) My personal experience of overcoming severe adversity dates to 2013, during my junior college years, when I was overwhelmed by depression. I struggled to cope with the stresses and demands of the A-level examinations. I only passed my papers and did not clear the first round of the ‘A' Level examinations. Consequently, I had to repeat another year in junior college. Those were some of the darkest days of my life, as I felt extremely daunted. I did not understand why I could not comprehend and retain knowledge like my peers. My depression worsened, and I found myself in tears almost every day in the restroom. I experienced major breakdowns as I wondered why I was not mentally capable like others. Things did not turn out well for me. I graduated without a full certificate, which prevented me from entering any university. I was too young to understand or cope with my emotions at that time. I felt emotionally handicapped, unsure how to rise above the adversities and societal pressures I faced. In 2018, I became schizophrenic. Yes, I became a mentally ill patient. I had to be treated and underwent severe medication to recover. However, as I grew older, my desire to enrol in a university and pursue tertiary education became stronger than ever. My medications and support from my family, especially my mother, who has been my most significant source of strength, allowed me to recover from my mental illness. I returned to school and earned a diploma. I found a decent job and successfully enrolled in a university that suits my learning capabilities. This is the story of my resilience, the positive adaptations, and intrinsic motivation to acquire knowledge, which enabled me to rise from my mental trauma. Today, I am honoured to share my story in a university module that teaches critical life skills, offering me a valuable opportunity to reflect on my lived experiences with resilience.
I resonate with Dr Lucy’s findings, which state that we focus on areas we can change.
During the times I was diagnosed with schizophrenia, I focused on reminding myself that I could return to a state where I could acquire knowledge. I practiced resilience with each doctor’s visit. After taking my medication, I took time to heal and concentrate on learning again. Scientifically, I believe the brain synapses strengthened with every effort, and magically, I recovered and relearned how to learn. In my case, the disruption to my homeostasis resulted in a resilient integration, the ideal outcome. Aside from what was discussed by Dr. Lucy, some major contributing factors are the support systems we need to surround ourselves with. In Dr. Lucy’s case, when she lost her daughter, she did not have a proper support system. This resulted in her struggle to return to normalcy being even more difficult. However, I feel that if she had a proper external source of support, her bounce-back ability would have been faster and stronger.
Dr. Lucy discusses how our mindset and behaviours can influence resilience. I believe that external factors, such as the environment we choose wisely during adversity, can also help to ease the pain and restore faith.

In conclusion, resilience develops due to various factors and strategies. As noted in this video, Dr. Lucy focuses on the emotional and mental strategies that help individuals overcome trauma. However, there are many facets of trauma apart from personal adversity. Different strategies are required depending on the type of adversity one is facing. Hence, while Dr. Lucy’s strategies are useful, they may not be relevant in other situations. External and biological factors also affect resilience building.

Video Reference: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://youtu.be/NWH8N-BvhAw?si=CaNnjoxzwlpKcMe5)

(a) In Hone’s (TEDx Talks, 2019) talk, her main message was that resilience can be built and strengthened through intentional thoughts and actions, even in the face of adversity. Drawing on her experience as a resilience researcher and a grieving mother, Hone shared how she coped with the tragic loss of her daughter. She outlined three key strategies for overcoming hardship. First, acknowledging that suffering is a natural part of life. Second, instead of dwelling on the negative, focus on what we can control and what we are grateful for. Third, asking ourselves whether our actions will help or harm our well-being, so that we can make choices that support healing and self-compassion. While these strategies did not change the reality of her pain, they helped her navigate the process of grieving while continuing to live a meaningful life.

(b) Hone’s three secrets for building resilience are largely relevant and accurate in supporting the development of resilience in individuals. In her first strategy, she emphasised that resilience begins with accepting adversity as an inevitable part of life – something everyone is likely to encounter at some point (TEDx Talks, 2019). This message prompted me to reflect on how we often personalise hardship, viewing it as something we must face alone, rather than recognising it as a shared human experience. This perspective is reinforced by the course, which highlights that even successful individuals experience repeated setbacks throughout their journeys (Ong, 2025). Adopting this realistic and growth-oriented mindset enables individuals to respond more constructively to disruptions in their homeostasis – a concept described in the course as “bouncebackability” (Vella & Pai, 2019). To build this capacity, I believe we must rely on our internal qualities like hardiness and a strong sense of coherence, which form the foundation for resiliency. As outlined in the course, these traits would help us stay mentally prepared for adversity and find meaning during challenging times, thereby strengthening our ability to adapt and recover over time (Ong, 2025; Mc Gee et al., 2018).

Next, Hone’s second strategy of focusing on what we can control and practicing gratitude resonated deeply with me (TEDx Talk, 2019). It reminded me of how easily we can become overwhelmed by negativity during tough times and made me realise that maintaining a hopeful mindset could influence the way we recover from adversity. This strategy is supported by the course, which mentions that attributes like optimism and positive emotions are contributors to “bouncebackability” in adverse circumstances (Ong, 2025). It also aligns with the broaden-and-build theory, which suggests that having a positive outlook enhances our adaptability and aids us in developing coping mechanisms, ultimately strengthening our resilience over time (Fredrickson, 2001). Additionally, according to Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, as introduced in the course, developing such a mindset helps us achieve resilient integration, the highest form of resilience. This is because reframing the situation and finding meaning in a setback, helps develop our cognitive flexibility, allowing us to not only recover, but also grow (Nakhostin-Khayyat et al., 2024). Overall, this strategy shows that resilience is not only about enduring hardship; it is also about how we choose to respond to it.

The final strategy of determining whether our actions are beneficial or harmful to us struck me as one of the most insightful approaches Hone shared (TEDx Talk, 2019). It reminded me of the importance of learning to pick our battles – choosing how to respond in ways that protect our well-being (Li, 2025). As someone who tends to be headstrong in my actions, I realised how easy it is to fall into habits that feel comforting but are actually unhelpful in overcoming the problem, such as holding onto anger or avoiding difficult conversations. By cultivating this strategy and making more intentional choices, it strengthens our capacity for active coping as we directly engage with adversity in a proactive manner, which the course highlights as a key aspect of resilience (Lieber, et al., 2023; Ong, 2025).

However, when viewed through the lens of Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, this final strategy does not fully align with achieving resilient integration, which requires both internal and external resources (Ong, 2025). In contrast, Hone’s strategy relies heavily on individual insight, which may be a challenge for some people. Factors like stress, limited social resources, or a pessimistic mindset can impair decision-making (Southwick & Charney, 2012; Ho et al., 2008). Therefore, while I find this strategy personally helpful in building resilience, I believe it is most effective when supported by structured coping strategies.

(c) I vividly recall a learning experience from the first month of my internship at a preschool centre during my diploma studies. One of my first responsibilities was to plan a lesson for a class of four-year-olds. As an ambitious intern eager to prove myself, I spent days preparing what I believed would be an engaging activity – a music lesson where the children would play with instruments. I had high hopes that the lesson would go smoothly. However, it turned out to be more challenging than I had anticipated. I struggled to manage the children’s behaviour, as many refused to follow my instructions. I became flustered, trying to stay on track with the lesson plan while feeling overwhelmed by the chaos unfolding in front of me.

After that tough teaching experience, I struggled to persevere. I felt demoralised and began to question whether I was cut out to be an educator. Looking back five years later, I now see how this experience connects closely to the course concepts of resilience. During that time, I had developed a pessimistic mindset in which I took the setback personally and blamed myself. As a result, instead of learning and adapting from the incident, I remained stuck in self-doubt. Through this course, I have learned how adopting such thinking can hinder my ability to recover from adversity and impede my progress toward resilient integration, the ideal outcome outlined in Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory. As such, staying optimistic is crucial, as it is associated with “bouncebackability,” which can help me respond more constructively to future challenges and continue growing as an educator (Ong, 2025).

Besides that, Hone’s strategies also helped me make better sense of the experience in hindsight. Her first strategy – accepting setbacks as an inevitable part of life – taught me to view the incident not as a personal failure, but as something many educators face, especially early in their careers (TEDx Talks, 2019). Recognising that challenges are a normal part of the learning process, I have come to see that resilience means viewing setbacks as opportunities for growth rather than signs of inadequacy. Also, Hone’s strategy of selective attention further reinforced the importance of being a reflective practitioner in this field. I now see how developing habits like journaling what went well and what I would do differently the next time, might have helped me cope more effectively. I also recall receiving feedback from my mentor, which gave me clarity in handling similar situations. These reflective practices promote active coping and play a valuable role in my professional growth (Ong, 2025).

All in all, both the course and Hone’s insights have deepened my understanding of resilience, helping me see challenges as opportunities to become a more adaptable and confident educator. As I continue my degree in this field, adopting this mindset encourages me to embrace growth through setbacks and stay committed to improving my practice in pursuit of peak performance.

Selected TED Talk: How to Relieve Stress when You’re Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc 
Part A
In the TED talk, speaker Nina, who is a work stress and burnout prevention consultant, currently studying for a PhD studying work-related stress, shares practical strategies to relieve stress effectively in daily life and work. Nina introduces three keys to stress relief, which are to let tension out, limit information in, and lower the barrier to entry for stress relief. Some examples of letting tension out are exercising and letting emotions out by journaling or talking to a friend. When relieving stress, it is important to limit taking in information as it may be a contributing factor to additional stress. Barriers to entry for stress relief should be reduced such that relieving stress is accessible at any time. Nina also believes that excessive or stressful media would compound stress rather than alleviate it by highlighting neuroscience research that shows proper breaks lead to better brain focus and reduce stress markers. By incorporating manageable and intentional stress relief, energy levels, focus and well-being will be boosted. 
Part B
Nina’s approach to stress relief of letting tension out, limiting information in and lowering the barrier to entry for stress relief are a form of emotion focused – approach coping, based on the two-dimensional coping framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Emotion focused approach coping refers to actively managing and improving one’s emotional reactions to a stressful situation. (Ong, 2025) Nina’s strategies fit the emotion focused – approach coping category as they do not solve the problem itself but instead, actively engages and improves the emotional responses relating to stress by promoting intentional activities such as physical movement, creative expression, reducing stress through limiting information intake, and making stress relief more accessible and easier to integrate into daily life. Nina believes that incorporating these intentional stress relief will increase energy levels, focus and well-being of the individual. This aligns with the course content as research has shown that individuals who employed approach coping strategies instead of avoidance coping strategies experienced better wellbeing, quality of life and lower levels of perceived stress. (Budimir et al., 2021) Nina believes that scrolling social media and consuming the internet will not relief stress and will instead contribute to stress by such content may trigger unhealthy comparisons or activate the fight or flight response which will disrupt proper rest and recovery and does not alleviate stress levels. However, I disagree with Nina as I believe that social media can be used as a coping strategy and consuming certain information can help to relief stress. 
Social media can be used as a coping strategy for both emotion-focused approach and problem-focused approach coping. For emotion-focused approach coping, individuals may watch uplifting videos, or engage in funny or relatable content as a way to relief tension and improve mood. For problem-focused approach coping, social media can be used to seek practical solutions, gather information or even connect with online support groups to help address the root cause of the stressor. (Lara et al., 2022) What should be avoided is emotion and problem focused avoidance coping methods though escaping and distracting from the problem through mindlessly scrolling and doomscrolling through social media and binge-watching videos to escape stress, which has been proven to have lower wellbeing, quality of life and higher levels of perceive stress (Ong, 2025) 
According to the transactional model of stress and coping, when an individual appraisal of potential stressful situation as stressful, a coping strategy will be used, leading to psychological changes within an individual as an outcome of coping with stress. (Ong, 2025) The use of social media does not necessarily contribute to stress when an individual’s primary appraisal does not perceive the content as threatening or relevant. When the individual views the content as entertaining, relaxing or supportive, it would be seen as helping to relieve stress rather than as a stressor. The example given by Nina is that watching content that trigger unhealthy comparisons or activate fight or flight response will not contribute to stress when content perceived is not threatening. 
Overall, I agree with Nina that letting tension out and lowering the barrier to entry for stress relief are great ways to regulate emotional needs from stress. However, certain information intake and the use of social media can also be great emotion focused approach coping methods when used appropriately. 
Part C
As a student, I often get stressed out from assignments and exams, especially towards the end of the semester. During these periods, I face time constraints and need to priories tasks effectively, which require time management. In the past, I often chose to skip track and field sessions to dedicate more time to studying.

column2:
The pervasive experience of stress in human life, theorised as an imbalance between perceived demands and available resources, often elicits negative associations (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). However, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal, in her compelling TED talk 'How to Make Stress Your Friend' (TED, 2013), reconceptualizes this conventional thought. This essay will critique McGonigal's arguments, analyse their alignment and divergence with established psychological theories of stress and coping covered in the course seminar, explore alternative perspectives such as the influence of oxytocin, a neurohormone, and apply these insights to my personal experience of stress management.
Citing Keller et al.’s (2012) longitudinal study, McGonigal highlighted that perceiving stress negatively is far worse than experiencing the actual stress itself (TED, 2013). By reappraising these stressors as energised body signs and to treat their stress response positively (Jamieson et al., 2012), people will become more confident and less anxious, leading to a healthier physical response. According to McGonigal, stress can also make a person feel more sociable, motivating people to seek and strengthen social support. Interestingly, McGonigal points out the influence of oxytocin, a neurohormone that is released when a person feels stressed, highlighting its roles in encouraging prosocial behaviours and fostering social connection. Furthermore, caring for others can help an individual build resilience against stress. In conclusion, embracing stress positively and using it to build courage and connection is the success road to a meaningful life.
The information shared on the TED talk aligns mostly with the lecture contents on stress. McGonigal asserted that if reappraised stressors can be seen as energised body signs, people will become less anxious. This directly echoes the core principle of Lazarus & Folkman’s (1984) transactional model of stress and coping. Lazarus & Folkman (1984) asserted that if the stressor is not perceived as a threat, then there will be no stress. Thus, McGonigal's strategy of cognitive reappraisal aligns with the fundamental idea that by altering one's perception (reappraising a threat as a challenge), the stress response can be fundamentally altered.
McGonigal also spoke about the importance of social support to help combat stress. This corresponds to Lazarus & Folkman’s (1984) model of whether they are perceived resources to cope with the stress, which is more clearly defined in McGonigal’s talk. This highlights a key alignment between McGonigal's perspectives and Lazarus & Folkman's theory: the critical role of appraisal and available resources in shaping the stress response (McGonigal, 2015; Niedenthal & Ric, 2017).
The other part is with regards to coping strategies. McGonigal asserts that if individuals can rise to life challenges and trust themselves to handle them, then their stress response will be healthier. In the seminar, the framework by Nes & Segerstrom (2006) was discussed. They provided a two-dimensional coping framework: problem and emotion focused coping and avoidant focused coping and approach focused coping, which is similar to McGonigal’s “fight” coping strategy (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). McGonigal also emphasised positive social support as a form of coping, which was not covered in Nes & Segerstrom (2006)’s framework. Given that Nes & Segerstrom’s framework was developed approximately two decades ago, it is plausible that the growing recognition and empirical validation of social support has been established as a crucial coping strategy in more recent research (Labrague, 2021; Li et al., 2021)
Other factors that may influence coping include personality and individual differences, government and social policies, chronosystem (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Chen et al., 2022; Childs et al., 2014). To cite an example, a hikikomori (an individual who is isolated at home for a prolonged period and refuses to step out of their house) may be stressed because he does not have money to buy food and his parents have passed away. While McGonigal offers strategies to empower people to take on the challenge, it is crucial to acknowledge situations where reappraisal alone cannot help to resolve the situation. As illustrated by the above case of a hikikomori, broader societal and governmental policies can create inescapable stressors, like lack of social support funds that transcend individual cognitive control (RocketNews24, 2014; Saito, 2019).
Another example where McGonigal’s framework may not be applicable is for individuals experiencing warfare, such as in Ukraine. For those whose houses have been destroyed by the bombs, experiencing war trauma and financial challenges daily, befriending stress on an individual basis may not be appropriate or sufficient given their profound trauma, instability and inescapable physiological burden (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Długosz, 2023; McEwen & Gianaros, 2011; Seleznova et al., 2023). Such severe circumstances often necessitate deeper psychological interventions and systemic support. 
As a personal reflection, a recent incident was that the Japanese language school that I manage had problems finding more students. I was very distressed with concerns about what is going to happen to the school and the students. While we have a comfortable pool of 70 students across two full-time teachers and one part-time teacher, we have a meticulous process of selecting students, making it even more difficult to recruit students easily.
After watching the video and attending the seminar, I realised that perhaps it is futile being distressed. If I had adopted McGonigal's perspective, I realise I can reframe my anxiety not as a debilitating emotion, but as my body's positive response, preparing me to proactively address the challenges of student recruitment. By reappraising the situation and adopting both problem-focused and approach-focused coping strategies (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006), I can redirect my attention towards the marketing process of attracting more students. Furthermore, re-evaluating our student selection and course marketing methods can help me navigate through this stressful period (Niedenthal & Ric, 2017; Troy et al., 2018). Reflecting on McGonigal's point about the social aspect of stress, I realise I can benefit more by seeking more support from my colleagues, leveraging the oxytocin response to strengthen our collective problem-solving. 
This essay has given me a chance to relook at stress from a different perspective. Although being a feeling-oriented person may make me more susceptible to stress and perceiving it negatively (Benham, 2006; Joo et al., 2012), I am confident that with better understanding and improved applications of these strategies, I can navigate stress positively throughout my life. This navigation, however, may be an ongoing process that requires continuous and conscientious effort, especially when confronted with external uncontrollable stressors such as financial challenges.

Psychologist Kelly McGonigal challenges the belief that stress is bad and inherently harmful. She shows research that stress is detrimental to our health only if we believe it is indeed harmful. In a broad-based study about stress, those who experienced high stress levels but did not perceive it as harmful had far lower mortality rates than even others with low stress. McGonigal posits that altering our mindset and perception of stress can make our physiological response better and healthier, transforming stress into something that energises and prepares us for challenges, rather than something debilitating. 
She mentions the hormone oxytocin, commonly known as the love hormone. However, it is instead a hormone released during stress, encouraging us to seek social support, strengthening our heart emotionally and physically. Reaching out while under stress or helping others improves resilience and wellbeing. Embracing stress and connecting with others transforms its potentially negative impacts into positive ones, making us stronger and more compassionate. The overarching message is that our perception, thoughts and response to stress is more important than stress itself, and cognitive reframing to view stress as helpful will lead to better health and a more meaningful life. 
McGonigal states that our perception and response to stress alters its impact on our health and wellbeing. This aligns with the course content, especially the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework (Nes and Segerstrom, 2006). The model shows our cognitive appraisal and coping strategies affect stress levels as well and is not solely due to external factors. McGonigal highlights the importance of mindset, where perceiving stress as a challenge rather than a challenge leads to healthier psychological outcomes. 
This aligns with the Transactional Model which posits that stress is a dynamic interaction between an individual and their environment, and not solely a direct response to an event. The model includes cognitive appraisal to evaluate how a situation affects one’s wellbeing, and if a situation is deemed stressful, a secondary appraisal is done to assess what can be done. If there are sufficient perceived resources to deal with stress, this results in eustress. If not, it causes distress. This matches McGonigal’s argument that stress is a subjective experience, shaped by how people interpret situations and their perceived ability to navigate them. Additionally, positive stress beliefs and a resilient mindset correlate with adaptive coping and lower distress (Chen et al., 2022). Cognitive reframing is to be aware of how we think, then to intentionally and actively alter how we interpret stressors. This relates to the goal setting theory, which proposes that specific and challenging goals with appropriate feedback leads to higher task performance and motivation. Through perceiving stress as a method to achieve our goals, this allows a flow state, performing optimally under eustress to bring positive outcomes, fostering a sense of control and resilience. 
However, McGonigal’s argument does not account for all individuals, especially those under chronic or overwhelming stress. Prolonged stress exposure can cause neurotoxic effects like impaired memory, increased risk of depression and physical illnesses such as cardiovascular disease (Lupien et al., 2018). This highlights that while mindset is indeed powerful and transformative, it cannot circumvent the physiological consequences of chronic, prolonged stress, especially for those with weak social support. Furthermore, a shift in mindset is only effective for those who have strong self-belief. It is difficult to change those who are chronically pessimistic, as they cling to the familiarity of their thinking and lifestyle. 
Ultimately, McGonigal’s message is important. Reframing stress as a resource to create eustress empowers individuals and increases resilience. This closely ties to the Two-Dimensional Framework of the Problem-focused and Emotion-focused approach coping. She suggests seeking support, positively reinterpreting stressors, and developing a plan to counteract and resolve stress, achieving peak performance in the process and to create a positive feedback loop for a more successful future. However, mindset shifts do have limits. For those facing chronic adversity, a perception shift is insufficient as it could be a genuine health risk. Though, effective coping, social support and interventions are essential. Hence, mindset shifts should complement efforts to reduce stressors for a more effective outcome. 
In my own life, stress has been a constant and it has greatly affected my life. As a deeply introspective and reflective person, my insight has led me to realise many things about myself. I often am hesitant to start on projects or work which I feel unconfident in, which is ironically due to my perfectionism. If I perceive the product to be insufficient given my perceived current ability, I tend to lean toward avoidance and leave the work to be done only when the stress of the deadline is greater than the stress of perfectionism. Over time, strides have been made, but this is a continual journey of improvement, aided by this course.
One notable event was my procrastination on one of my group projects. It was difficult as it required high technical knowledge and understanding of the topic. At the time, I had perceived this stressor as a threat while perceiving that I lacked the resources for coping, resulting in distress and emotion-focused avoidance, as I would procrastinate or distract myself to reduce the negative feelings. However, this left me constantly dissatisfied and there was a constant nagging feeling within me.
The deadline neared, and my groupmates were starting to get anxious as well, which caused additional stress. Some began to chase me to complete my share of the work. I was aware that I did not want to live my life this way, and that I needed to take a first step toward change, however uncomfortable. After reflecting, I understood the mechanisms of my thinking and actions. There was a fear of failure, and a fear of falling below expectations of both myself and others. After overcoming various mental hurdles, I accepted that to succeed, it would first require failure and various setbacks. There was a clear perception shift due to a new goal of wanting to do better (aligning with Goal Setting theory), where I internalized that failures were not indicative of negativity about my identity, but rather was a step forward and a sign of courage that I was willing to put in effort to improve. This aligns with the mindset shift mentioned by McGonigal, where the cognitive reframing allowed me to view my stressors as motivators instead, putting me on an upward trajectory with each challenge overcome. 
I used failure as fuel, devising a plan for myself to remain productive to achieve better performance in my work. I intentionally schedule “focus time” into my day to actively engage in flow state. I break down tasks into manageable components of sufficient difficulty to challenge me at my current skill level, and accomplishing the tasks gives me a great sense of control and satisfaction. Doing this allowed me to keep up to date on tasks, and to fulfil my responsibility in the project, achieving a desirable result. I am also very fortunate to have a strong support network, where I can discuss my views, talk about my stresses and receive advice accordingly. I also actively give back and support peers as I feel it is only right and courteous to do so. Through the TED talk, I have come to realise that part of the reason that support systems work so well is due to the release of oxytocin and its physiological benefits where it buffers against stress (Takayanagi & Onaka, 2021). This has yet again increased awareness of how my environment affects me and can direct me to improve as a person. 
A key takeaway from my experiences, learning and reflection is that our mechanisms largely decide our outcomes. The way we perceive and deal with problems is vital to whether we perform well or not. Though there are many factors involved, I believe that if one has strong enough self-belief while acting in alignment with their goals, if they are intentional in their actions and willing to sacrifice for a better result, they will be able to overcome any self-induced stress. However, we must be cognisant that stress may indeed be overwhelming, limiting one’s ability to cope adequately.

Reflection Essay on "What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience" by Charles Hunt
The talk that Charles Hunt shares is about his own personal life story and how he explores how personal adversity and trauma help him in shaping Resilience, which includes the loss of his father and being homeless. He shares that we can grow stronger through a tough experience in life. By learning how to be resilient and how to be able to pick ourselves up from the challenges is not something thing that we know when we come into this world but along the way growing up.  Hunt also shared that instead of looking at the challenges or problems we face as a stumbling block why not see it as an opportunity to grow? He believes that a person’s mindset, determination and self- reflection are important as they help in overcoming difficulties. Listening to his talk, it inspires me as an individual to acknowledge my ability to reshape my own life and tell myself that my response to the challenges is important and will define me. The talk clearly shown that Resilience is not given but slowly accumulates along the way and we have the power to turn whatever pain into progress.
In the NCO 112 module, there were some concepts which were aligned with Hunt’s sharing, especially on the metatheory of Resilience, and transaction model of stress and coping. In the metatheory by Richardson, he stated that people who overcome hardship and reintegrate will become resilient. In the talk where Hunt shares, he faced being homeless, abandonment and the loss of his family member, yet he has chosen to face and pick himself up from this setback. This allows him to use this as a foundation for his own career and personal development which aligns with the belief that adversity can help in elevating a person’s limit of functioning when it is handled well. Hunt’s Story has also illustrated the Transaction Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus & Folkman, 1984 has shown insight into Hunt’s first assessment, identifying life challenges as a life obstacle and then slowly evolving into a second assessment which allows him to adapt the coping method and to improved personal capabilities.
Hunt at first was lacking the coping methods, but with his continuous effort and trying to better manage his stress, he comes up forming a supportive community, where he found his purpose in helping others and engaged with problem solving instead of avoiding it. This changes in the mindset moves toward a eustress, where the stress part is a motivation to become positive.
Hunt’s sharing also shown the different important traits that the course is aligned with as essential for Resilience. Traits such as cognitive flexibility, optimism, self-efficacy, and learning from experience. He was able to find strength through his vulnerability shown in the concept of growth mindset by Dweck,2006, where the failure are views as point of stepping stone to get better.
Although Hunt’s story is inspiring, but it can be potentially a risk of overlooking some other social factors that cause Resilience to weaken.  In Sameroff and Rosenblum, 2006 it shared that factors such as knowledge, environment surrounding and poverty can hinder a person’s capacity to recover. Hunt was able to access to guidance and education which many others who went through the same challenges may not have. It is important that we look beyond the social context, even that Hunt’s message supports psychological theories that were covered in the module.
Hunt’s TED talk presented a powerful illustration of the theories and ideas of resilience and peak performance, which are cover in the NCO112 module. It strongly argued that how adversity can help in person’s development with the right mindset and support.
I met with an accident in June 2023 while playing go-kart in Malaysia. It became a life changing experience for me when the vehicle overturned and landed on my upper left arms, this impact has resulted me with my left arm bone being broken into two pieces. At the moment, fear surrounded me as the injury was quite bad and beyond the physical pain, I was struggling with the emotion toll of the feeling of being a handicapped. This deeply affected my confidence and mental wellbeing, as I needed to wrestle with depression and doubt the ability to recover fully or worse lose one side of my mobility.
This added to the challenges when I was about to transit to my part time studies in SUSS for my degree course in July 2023 while I am continued to work full-time. Managing recovery, getting into academic demands and taking up new work responsibilities at that time has increased my stress. The Transaction Model of stress and coping arises when the expectation outweighs the coping methods, which happened to me. I initially thought I could manage my recovery while studying and working at the same time. It was far beyond what I could imagine as I felt pressure from the academic demand, pains and work obligation as I relied on emotion focused method. As time went by, I started to look for other alternatives to the problem focus method and kept looking out for way to resolve rather than to let the stress overwhelm me.
Hunt’s sharing has hit a deep connection with my experiences where he talks about reframing my adversity, this come to my realisation that I can use the accidents to strengthen my resilience in different areas of my life such as my studies, emotional mental stability and recovery from my injury instead of seeing it as a permanent loss. In Csikszentmihalyi’s concept it becomes relevant to me. By maintaining my focus and keep my distress from turning to hopelessness, I set myself to focus on the recovery processes by engaging with physiotherapy and concentrating on getting my degree in SUSS.
In this module, it helps me to understand resilience about adjusting, growing and learning from past adversity and not just about enduring. Hunt’s stress on personal perseverance, in my own experiences, has made me understand the importance of friends, families and school resources are important to help me stay rooted. I will aim to embrace coping methods, managing self-reliance and the understanding that resilience is developed when it is supported with personal effort and the support from others.

a)The TED talk was trying to provide listeners with different perspectives to handle setbacks, and with the 3 strategies she introduced to handle those setbacks, it brings out the resilience in people. The strategies highlighted are acceptance of the suffering faced, attention management by focusing on the positive aspects of the issue on hand, and self-assessment to assess the quality of actions taken during that circumstance. These strategies were researched and identified by Lucy herself through her personal first-hand experience with a resilience episode of losing her own daughter after deciding to turn her back on typical advice given to her as a victim of that situation. In the talk, she also encouraged people to be an active participant on their grieving process. 


b)Both the TED talk and the course aimed to provide techniques and strategies to achieve what the Study Guide called “resilient integration” (Ong, 2025), which takes into account the experiences felt due to the adversity faced, and learning from such experiences to develop better resilience. The basis of the content demonstrated both clearly articulating the possibility to develop resilience through setbacks, using positive outlooks to the situations experienced.

In fact, the three strategies documented in the TED talk were of similar essence compared to the areas highlighted by Kunzler et al. (2020) in the Study Guide that are associated with resilience, which included optimism, active coping, positive emotions and self-efficacy. (Ong, 2025) These areas, combined with the strategies elaborated in the TED talk, allows for readers and listeners to make use of them to recover after facing a setback. 

Resilience can be cultivated by the 7 “Cs”, which includes Competence, Confidence, Connection, Character, Contribution, Coping and Control. (Duszynski-Goodman, 2023) It involves the ability to believe in one’s ability to know that they are capable of handling adversity and staying true to their beliefs and act on their beliefs through mindfulness. (Duszynski-Goodman, 2023) This also backs the TED talk and course content in the key competencies one should have or strive to achieve to have resilience. 

However, we can see that though the TED talk and the course content are largely similar, we can still see some pointers that are not being highlighted in the talk. One of which is the point of Religiosity as mentioned in Ong, 2025. This point highlighted the use of religion in the form of participating in religious activities and practices (Ong, 2025) to foster resilience. Religious coping was reported as one of the most common forms of coping in times of crisis. (Dolcos et al., 2021) This would mean that Religiosity would have been highly regarded in terms of the methods of cultivating resilience, which was not highlighted in the TED talk. 



c)One episode that I experienced regarding resilience would be a time where I experienced a period of setbacks due to a mistake I made during a precision drill performance competition in Secondary School. While the result was a good one, having created an unclean performance and being at the centre of discussions regarding the worthiness of our results sent me down the spiral. For context, the previous competition winners would usually have the cleanest performance with negligible mistakes seen, but my mistake in the actual display failed to maintain that “high-class” performance status expected from the winner of the competition. Especially when the performance was a team effort, I felt that I eventually let the team down following our months of hard work. Given the nature of the competition and the attitude of the seniors that put in as much effort as we did, one of them did subtly blame me for the teams’ “failure” before the announcement of the results, which significantly affected me.

While I cannot say I am no longer affected by it, I believe I made a fair share of personal adjustments to my mindset to help me overcome such issues in the future, first of which is like what was mentioned in the TED talk, which is to accept that I was hurt by the incident. Being able to recognise that the hurt was the cause of the emotions was very important as I would now be able to try and compartmentalise my thoughts and have an avenue to pin-point the cause of the emotion, and re-engineer my thoughts and emotions again when I am outside the situation. I realised that the thoughts I had were a buildup of expectations and the authoritative nature of the CCA I was in. 

Having this thought, I was more able to critically manage and reflect on the situation, where I found out that though it was a period where I had extreme negative thoughts and perceptions of myself, I also managed to get over it by looking at the positive side of the situation. I managed to perform under pressure and not let my mistake deter me from continuing the rest of the choreography and exhibited a smooth and confident display of precision till the end of the display. This was something I thought I would never be able to do. I thought I would just let loose and complete the rest of the choreography half-heartedly given that damage has already been done. These feelings and perceptions would eventually help me in difficult situations that I have faced in the future, such as making critical decisions during NS and manoeuvring different peer characters during group projects in SUSS.

Selected TED talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)

Q1a. Summary
In her TED Talk, Lucy Hone presents three key resilience strategies from research and personal experience and demonstrates how these strategies enabled her to cope with the sudden death of her 12-year-old daughter. The first strategy involves acknowledging that hardships can happen as part of life. The second strategy pertains to the deflection of focus on what is controllable and what remains positive. The third encourages individuals to regularly ask themselves if their actions and thoughts are helping or harming them. Hone is eager to emphasise that these strategies entail an active attempt to adopt a mindset that enhances strength and healing, rather than avoidance or denial. Importantly, she reiterated that resilience is less a fixed trait than an intentional practice accessible to anyone who wants to cultivate it.

Q1b. Discussion
Lucy Hone's stance on resilience is in alignment with the core concepts taught in our course, particularly the focus on self-regulation, attitude, and the ability to cope with setbacks. Her belief that resilience involves intentional choices aligns with the growth mindset by Dweck (2006), where success can be developed through effort and adaptability and not fixed abilities. Similarly, her third strategy self-checking, aligns with self-regulation. NCO112 discusses how high achievers continuously examine and update their habits, thoughts, and behaviours to maintain performance under pressure. Hone's guidance is consistent in this sense by encouraging metacognition and personal agency to shift away from helplessness towards action. 

Her second strategy, focusing attention on what is controllable, parallels stress management covered in the course. By consciously redirecting attention to areas of agency, stress can be coped with a problem-oriented or emotions approach (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Her advice embodies cognitive reappraisal, a process of emotional regulation that has been shown to buffer against the effects of stress and trauma (Troy et al., 2018). For instance, instead of thinking “I failed this assignment, so I must be stupid,” a person using cognitive reappraisal might think, “This assignment was tough, but it’s a chance to learn and improve for next time.” This shift in thinking helps reduce feelings of shame or frustration and promotes a more balanced emotional response. It empowers people by reframing adversity to mitigate emotional suffering. It is the intentional, conscious exercise that sets high achievers apart from burnout performers (Heydari & Beigzadeh, 2024). 

However, while empowering, Hone's advice fails to address how structural or environmental variables shape resilience. Ungar (2018) finds that resilience is not merely an intrapersonal quality, as it's shaped by systems like environment, social support, and education. Individuals from underprivileged backgrounds or with systems-related obstacles might not find Hone's answers enough in themselves. Reinforcing this notion, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) suggests that intrapersonal and extrapersonal elements are in dynamic interaction—the full biopsychosocial model—when thinking about peak performance (Ong, 2025). Hence, resilience will need to be theorised contextually, with consideration of how external relationships facilitate adaptive processes. Hone's message may do a disservice to the complexity of resilience across different populations. 
Despite these limitations, her message remains valuable and simplifies key psychological concepts in an accessible way, encouraging people to develop resilience. When integrated with the more nuanced and systemic models presented in our course, her ideas become powerful tools for personal growth. Together, they remind me that resilience is not just a concept to study but a vital skill to practice. 

Q1c. Reflection
One personal experience occurred over my last year of polytechnic, when my mother was diagnosed with stage three cancer and depresssion. I remember worrying and feeling overwhelmed, especially with the long waiting times for her medical reports. At the same time, I was attempting to juggle part-time work, pressure from my final-year project, broken family dynamics and extracurricular commitments. It felt like everything was happening all at once, and I couldn’t afford to stop. Looking back, I now understand that I had no effective coping strategies and would usually self-blame, believing that I wasn't doing my best as a daughter and as a student. My thoughts became increasingly negative and self-critical, and I was constantly exhausted, both emotionally and physically. 

Hone's TED Talk helped me reframe this experience. Her first principle—"Resilient people know that suffering is part of life" was especially validating. My struggles then were something I saw as a deficiency, something that isolated me from others who were coping with it better. The assertion that trouble is a global human experience shifted my mindset. It helped me accept that it was okay to suffer, and that my reaction wasn't a failure on my part but a natural response to a challenging situation. 
The biopsychosocial emphasis of the course on optimal performance also helped me make sense of the entire scope of what I was experiencing. Emotionally, I was so stressed, but I wasn't taking care of my physical and social well-being, either—skipping meals, disrupting sleep cycles, and excluding friends. Those bad habits made things worse. 

Hone’s third principle, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” resonated deeply with me. Had I asked myself that question during that difficult period, I might have been more mindful to how my actions were contributing to my burnout. At that time, I perceived my emotional exhaustion as an indicator of not being resilient enough back then. Now I see that resilience is not necessarily about not being affected by adversity, but about how one recovers, learns, and adapts in relation to it. This has also helped me appreciate the value of emotional regulation strategies, like reframing my thoughts to facilitate healthier reactions to stress rather than dismissing difficult emotions. 

Reflecting on this, one of the most meaningful insights I have gained is that resilience also involves acknowledging pain, allowing space for vulnerability, and intentionally taking steps that support healing and growth. In hindsight, although I lacked the knowledge and coping mechanisms I now possess, I remain proud of how I navigated that difficult period with the emotional endurance and inner strength available to me at the time. As the common saying goes, “There are no regrets in life, just lessons.”

In the TED Talk, The Three Secrets of Resilient People, Lucy Hone shares her deeply personal and tragic story of resilience in the face of a life-altering incident. After losing her 12-year-old daughter in a car accident, Bones found that existing were victimising her, instead of giving her advice on how to control what she could. She turned to her academic background and life experiences instead, and found out that anyone can develop resilience. Three strategies allowed Bones to survive losing her child. These strategies can be applied by simply adapting them to our circumstance. Firstly, instead of asking “Why me?”, Bones accepted that hardship is part of the human experience, making it easier to move forward. Secondly, resilience is about making a conscious choice on focusing on matters you can control. Rather than being swallowed up in grief or anxiety, focusing on the good can help us stay grounded. Thirdly, constantly ask: “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?”. Bones realised this when she kept looking at pictures of her deceased daughter realising it was harmful. This question helped her steer clear of self-destructive behaviour and thought spirals.
During this course, we spoke about going through adversity and coming out stronger as part of resilience, despite the pain. There is usually a sense of growth or continuation, like the story does not end despite adversity. Bones’ story perfectly exemplifies this, as she did not drown in grief, instead actively living and growing despite it.Bones also mentioned the positive effects of resilience, like her strategies helping her cope in her darkest hours. This aligns with class material on resilience protecting people in high-stress environments. While not mentioned in the TED Talk, resilience also improves quality of life, work happiness, and job performance, and Bones’ strategies can help achieve these goals. Bones specifically mentioned the importance of stepping out of your comfort zone. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency states that resilience is only built when you are pushed into unfamiliar and difficult territory (Richardson, Glenn, 2002). Bones’ story was one of extreme hardship, and her decision to confront it head-on helped her achieve resilient integration, which we discussed in class. Bones found tools, which gave her meaning, and a reason to continue growing. 
In class, we discussed personal qualities associated with resilience. Bones used optimism to intentionally focus on the good. Cognitive flexibility was utilized when she willingly adjusted her self-destructive thoughts and actions. Bones used self-efficacy when she believed she could shape her responses. She used an active coping style, rather than sitting in her grief and letting it consume her.  Despite Bones’ success story, her tragedy is one-dimensional and not applicable to everyone due to the variations in support systems, mental tools, and ability to reflect and contemplate. George Bonanno, a resilience researcher, points out that everyone reacts to trauma and hardship differently, and there is no one fixed path to resilience (Bonanno, 2021). While some may be able to use internal strategies, others require professional help, medication, or strong support systems to avoid spiraling. 
Southwick and Charney also point out how science plays a part in resilience. Biology, social networks, and community resources significantly impact how resilient we are, which was not covered by Bones. This neglects the population who face systematic issues like poverty, chronic illness, or discrimination that deter them from seeking help (Southwick, Charney, 2012). Despite this, Bones provides resilience strategies that a majority can utilize, and effectively expresses the effort needed for her to overcome tragedy, removing the mysteriousness of resilience.
While nothing compared to Bones’ story, I had my own experience with stress and failure that could have been approached differently had I known about this TED Talk. During year two in SUSS, I failed a core marketing module. While it was a difficult module, I had not expected to fail, since I had never failed anything academically before and it affected me alot. I would avoid my friends from that module, ignore homework and emails, and did not tell my parents, instead paying the reattempt fee myself, as I felt like I had let myself, and people who believed in me, down. 
After listening to class material and Bone’s talk, I realise I was engaging in self-destructive behaviours and thoughts, not helping myself get out of the loop. Bones’ strategies would have been invaluable to me at that time, allowing me to see and do things differently. I would have known to remind myself that setbacks are natural, and not the end. I would not have associated failing academically with my own self-worth, instead rationalizing it as a slip up. I could have focused on the good, like friends, family, and other classes, and that I still could retake the module. Active coping, a lesson from class, would have helped me too. I could have consulted the lecturer or studied with friends, showing self-efficacy. 
This reflection helped me realise resilience does not only apply to massive and life-altering tragedies, but also to everyday challenges. Small incidents build up over time, and with the right mindset and strategies, we avoid drowning under the pressure. By using Bones’ three strategies of accepting the situation, focusing on the good, and taking proactive steps to move forward, alongside class material of understanding the characteristics of resilience and how to apply them, I am now more prepared to face life’s challenges in healthier ways. 
In conclusion, Bones’ TED Talk reveals that resilience is not a special trait unattainable by the everyday person. We all struggle from adversity, and thus build resilience when we face them. However, to avoid unhealthy coping mechanisms, we must stick to tried and tested strategies. There is no easy way out, and effective strategies require self-awareness, effort, and choice. While Bones’ is not marketing a universal solution, her strategies are a good foundation to start on, and more importantly, they shine hope on others’ seemingly impossible situations. If she could overcome such a tragedy using her own willpower, then so can I, by altering her tools to suit my specific situation. Reflecting on my hardships, I realise that resilience is not about bouncing back from a setback, but also surging forward, using the hardship as a stepping stone to better ourselves in the future.

Title: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
Speaker of the TED Talk: Nina Nesdoly
YouTube link: (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)
(a) Short summary of TED Talk
Nina Nesdoly shares in her TED talk three ways a person could do to help them reduce stress when they are feeling overwhelmed. First, stress could be reduced by letting tension out. For instance, communicating with a close friend or having a physical workout could help to lower tension and reduce stress. Second, stress could be reduced by restricting the flow of information in. For example, taking a break away from information that causes stress such as the news could help to lower stress and improve productivity. Third, stress could be reduced by decreasing one’s barrier to entry. To specify, the activity which helps one to reduce stress does not have to be complicated. It can be as simple as journaling in point forms. The point is to take the first step in reducing stress in ways which one finds comfortable because it would help in bringing about increased energy for one to survive through their workday with higher concentration (Nesdoly, 2023). 

(b)
The TED talk content by Nina Nesdoly aligns with the course content on stress. In this case, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) states that stress could emerge in a person when there is an imbalance in the resources which the person has to endure with the demands. When a person is feeling overwhelmed as mentioned in the TED talk, it would suggest that the person could have undergone a primary appraisal and assessed their circumstances as threatening to them. This could result in the person to undergo in a secondary appraisal whereby the person could feel that they do not have enough resources to handle the situation. As a result, this could lead to a person feeling distress which is considered as negative result of stress. Besides, the three ways which Nina Nesdoly presents to the audience in the TED talk are coping measures to help a person achieve Eustress. To demonstrate, the TED talk suggests problem focused-approach coping strategy as suggested by Nes and Segerstrom (2006) such as engaging in a physical workout. This helps the person to cope with the stress as the stress is released through exercise. Furthermore, emotion focused-approach coping strategy such as communicating with a close friend provides emotional support to the person which helps in coping with stress (Ong, 2025).

Similarly, research has shown that nursing students have a higher tendency to adopt problem focused-approach coping strategy to handle stress. An overall improvement in well-being, learning and work performance has been reported as the advantages of utilising problem focused-approach coping strategy. In addition, the approach deals with the root cause of the problem that results in stress. In this case, the search for meaning when one is dealing with difficult circumstances and coming up with the use of different plans to tackle issues. Hence, problem focused-approach coping strategy would be regarded as the most effective method in coping with stress. However, emotion focused coping strategy handles with the feelings of the person that is associated with stress which does not deal with the root cause of the stress. For instance, nursing students were reported to have greater stress when they regularly used emotion focused coping strategy to cope with their stress. Some of the behaviours which the students had took on are watching movies, TV or sleeping to distract themselves. Furthermore, studies have also pointed that emotion focused coping strategy could result in damage to one’s health. Therefore, it could be regarded as the approach that is the least effective in coping with stress (Labrague et al., 2016). Additionally, another research considered active coping strategy to be more effective in tackling stress in contrast with avoidant coping. To illustrate, reframing negative thoughts into positive thoughts in a stressful event and making plans on how to deal with the stress are considered active coping strategies. On the other hand, avoidant coping is less effective as it causes a person to have behavioural disengagement, denial and venting (Al-Dubai et al., 2011). Thus, this suggests that it would be prudent to adopt emotion focused-approach coping as it could provide emotional support for the person from their social support system to help them in generating more positive emotions in dealing with stressors. Moreover, it would be more beneficial to avoid resorting to emotion focused-avoidance coping as attempting to create distraction through harmful behaviours such as excessive drinking would only help to cope with the problem in the short-term (Ong, 2025).

(c)
I recalled that during the period in year 2 semester 1, I felt extremely stressed out particularly when I had to prepare for my closed book exams. I have always felt that my weakness is in memorising. I struggled with trying to memorise the load of content taught for the exams and broke down several days before the exams. I remembered that before the exams, I had been working very hard to complete deadlines that come one after another and did not give myself a proper break. I also stopped engaging in my hobby which brought me joy such as gaming with friends, spending time with family and friends and exercising as I felt that there was simply not enough time. Applying the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984), I felt stressed because there was imbalance between the demands and resource which I had to cope. In my primary appraisal, I was worried that I would fail my exams because I could not memorise enough content and viewed it as threatening to me. In my secondary appraisal, I felt that I did not have sufficient resources to cope with the preparation of the exams and experienced distress. I had also adopted emotion focused-avoidance coping through social withdrawal. For example, I stopped spending time with my family and friends and gaming with my friends when I felt overwhelmed. As a result, this has caused me to distance myself away from my social support network and feel more stressed (Ong, 2025).

I could learn from my experience by adopting problem focused-approach coping such as having a better study plan to deal with exams in the future. Instead of cramming information in a week before the exam, I could periodically review and memorise content in the weeks leading up to the exam which could help me to retain information better. Furthermore, I could ensure that I allocate more time for studying exams such as blocking out additional days and aiming to complete my ECAs and assignments earlier. Besides, I could practise active coping by journalling down my thoughts when I feel stressed into my diary which could help me to comprehend the situation better. What’s more, I could also adopt emotion focused-approach coping by confiding with my close friends about my stressful situation. My close friends could help provide me with emotional support by encouraging me or being a listening ear. In addition, I could practise positive reinterpretation by reframing my negative thoughts into positive thoughts (Ong, 2025). The TED talk has also taught me the importance on reducing stress in a timely manner. In my experience, I had overworked myself as I kept pushing away the need to destress because I felt that I did not have enough time. Consequently, this has caused me to bottle up too much stress and become overwhelmed by it which led me to break down days before my exams. Further, I learned that reducing stress does not have to be complicated, it can be as easy as journaling down my thoughts into my diary whenever I feel stressed. Moreover, it is beneficial to take sufficient breaks as it could help me to reduce my stress and increase my productivity when I come back refreshed from my break. I could also reduce tension by going for a jog in the nature park to lower my stress.

For the purpose of this assignment, the video of choice for discussion is as follows:
Title: The Three Secrets of Resilient People
Speaker: Dr. Lucy Hone
Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw


In the TED talk by Dr. Lucy Hone, an author and a researcher who did resilience research and over the years helped or supported people going through different types of adversity in their lives. Through her professional expertise and personal experience, she shared her thoughts about what it means to be resilient, how to navigate the stages of her grief and how it eventually led her to develop three key resilient strategies.

Dr. Lucy Hone said that “Adversity does not discriminate” and acknowledges that everyone goes through tough times. After losing her daughter suddenly in a car accident, she further explained how she was told that it was expected to take five years of grief, which left her feeling powerless. During that pain and anguish, she wanted to have hope, and this helped her to become actively involved in her own journey to overcome parental loss. 

Through her talk, the main message she was trying to convey to others is that it is possible to rise up from adversity, that there are workable strategies for us to adopt and it is possible to make ourselves think and act in specific ways to help us navigate through our tough times. She also shared three strategies that can be used to build our resilience.

--

In the APA Dictionary of Psychology, resilience is defined as “The process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA,2020). There are two components to resilience – adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013).

In her video, the first strategy that Dr. Hone shared is that resilient people acknowledge that suffering and going through hardships are part of life. The moment this happens, one will experience a shift in mindset, which can help lift any feelings of isolation or victimization, then replaces these with hopes that one can go through tough times and instead of avoiding, they confront these challenging situations. This mindset may not be easy for everyone, but the key is acceptance, which hopefully becomes the catalyst to start making our brains work towards a more problem-solving approach. 

The second strategy was to focus on the things that we can control. It is easy to let things spiral when we are faced with adversity and when we become “frozen” from not knowing what to do or feel next. This feeling that everything is out of control, may eventually lead to an extended period of unhealthy depressive state and this will affect one’s mental, emotional and physical health. Hence, resilient people are good at identifying the good or the positive, in every emotion that surrounds them.

These first two strategies are aligned with the two components of resilience mentioned above and what was shared during the seminar lessons. Acknowledging that adversity and having to face one, is part of living and this is the first step that will help change our mindset. The videos we watched about the athlete and the parachutist showed that they did not give up and left their passion and instead gave themselves time to recuperate and do what is necessary to regain their strength and self-confidence. 

They also demonstrated how important it is to choose to look at the positive side of things instead of burying deeper into negativity. It is easier to be clouded by negative thoughts and wondering why things happen, but it is essential to be able to shift one’s energy to positivity and work towards overcoming obstacles they were facing. Having a choice is a blessing – and one should always aim to exercise our gift of choice and choose to look at the positive or to work on things are within our control.

With the right mindset and the ability to seek the positive, the third strategy that Dr. Hone shared was that resilient people can ask themselves if a thought or an action is harmful or helpful to themselves. This question is self-reflective, and one can assess whether their thoughts and actions contribute positively to their well-being. It is important to feel that we are in control of our lives again by making conscious decisions that have a positive impact on life.

I agree with Dr. Hone that these strategies do not mean that the pain will magically go away but minimally, they provide a structure to how one can start building resilience. Being constantly grateful or practicing gratitude as often as we can, will also help us to see the good in what we do, which we may have missed to see and be thankful for. 

However, I also think that having a strong support system is important and this comes even before one can start to adopt the strategies shared. With reference to the metatheory that we learnt in this module, there are four possible outcomes whenever a disruption occurs. I strongly feel that one of the most critical factors that contributes to which outcome will eventually happen, highly depends on the type of support system we have during the time of adversity. 

--

My parents divorced at one of the most critical points of my life and for a period of time, I blamed them for causing an unfortunate series of events. At the age of 15, I was unable to fathom what was happening and why it was happening. I was supposed to be preparing for a major national exam which will be pivotal in my academic journey and while I was only an occasional-A student, I knew I wanted to study hard so that I could be accepted in the school of my choice. Instead, I was faced with huge uncertainties, feelings of anger and resentment while at the same time, being forced to “grow up” as I also had a younger sibling to care for. Looking at my sibling, during those times, was what helped me focus more energy on the positive side of things instead of just being in the state of self-pity. While gratitude was the third strategy shared by Dr. Hone, I realised now that it was my first strategy during that time. I wrote down all the things that I was still grateful for despite all that happened, and I listed all the things that I could do as a 15-year-old and let the things I am unable to control to the adults. 

Things never turned out the way I planned it to be when I wrote in my book of dreams, but it made me a more resilient person who can bounce back up each time I fall.
